m: to become less intense, severe, or widespread; to lessen
x: We waited in the café until the rain abated enough for us to walk home.
Her anxiety about the presentation abated once the first few slides went smoothly.
The professor paused the lecture until the noise from the construction site had abated.
Health officials warned that the outbreak showed no sign of abating despite the new restrictions.
In Dhaka, the flooding usually abates only after the heaviest weeks of the monsoon have passed.
tc: Forecasters expected the storm to ______ overnight, but instead it grew stronger as it approached the coast.
'But instead it grew stronger' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean weaken or lessen.
se: The protesters agreed to go home once the tension in the square began to ______.
subside
Both 'abate' and 'subside' mean to become less intense, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: departing from what is normal, usual, or expected
x: The dog's aberrant behavior, refusing food and hiding under the bed, prompted us to call the vet.
Our usually punctual manager's aberrant lateness this week made everyone wonder whether something was wrong at home.
Researchers excluded one aberrant result from the study because it was clearly caused by a faulty sensor.
Scientists are investigating aberrant weather patterns that have brought snow to regions that rarely see frost.
After the argument, his cold and aberrant behavior left his friends confused about what had changed.
tc: Unlike the rest of the data, which followed a predictable pattern, one ______ reading fell far outside the expected range.
'Unlike the rest of the data' and 'far outside the expected range' show the reading departs from the norm.
se: Doctors were alarmed by the patient's ______ heart rhythm, which differed sharply from a healthy pattern.
abnormal
Both 'aberrant' and 'abnormal' describe something that departs from the normal pattern.

m: to deliberately hold back from doing or enjoying something, especially voting or indulging
x: Many families in Bangladesh abstain from food and drink from dawn to sunset during Ramadan.
Three board members abstained when the proposal to cut salaries was put to a vote.
During exam week, she abstains from social media so she can concentrate on her revision.
Several countries abstained from the United Nations resolution rather than openly oppose it.
He decided to abstain from alcohol for a year, hoping it would improve his health and his relationships.
tc: Although he loved sweets, he chose to ______ from dessert for the whole month to keep his promise to his doctor.
'Although he loved sweets' sets up a contrast, so the blank must mean deliberately hold back.
se: Patients are asked to ______ from eating for at least eight hours before the blood test.
refrain
Both 'abstain from' and 'refrain from' mean to deliberately avoid doing something.

m: difficult to understand because it is obscure or highly complex
x: The instructions for assembling the bookshelf were so abstruse that we gave up and watched a video instead.
Our team lead rewrote the abstruse technical report so that clients without an engineering background could follow it.
Even graduate students struggled with the professor's abstruse lectures on quantum field theory.
Critics argue that the new tax law is written in abstruse language that ordinary citizens cannot understand.
She found his love letters oddly abstruse, full of philosophical references she had to look up.
tc: The author's earlier books were ______ and full of jargon, but her latest one is so clear that even beginners enjoy it.
The contrast with 'so clear that even beginners enjoy it' shows the blank means hard to understand.
se: Few readers could follow the philosopher's ______ argument, which relied on concepts that only specialists understand.
recondite
Both 'abstruse' and 'recondite' mean difficult to understand and known only to a few.

m: the ability to make good judgments and quick decisions, especially in business
x: Her business acumen turned a small tea stall near the university into a chain of busy cafés across Dhaka.
The firm promoted him quickly because his financial acumen saved the company millions in his first year.
Doctors need clinical acumen as much as textbook knowledge to diagnose rare diseases correctly.
Voters questioned whether the young candidate had the political acumen to manage a divided parliament.
I've always admired my grandmother's acumen when it comes to judging people's true intentions.
tc: Although he had no formal training in finance, his ______ allowed him to spot profitable investments that experts overlooked.
Spotting investments that experts missed despite no training points to sharp practical judgment.
se: Investors trusted her because of her ______, which had helped her make sound decisions through several market crashes.
shrewdness
Both 'acumen' and 'shrewdness' mean sharp, practical judgment, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to warn or reprimand someone firmly but usually without harshness
x: My mother admonished me for leaving the gas stove on after making tea.
Our manager admonished the team for missing the deadline but praised the quality of the design.
During the exam, a proctor admonished two students for whispering to each other.
Halfway through the trial, the judge admonished both lawyers to stick to the evidence.
She gently admonished her friend for always cancelling plans at the last minute.
tc: Instead of praising the intern for his initiative, the supervisor decided to ______ him for acting without permission.
'Instead of praising' signals the opposite, so the blank must mean to reprimand.
se: The teacher had to ______ the boys repeatedly for throwing paper planes during the lesson.
scold
Both 'admonish' and 'scold' mean to tell someone off for bad behavior.

m: to make something poorer in quality by adding an inferior or impure substance
x: Shoppers in Bangladesh often worry that vendors adulterate milk and fruit with harmful chemicals to extend shelf life.
The supplier was fined after inspectors discovered it had adulterated its olive oil with cheaper vegetable oil.
In the lab, we learned simple tests to detect whether honey has been adulterated with sugar syrup.
Authorities warned that counterfeit medicines are often adulterated with chalk or other useless fillers.
He felt that mixing business with friendship would adulterate the trust they had built over twenty years.
tc: Unlike the honest merchants who sold pure saffron, the dishonest trader would ______ his spice with dyed corn silk to increase his profits.
The contrast with 'pure saffron' and the added corn silk show the blank means to make impure.
se: Unscrupulous dealers sometimes ______ the petrol with kerosene to sell it at a higher margin.
contaminate
Both 'adulterate' and 'contaminate' mean to make the fuel impure by mixing in another substance.

m: concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty
x: We chose the blue sofa for aesthetic reasons, even though the grey one was more comfortable.
Our architects must balance aesthetic considerations with the client's strict budget.
Her thesis examines the aesthetic principles behind traditional Japanese garden design.
Critics argued that the new bridge was an aesthetic disaster that ruined the city's skyline.
He appreciated her aesthetic sense, which turned their small flat into a warm and beautiful home.
tc: Although the building is perfectly functional, its ______ appeal is limited; most people find its concrete walls ugly.
The contrast between 'functional' and 'ugly' shows the blank concerns beauty.
se: The museum values the vase not for its age but for its ______ qualities, such as its elegant shape and color.
artistic
Both 'aesthetic' and 'artistic' refer to qualities of beauty, so the meaning stays the same.

m: to increase the power, status, or wealth of; to make something seem greater than it is
x: He tends to aggrandize his role in every story, as if he alone had solved the problem.
Some executives use company resources to aggrandize themselves rather than to reward their staff.
Historians criticized the biography for aggrandizing a minor general who had won only a single battle.
The dictator built enormous statues to aggrandize his image and silence any dissent.
She was tired of friends who used every conversation to aggrandize their own achievements.
tc: Rather than modestly acknowledge his team's work, the director tried to ______ his own role in the project's success.
'Rather than modestly acknowledge' signals the opposite of modesty, so the blank means to make seem greater.
se: Politicians often try to ______ their minor achievements during election campaigns.
exaggerate
Both 'aggrandize' and 'exaggerate' mean to make the achievements seem bigger than they are.

m: brisk and cheerful readiness or eagerness
x: When I offered to buy lunch, my younger brother accepted with remarkable alacrity.
She accepted the job offer with alacrity, signing the contract the same afternoon.
Our students responded to the extra-credit assignment with surprising alacrity.
Emergency crews moved with alacrity after the earthquake, reaching the worst-hit villages within hours.
He agreed to meet her parents with an alacrity that showed how serious he was about the relationship.
tc: Expecting the children to resist, their mother was surprised by the ______ with which they began cleaning their rooms.
'Expecting the children to resist' and 'surprised' signal the opposite of reluctance, so the blank means eagerness.
se: The volunteers responded with such ______ that the shelter was fully stocked within a day.
eagerness
Both 'alacrity' and 'eagerness' describe a quick, willing response.

m: to make pain, suffering, or a problem less severe
x: A cup of hot ginger tea usually helps alleviate my sore throat.
The company hired three new engineers to alleviate the pressure on its overworked staff.
Researchers are testing whether regular exercise can alleviate symptoms of depression in teenagers.
The new flyover was supposed to alleviate Dhaka's traffic congestion, but the jams have simply moved elsewhere.
Talking to a close friend alleviated some of the guilt she had been carrying for months.
tc: The doctor hoped the new medication would ______ the patient's pain, but it only made it worse.
'But it only made it worse' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean to reduce the pain.
se: The government introduced cash transfers to ______ the hardship faced by families who had lost their jobs.
relieve
Both 'alleviate' and 'relieve' mean to make hardship less severe.

m: to combine or unite separate parts into one whole
x: We decided to amalgamate our two small kitchens into one large cooking space.
Last year the two banks amalgamated to form the country's largest lender.
The new course amalgamates material from economics, psychology, and engineering.
Officials plan to amalgamate several rural schools to cut costs and share resources.
Over the years, their separate circles of friends gradually amalgamated into one close group.
tc: Rather than keep the three departments separate, the board decided to ______ them into a single division.
'Rather than keep... separate' and 'into a single division' show the blank means to combine.
se: The two rival clubs agreed to ______ and form one stronger team for the new season.
merge
Both 'amalgamate' and 'merge' mean to join together into one.

m: open to more than one interpretation; not clear in meaning
x: Her text saying 'fine' was so ambiguous that I couldn't tell whether she was angry or not.
Our contract contained an ambiguous clause about overtime pay that led to months of dispute.
Examiners removed the question because its wording was ambiguous and allowed two correct answers.
The ministry's ambiguous statement left journalists unsure whether the policy had actually changed.
After our first date, he gave me an ambiguous smile that could have meant interest or polite boredom.
tc: The witness's answer was so ______ that the lawyers on both sides claimed it supported their case.
Both sides reading the answer in their favor shows it had more than one possible meaning.
se: The instructions were ______, so half the class did the assignment one way and half did it another.
unclear
Both 'ambiguous' and 'unclear' explain why students understood the instructions differently.

m: having mixed or contradictory feelings about something or someone
x: I'm ambivalent about moving to the new apartment: it's bigger, but it's much farther from work.
Many employees feel ambivalent about the merger, welcoming the higher salaries but fearing layoffs.
She remained ambivalent about pursuing a PhD, torn between research and a well-paid industry job.
Public opinion is ambivalent about the new technology, which promises convenience but threatens privacy.
He felt deeply ambivalent toward his father, admiring his success yet resenting his long absences.
tc: Because she both loved the city's energy and hated its noise, Maya felt ______ about living downtown.
'Both loved... and hated' shows mixed feelings, which is what the blank means.
se: Torn between excitement and fear, he was ______ about accepting the job overseas.
conflicted
Both 'ambivalent' and 'conflicted' describe having mixed feelings, matching 'torn between excitement and fear'.

m: to make a bad or unpleasant situation better
x: Adding a few plants and a brighter lamp ameliorated the gloom of my tiny rented room.
The new manager introduced flexible hours to ameliorate the low morale in the department.
Scholars debate whether foreign aid truly ameliorates poverty or simply creates dependence.
City planners hope that new drainage canals will ameliorate the waterlogging that follows every monsoon storm.
A sincere apology did much to ameliorate the tension between the two old friends.
tc: The reforms were meant to ______ conditions in the prisons, but critics say the overcrowding has only gotten worse.
'But... has only gotten worse' contrasts with the intended effect, so the blank means to improve.
se: The charity works to ______ the living conditions of families in the city's poorest neighborhoods.
improve
Both 'ameliorate' and 'improve' mean to make conditions better.

m: something that belongs to a different time period from the one in which it appears
x: My grandfather's habit of writing letters by hand seems like a charming anachronism in the age of email.
Some staff see the weekly paper memo as an anachronism in an office that runs entirely on chat apps.
Students were asked to spot the anachronism in the film, where a Roman soldier wears a wristwatch.
Critics argue that hereditary titles are an anachronism in a modern democratic society.
In her eyes, his old-fashioned ideas about marriage were an anachronism she could not accept.
tc: In an office full of laptops, the old typewriter in the corner seemed a curious ______, a leftover from an era long past.
'A leftover from an era long past' defines something out of its proper time.
se: To younger voters, the law banning dancing on Sundays is simply a strange ______ from a bygone era.
relic
Both 'anachronism' and 'relic' describe something that belongs to an earlier time.

m: comparable or similar in certain respects, so that a comparison can be made
x: Learning to drive in a new city is analogous to learning a new language: it takes patience and practice.
Our situation is analogous to that of the startup that grew too fast and ran out of cash.
The professor explained that the heart's function is analogous to that of a pump moving water through pipes.
Some economists see the current crisis as analogous to the banking collapse of 2008.
She felt that her loneliness abroad was analogous to what her mother had experienced decades earlier.
tc: Fins play a role for fish that is ______ to the role wings play for birds: both let the animal move through its surroundings.
The colon introduces the shared function, showing the two roles are comparable.
se: The scientist argued that the way ants share tasks is ______ to the division of labor in a human factory.
comparable
Both 'analogous to' and 'comparable to' mean similar enough to be compared.

m: something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected
x: A sunny, dry week in the middle of July is an anomaly in Dhaka.
The accountant noticed an anomaly in the expense reports and asked for the original receipts.
Researchers first dismissed the data point as an anomaly, but repeated tests confirmed it.
Astronomers detected a gravitational anomaly that may indicate a hidden planet.
Among her career-obsessed friends, her decision to travel for a year was seen as an anomaly.
tc: Because nearly every patient responded well to the drug, the one who got worse was regarded as an ______.
'Nearly every patient responded well' shows the one exception departs from the norm.
se: The record low temperature was considered a strange ______ in an otherwise mild winter.
aberration
Both 'anomaly' and 'aberration' mean something that departs from the usual pattern.

m: a deep-seated feeling of dislike or hostility
x: My cat has a strong antipathy toward the vacuum cleaner and hides whenever it comes out.
Her antipathy to long meetings was well known, so she kept every agenda short.
Many students share an antipathy for exams that test memorization rather than understanding.
The documentary explores the historical antipathy between the two neighboring countries.
Despite his antipathy toward his sister's husband, he stayed polite for the sake of the family.
tc: Though the two scientists once collaborated closely, a bitter dispute over credit turned their friendship into lasting ______.
'Though... collaborated closely' and 'bitter dispute' signal a shift to the opposite of friendship.
se: He never hid his ______ toward bureaucracy, complaining about paperwork at every meeting.
hostility
Both 'antipathy' and 'hostility' express strong dislike, and both pair naturally with 'toward'.

m: lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern
x: The low turnout at the local election reflected widespread apathy among young voters.
After months of unanswered complaints, a mood of apathy settled over the office.
Teachers struggle to overcome student apathy in classes that seem irrelevant to their future careers.
I couldn't understand his apathy about the house, which he left dirty and unrepaired for months.
Her apathy toward their anniversary hurt him more than any argument could have.
tc: Organizers had expected passionate debate, but the meeting was marked by such ______ that hardly anyone spoke.
'Had expected passionate debate, but' signals the opposite, so the blank means lack of interest.
se: The charity's biggest obstacle was not a lack of money but public ______ toward the issue.
indifference
Both 'apathy' and 'indifference' mean a lack of concern.

m: to calm or satisfy someone, often by giving in to their demands
x: To appease my hungry little sister, I gave her a biscuit before dinner was ready.
The company offered a small bonus to appease employees angry about the cancelled holiday.
The university extended the library's opening hours to appease students protesting before exams.
Critics accused the government of trying to appease extremists instead of confronting them.
He bought her flowers to appease her after forgetting their dinner plans yet again.
tc: Instead of standing up to the bully, the principal tried to ______ him with privileges, which only encouraged him further.
'Instead of standing up to' signals giving in, so the blank means to calm by making concessions.
se: The airline gave every passenger a meal voucher to ______ the angry crowd at the gate.
placate
Both 'appease' and 'placate' mean to calm angry people by giving them something.

m: based on random choice or personal whim rather than reason or a consistent system
x: The order in which we hung the family photos was completely arbitrary; we just used whatever space was free.
Employees complained that promotions seemed arbitrary, with no clear criteria for who got ahead.
Choosing a cut-off score of seventy percent is somewhat arbitrary, the professor admitted.
Human rights groups condemned the arbitrary arrest of journalists without charge or trial.
Her father's rules felt arbitrary to her, changing from week to week depending on his mood.
tc: Rather than follow a consistent policy, the referee made ______ calls that seemed to depend only on his mood.
'Rather than follow a consistent policy' and 'depend only on his mood' define the blank as based on whim.
se: The landlord's ______ rent increases, imposed without any explanation, angered the tenants.
random
Both 'arbitrary' and 'random' describe increases made without any reason or pattern.

m: understood by only a few people; mysterious or obscure
x: My uncle loves explaining cricket's arcane rules about rain-shortened matches to anyone who will listen.
Only the senior accountant understood the arcane tax codes that governed the firm's overseas income.
The library's rare-book room holds arcane texts on medieval alchemy that few visitors can read.
Voters rarely follow the arcane procedures by which parliamentary committees approve the budget.
Their friendship was full of arcane inside jokes that no one else could understand.
tc: Unlike the familiar rules of football, the ______ regulations of the ancient game were known only to a handful of scholars.
'Unlike the familiar' and 'known only to a handful' show the blank means understood by few.
se: The lawyer spent years mastering the ______ rules of maritime law, which few in her field understand.
esoteric
Both 'arcane' and 'esoteric' describe knowledge understood by only a small group.

m: requiring great effort; difficult and tiring
x: Carrying the groceries up five flights of stairs was more arduous than I had expected.
After an arduous week of audits, the whole accounts team left the office early on Friday.
Writing a doctoral thesis is an arduous process that can take five years or more.
Rescuers faced an arduous climb to reach the hikers trapped on the mountain.
Rebuilding trust after the betrayal was an arduous task for both of them.
tc: Hikers who expected an easy stroll were shocked by the ______ climb, which left even the fittest among them exhausted.
The contrast with 'an easy stroll' and the result 'exhausted' show the blank means very difficult and tiring.
se: After a long and ______ trek through the mountains, the volunteers finally reached the remote village.
grueling
Both 'arduous' and 'grueling' describe a journey that is extremely tiring and difficult.

m: able to express ideas clearly and effectively in speech or writing
x: My nine-year-old niece is remarkably articulate and can argue for a later bedtime like a lawyer.
The most articulate member of the team was chosen to present the proposal to the clients.
Professors look for articulate students who can explain complex ideas in plain language.
The activist gave an articulate speech that persuaded many skeptics to support the cause.
Even in the middle of an argument, she remained calm and articulate about how she felt.
tc: Although he was shy and hesitant in private, on stage he became confident and ______, explaining his ideas with perfect clarity.
'Although... shy and hesitant' sets up a contrast, and 'explaining his ideas with perfect clarity' defines the blank.
se: The debate judges praised her as the most ______ speaker, noting how clearly she made every point.
eloquent
Both 'articulate' and 'eloquent' describe someone who expresses ideas clearly and well.

m: practicing strict self-denial and avoiding pleasure or luxury
x: My roommate lives an almost ascetic life, owning only a mattress, a laptop, and two shirts.
Despite earning a large salary, the CEO kept an ascetic office with bare walls and a plain desk.
The course examines ascetic traditions in Buddhism, Christianity, and Sufism.
Monks in the remote monastery follow an ascetic routine of prayer, silence, and simple meals.
Her ascetic habits, like skipping dessert and refusing gifts, sometimes made her friends uncomfortable.
tc: Unlike his brother, who loved fine food and expensive cars, Rafiq lived an ______ life of plain meals and few possessions.
'Unlike his brother, who loved fine food' signals the opposite of indulgence, and 'plain meals and few possessions' confirms it.
se: The philosopher was known for his ______ lifestyle, sleeping on a wooden floor and eating one simple meal a day.
austere
Both 'ascetic' and 'austere' describe a life of strict simplicity without comforts.

m: to make an unpleasant feeling less intense; to satisfy an appetite or desire
x: A plate of hot rice and dal quickly assuaged my hunger after the long bus ride from Sylhet.
The CEO held a town-hall meeting to assuage employees' fears about job cuts.
Her tutor's encouraging feedback did much to assuage her anxiety before the final exam.
Officials released new safety data in an attempt to assuage public concern about the vaccine.
Nothing he said could assuage her grief after the loss of her grandmother.
tc: The doctor's reassurances were meant to ______ his worries, but her vague answers only made him more anxious.
'But... only made him more anxious' contrasts with the intended effect, so the blank means to lessen worry.
se: He donated a large sum to the charity, hoping to ______ the guilt he felt about his past behavior.
ease
Both 'assuage' and 'ease' mean to make a painful feeling less intense.

m: able to assess situations accurately and turn them to one's advantage; shrewd
x: An astute shopper, my aunt always knows which market stall has the freshest fish at the lowest price.
Thanks to an astute investment in cloud software, the firm doubled its profits within two years.
The professor praised her astute observation that the data contradicted the author's main claim.
Political analysts called the candidate's decision to focus on local issues an astute move.
He is astute enough to notice when his friends are hiding something, even if they smile.
tc: Whereas most investors missed the warning signs, one ______ analyst predicted the crash months in advance.
'Whereas most investors missed the warning signs' contrasts with someone sharp enough to see them.
se: The detective was ______ enough to notice that the suspect's story did not match the evidence.
shrewd
Both 'astute' and 'shrewd' mean sharp at noticing and judging things accurately.

m: showing a bold willingness to take risks; sometimes rudely daring
x: In an audacious move, my cousin quit her stable job to open a bakery in a crowded neighborhood.
The startup's audacious plan to compete with global giants surprised even its own investors.
Her audacious thesis challenged a theory that had gone unquestioned for fifty years.
Thieves carried out an audacious robbery in broad daylight, escaping with paintings worth millions.
He made the audacious decision to propose to her on their second date.
tc: Whereas most of his colleagues played it safe, the young architect submitted an ______ design that broke every convention.
'Whereas most... played it safe' and 'broke every convention' show the blank means boldly risky.
se: The general's ______ plan to attack at night caught the enemy completely off guard.
daring
Both 'audacious' and 'daring' describe a bold, risky plan.

m: severely plain and without comfort or decoration; also stern and strict in manner
x: The hotel room was austere, with nothing but a narrow bed, a chair, and a bare bulb.
Our new headquarters has an austere design: grey concrete, steel furniture, and no artwork.
Students feared the austere headmaster, who rarely smiled and never tolerated excuses.
The government introduced austere budget measures, cutting spending on health and education.
Growing up with an austere father, she learned early to keep her feelings to herself.
tc: Unlike the lavish palace with its gold ornaments, the monk's cell was ______, containing only a mat and a small lamp.
'Unlike the lavish palace' and 'only a mat and a small lamp' show the blank means plain and bare.
se: Visitors were struck by the ______ decor of the chapel, which had bare stone walls and simple wooden benches.
plain
Both 'austere' and 'plain' describe decor with no ornament or luxury.

m: acting independently; having the freedom to govern or control itself
x: My teenage son wants to be fully autonomous, but he still asks me to wash his clothes.
Each regional office is autonomous and can hire staff without approval from headquarters.
Engineers at the lab are developing autonomous robots that can navigate warehouses without human help.
The region has been autonomous since 1990, with its own parliament and police force.
She values being autonomous in her relationship, keeping her own friends and interests.
tc: Although the province remains part of the country, it is largely ______, making its own laws on education and taxes.
'Making its own laws' defines the blank as self-governing.
se: The central bank is ______, so the government cannot dictate its interest-rate decisions.
independent
Both 'autonomous' and 'independent' mean free from outside control.

m: to state or assert firmly that something is true
x: My grandmother avers that a spoonful of honey every morning keeps all illness away.
In the meeting, the manager averred that no one would lose their job because of the merger.
The author avers that the ancient manuscript was written centuries earlier than scholars believed.
The witness averred under oath that she had seen the defendant leave the building at midnight.
He averred that he had never loved anyone as much as he loved her.
tc: Although the evidence suggested otherwise, the suspect continued to ______ that he had been at home all evening.
'Although the evidence suggested otherwise' shows he kept firmly stating his claim.
se: Several experts ______ that the painting is genuine, though a few still doubt it.
assert
Both 'aver' and 'assert' mean to state confidently that something is true.

m: so lacking in originality as to be boring or obvious
x: We spent the whole dinner making banal small talk about the weather and the traffic.
The marketing team rejected the slogan as too banal to stand out from competitors.
Her essay was well written, but its conclusions were banal and added nothing new to the debate.
Critics dismissed the film as a banal love story dressed up with expensive special effects.
He hated writing birthday cards because everything he wrote seemed banal and insincere.
tc: Though the novel's premise sounded fresh, its dialogue was ______, consisting mostly of worn-out phrases and predictable jokes.
'Though... sounded fresh' signals contrast, and 'worn-out phrases' defines the blank as unoriginal.
se: The speaker's ______ advice to 'follow your dreams' failed to inspire the graduates.
trite
Both 'banal' and 'trite' describe advice that is overused and unoriginal.

m: to give a false impression of something; to contradict or show to be false
x: My grandmother's energy belies her age; she still walks two miles every morning.
His calm voice during the presentation belied how nervous he really felt.
The study's modest title belies the importance of its findings for cancer research.
Strong export figures belie claims that the economy is heading into recession.
Her cheerful messages belied the loneliness she felt in her first months abroad.
tc: The restaurant's shabby exterior seems to ______ the quality of its food, which is among the best in the city.
The contrast between the 'shabby exterior' and food 'among the best' shows the appearance gives a false impression.
se: His relaxed manner tends to ______ the intense pressure he is under at work.
mask
Both 'belie' and 'mask' mean to hide the truth behind a misleading appearance.

m: gentle and kindly; also harmless or not dangerous
x: Our neighbor's huge dog looks fierce, but he's completely benign and loves children.
The new CEO turned out to be a benign leader who listened to staff before making decisions.
Doctors confirmed that the lump was benign, so no further treatment was needed.
Experts say most of the chemicals found in the river are benign at such low levels.
He looked at his granddaughter with a benign smile as she struggled to tie her shoes.
tc: Although the doctors initially feared the growth was cancerous, tests showed it was entirely ______.
'Although... feared... cancerous' signals the opposite, so the blank means harmless.
se: Most of the bacteria living on our skin are ______ and pose no threat to our health.
harmless
Both 'benign' and 'harmless' mean not dangerous, matching 'pose no threat'.

m: to support or strengthen something
x: A good night's sleep and a strong cup of tea bolstered me before the long drive.
The company hired a respected economist to bolster its credibility with investors.
Citing recent studies will bolster the argument in your research paper.
The government cut interest rates to bolster the struggling economy during the recession.
Her friends' encouragement bolstered her confidence before the job interview.
tc: The lawyer hoped the new witness would ______ her case, but his testimony actually weakened it.
'But his testimony actually weakened it' contrasts with the hope, so the blank means to strengthen.
se: The coach's speech helped ______ the team's morale after a string of defeats.
boost
Both 'bolster' and 'boost' mean to strengthen or raise morale.

m: using high-sounding, pompous language with little real meaning
x: My uncle's bombastic toasts at weddings always go on far too long.
The manager's bombastic emails, full of buzzwords, rarely contained any useful instructions.
Our writing tutor warned us that bombastic prose will never hide a weak argument.
Voters grew tired of the candidate's bombastic promises, which he never explained how to keep.
Her poems were heartfelt and simple, unlike the bombastic verses her ex-boyfriend used to send her.
tc: Instead of speaking plainly, the politician delivered a ______ speech full of grand phrases that meant very little.
'Instead of speaking plainly' and 'grand phrases that meant very little' define the blank.
se: Readers found the novel's ______ style exhausting, with every sentence stuffed with inflated words.
pompous
Both 'bombastic' and 'pompous' describe language that is inflated and self-important.

m: rough, rude, and bad-mannered
x: His boorish habit of talking with his mouth full embarrassed everyone at the dinner table.
HR received several complaints about the sales director's boorish behavior at the office party.
The seminar was spoiled by one boorish student who kept interrupting the speaker.
Fans condemned the boorish chanting of a small group of supporters during the match.
She ended the relationship after his boorish comments about her family.
tc: Expecting a polished gentleman, the hosts were shocked by the guest's ______ manners: he belched loudly and insulted the cook.

m: a bitter, forceful verbal or written attack
x: My uncle launched into a diatribe about traffic as soon as he walked through the door.
The director's email was less a memo than a diatribe against lazy employees.
The reviewer's diatribe against the novel seemed driven more by personal dislike than by literary judgment.
The columnist published a furious diatribe against the new censorship law.
After the breakup, she wrote a long diatribe about him that she wisely never sent.
tc: Rather than offering calm, constructive criticism, the commentator delivered a furious ______ against the referee.
The contrast with 'calm, constructive criticism' and the word 'furious' show the blank means a bitter attack.
se: The senator's speech turned into a long ______ against the media.
tirade
Both 'diatribe' and 'tirade' mean an angry, extended attack in words, so the meaning is the same.

m: a sharp division or contrast between two things
x: There's a strange dichotomy between how much people say they value sleep and how little they get.
The company struggles with the dichotomy between short-term profits and long-term growth.
The course challenges the traditional dichotomy between nature and nurture.
The report highlights the dichotomy between gleaming city towers and the slums beside them.
He felt a painful dichotomy between the son his parents wanted and the man he really was.
tc: Many philosophers reject the strict ______ between mind and body, arguing that the two cannot really be separated.
'Cannot really be separated' is the opposite of a sharp division, which is what the blank must mean.
se: The novel explores the ______ between rural tradition and urban modernity.
contrast
Both 'dichotomy' and 'contrast' express a sharp opposition between two things, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: shy and lacking confidence in oneself
x: He was too diffident to ask the waiter to replace his cold soup.
A diffident new hire, she rarely spoke in meetings despite having excellent ideas.
Diffident students often understand the material well but hesitate to answer in class.
The young scientist gave a diffident speech when accepting the award, thanking everyone but herself.
He was so diffident that he never found the courage to tell her how he felt.
tc: Though brilliant on paper, the candidate was so ______ in interviews that he barely made eye contact with the panel.
Barely making eye contact contrasts with 'brilliant on paper' and shows the blank means shy and unconfident.
se: The ______ boy hid behind his mother whenever visitors came to the house.
shy
Both 'diffident' and 'shy' describe someone timid and lacking confidence, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to wander away from the main subject in speech or writing
x: Sorry, I digress; let's get back to planning the trip before everyone falls asleep.
The presenter kept digressing into stories about his old job, and the meeting overran.
Our history teacher would often digress, but his tangents were the best part of the lessons.
The minister digressed from his prepared remarks to attack journalists.
When she's nervous, she tends to digress, and her husband finds it charming.
tc: The professor warned students not to ______ in their essays, since points would be lost for any material unrelated to the question.
Losing points for 'material unrelated to the question' shows the blank means wander off topic.
se: Speakers who ______ from the main point quickly lose their audience's attention.
stray
Both 'digress' and 'stray' mean to move away from the subject, so the sentence means the same.

m: slow to act or tending to cause delay
x: My dilatory roommate still hasn't paid his share of last month's electricity bill.
The project fell behind schedule because of the contractor's dilatory approach.
Dilatory students who leave their research until the last week rarely produce good theses.
Lawyers accused the government of using dilatory tactics to postpone the trial.
She grew tired of his dilatory replies to her messages and decided to move on.
tc: Frustrated by the agency's ______ response, the residents organized their own flood relief instead of waiting any longer.
Residents refusing to wait 'any longer' shows the agency's response was slow.
se: The committee was criticized for being ______ in releasing the inquiry's findings.
slow
Both 'dilatory' and 'slow' mean taking too long to act, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: showing care and steady effort in one's work or duties
x: She's a diligent gardener who waters her plants every morning before work.
Diligent employees who quietly meet every deadline are often the first to be promoted.
Thanks to diligent revision, he raised his GRE score by fifteen points.
Months of diligent reporting by local journalists finally exposed the corruption scandal.
Her diligent care for her ailing father won the admiration of the whole family.
tc: Unlike his careless classmates, Imran was remarkably ______, double-checking every calculation before submitting his work.
The contrast with 'careless' and the detail of double-checking show the blank means careful and hardworking.
se: Only after a ______ search of the archives did the historian find the missing letter.
painstaking
Both 'diligent' and 'painstaking' describe a careful, thorough search, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to free someone from a mistaken belief
x: Let me disabuse you of the idea that I'm a morning person.
The first week at the firm quickly disabused him of any notion that consulting was glamorous.
Our lecturer set out to disabuse students of common myths about evolution.
The latest report should disabuse anyone of the belief that the economy is recovering quickly.
Living together soon disabused her of the fantasy that he was perfect.
tc: The new recruit believed sales would be easy, but a month of rejections was enough to ______ him of that illusion.
A month of rejections removes his false belief, so the blank means free from a mistaken idea.
se: It took a patient tutor to ______ the students, who wrongly believed that summer happens because Earth moves closer to the sun.
correct
Both 'disabuse' and 'correct' mean to rid people of a false belief, so the sentence means the same.

m: to perceive or recognize something, especially with difficulty
x: In the fog, I could barely discern the outline of the approaching bus.
It's hard to discern what the client actually wants from his vague emails.
Researchers could discern no clear pattern in the survey responses.
With modern telescopes, astronomers can now discern planets orbiting stars hundreds of light-years away.
Over time she learned to discern when her son was lying.
tc: The handwriting was so faded that even the archivist, using a magnifying glass, could barely ______ a few words.
'So faded' and 'could barely' show the blank means perceive with difficulty.
se: Careful readers can ______ the author's irony beneath the polite tone.
detect
Both 'discern' and 'detect' mean to notice something not obvious, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: not in agreement or harmony; clashing
x: The neighbors' discordant music kept us awake half the night again.
Discordant views within the team made it hard to agree on a strategy.
The new findings strike a discordant note with decades of earlier research.
Discordant voices within the ruling party have begun to question the leader's plans.
Their discordant ideas about money eventually drove the couple apart.
tc: Amid the warm speeches praising the merger, one director's sharp criticism struck a ______ note.
Sharp criticism amid warm praise clashes with the mood, so the blank means out of harmony.
se: The witnesses gave ______ accounts of the accident, each contradicting the other.
conflicting
Both 'discordant' and 'conflicting' describe accounts that disagree, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to harm the reputation of someone or cause people to doubt something
x: He tried to discredit his neighbor's complaint by claiming she always exaggerated.
A rival firm spread rumors to discredit our product before its launch.
Later, larger studies thoroughly discredited the theory that vaccines cause autism.
The lawyer attempted to discredit the witness by pointing out inconsistencies in her story.
Her ex tried to discredit her among their mutual friends, but nobody believed him.
tc: Unable to refute her arguments, her opponents tried to ______ her by digging up embarrassing details from her past.
Digging up embarrassing details to damage her reputation shows the blank means destroy her credibility.
se: The defense team sought to ______ the expert's testimony by questioning his qualifications.
undermine
Both 'discredit' and 'undermine' mean to weaken trust in the testimony, so the meaning is the same.

m: a difference or lack of agreement between things that should match
x: There's a discrepancy between the price on the shelf and the one at the till.
The auditors spotted a discrepancy of two million taka in the company's accounts.
Researchers could not explain the discrepancy between the two sets of results.
Journalists noted a discrepancy between official death tolls and hospital records.
She noticed a discrepancy between what he told her and what his friends said.
tc: The detective became suspicious when she noticed a ______ between the suspect's story and the timestamps on the security footage.
Suspicion arising from comparing the story with the footage shows the blank means a mismatch.
se: The bank is investigating a ______ in the figures reported by the two branches.
inconsistency
Both 'discrepancy' and 'inconsistency' mean figures that do not match, so the sentence means the same.

m: not sincere or honest, especially by pretending to know less than one does
x: It's disingenuous of you to say you didn't know about the party when you helped plan it.
The company's claim that it valued staff well-being seemed disingenuous after the layoffs.
Critics called the author's apology disingenuous, since he kept repeating the same claims.
It would be disingenuous for officials to blame the floods entirely on the weather.
His disingenuous compliments about her cooking only made her trust him less.
tc: The minister's claim to have been unaware of the scandal was ______, since emails showed he had been briefed weeks earlier.
Emails proving he knew show the claim was insincere.
se: It is ______ to praise transparency while hiding your own financial records.
hypocritical
Both 'disingenuous' and 'hypocritical' describe pretending to hold values one does not practice, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: not influenced by personal advantage; impartial
x: We asked a disinterested friend to settle the argument about who should pay.
The company hired a disinterested consultant to review its hiring practices.
Peer review depends on disinterested experts judging research on its merits.
The election commission must be a disinterested body, free from party influence.
As her sister's lawyer, he couldn't give disinterested advice about the family dispute.
tc: Because the judge owned shares in the company, critics argued he could not be a ______ arbiter of the case.
Owning shares gives him a personal stake, so the blank means impartial.
se: The dispute was settled by a ______ referee with no ties to either club.
neutral
Both 'disinterested' and 'neutral' mean taking no side, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to speak of someone or something as having little worth
x: She never disparages her ex-husband in front of their children.
Good managers don't disparage competitors' products; they just improve their own.
Some academics disparage popular science books as oversimplified, yet many researchers first discovered science through them.
Opponents disparaged the new metro project as a waste of public money.
His habit of disparaging her friends caused many of their arguments.
tc: Although he publicly praised his rival's novel, in private he would ______ it as clumsy and overrated.
The contrast with 'publicly praised' and the words 'clumsy and overrated' show the blank means belittle.
se: Politicians often ______ the achievements of their predecessors to make their own look better.
belittle
Both 'disparage' and 'belittle' mean to make something seem unimportant, so the meaning is the same.

m: essentially different in kind and not easily compared
x: My roommates have disparate tastes in music, so we never agree on a playlist.
The merger brought together two disparate corporate cultures, and clashes began within weeks.
The course draws on disparate fields such as biology, economics and philosophy.
The coalition united disparate groups, from farmers to students to factory workers.
Despite their disparate backgrounds, the two friends found they had a lot in common.
tc: The anthology brings together such ______ writers that it is hard to find any theme linking them.
Being unable to find a common theme shows the writers are very different.
se: The museum's collection includes objects from wildly ______ cultures.
different
Both 'disparate' and 'different' describe cultures that have little in common, so the sentence means the same.

m: to hide one's real feelings or motives; to pretend
x: Children are terrible at dissembling; you can always tell when they've broken something.
When the boss asked about the missed deadline, he chose to dissemble rather than admit his mistake.
In the novel, the heroine must dissemble to survive in a court full of spies.
Officials dissembled for weeks before admitting the scale of the outbreak.
She tried to dissemble her disappointment, but her eyes gave her away.
tc: Unlike her brother, who always said exactly what he felt, Mina had learned to ______, hiding her true opinions behind polite smiles.
The contrast with saying exactly what he felt and 'hiding her true opinions' show the blank means disguise one's feelings.
se: A good poker player must be able to ______ when holding a strong hand.
dissimulate
Both 'dissemble' and 'dissimulate' mean to conceal one's true feelings, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to spread information or ideas widely
x: Our neighborhood group uses a messaging app to disseminate news about water cuts.
HR will disseminate the new policy to all staff by email.
Scientists have a duty to disseminate their findings to the public, not just to other researchers.
Health workers disseminated information about cholera prevention across the flooded villages.
She was hurt to learn that her best friend had disseminated her secret to half the class.
tc: The charity printed thousands of leaflets in order to ______ basic health advice as widely as possible.
Printing thousands of leaflets to reach people 'as widely as possible' shows the blank means spread.
se: The ministry plans to ______ the safety guidelines through radio and television.
spread
Both 'disseminate' and 'spread' mean to share information widely, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a lack of agreement or harmony; a clash between things
x: The dissonance of car horns and street vendors is the soundtrack of my morning commute.
There was obvious dissonance between the director's upbeat speech and the falling sales figures.
Psychologists use the term cognitive dissonance for the discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs.
The policy reveals a dissonance between the government's green promises and its support for coal.
She felt a growing dissonance between the life she had planned and the one she was living.
tc: The ______ between the charity's lofty mission statement and its lavish executive salaries alarmed many donors.
The clash between a lofty mission and lavish salaries shows the blank means a lack of agreement.
se: Critics noted the ______ between the film's cheerful music and its grim subject.
incongruity
Both 'dissonance' and 'incongruity' mean an uncomfortable mismatch, so the meaning is the same.

m: inclined to insist that one's opinions are undeniably true
x: My uncle is so dogmatic about diet that he lectures everyone at the dinner table.
A dogmatic manager who won't consider new ideas can stifle a whole team.
Good scientists avoid being dogmatic and change their minds when the evidence changes.
The party's dogmatic stance on economics left little room for compromise.
Their arguments were endless because both were dogmatic about how to raise the children.
tc: Whereas his mentor was willing to revise her views, Dr. Rahman was ______, refusing to consider any evidence that contradicted his theory.
The contrast with 'willing to revise' and 'refusing to consider any evidence' show the blank means rigidly opinionated.
se: The professor was so ______ that students stopped offering alternative interpretations in class.
opinionated
Both 'dogmatic' and 'opinionated' describe someone who insists on his own views, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to deceive or trick someone into believing or doing something
x: My little brother duped me into doing his homework by pretending he was sick.
Thousands of investors were duped by the fake cryptocurrency scheme.
The study shows how easily people can be duped by fake headlines that look official.
Fraudsters duped elderly villagers into handing over their land deeds.
She felt foolish for letting him dupe her with sweet words for so long.
tc: The con artist was skilled enough to ______ even experienced bankers, persuading them to approve fake loans.
'Con artist' and 'fake loans' show the blank means deceive.
se: Scammers often pose as bank officials to ______ customers into revealing their passwords.
trick
Both 'dupe' and 'trick' mean to deceive someone into acting, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: cheerful and full of energy and excitement
x: Our ebullient tour guide kept everyone laughing despite the steady rain and long queues.
The ebullient new sales director quickly lifted the mood of the office.
Ebullient after passing her viva, she treated her lab mates to dinner.
Fans were ebullient as the team returned home with the trophy.
His ebullient personality made him the life of every family gathering.
tc: Normally quiet and reserved, Farah was uncharacteristically ______ at the party, chatting and laughing with everyone.
'Normally quiet and reserved' contrasts with chatting and laughing, so the blank means lively and cheerful.
se: The crowd was in an ______ mood after the surprise victory.
exuberant
Both 'ebullient' and 'exuberant' mean full of joyful energy, so the sentence means the same.

m: drawing from a wide and varied range of sources
x: Her flat is decorated in an eclectic style, with Moroccan rugs next to Scandinavian chairs.
The firm hires people with eclectic backgrounds, from musicians to physicists.
The professor's eclectic reading list included novels, scientific papers and old newspapers.
The festival offered an eclectic mix of folk, jazz and electronic music.
His eclectic taste in friends meant his birthday parties were always full of surprises.
tc: Rather than following a single school of thought, the architect took an ______ approach, borrowing from Gothic, Islamic and modernist styles.
Borrowing from several styles rather than one shows the blank means drawing from varied sources.
se: The café's customers are a truly ______ crowd of students, artists and retirees.
diverse
Both 'eclectic' and 'diverse' describe a varied mix, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: shameless boldness; insolent nerve
x: He had the effrontery to ask me for another loan when he still hadn't repaid the first one.
She was stunned by the effrontery of a junior colleague who took credit for her presentation.
The examiner could hardly believe the effrontery of a student who argued after being caught cheating.
Voters were outraged at the effrontery of officials who raised their own salaries during a recession.
After cheating on her, he had the effrontery to accuse her of being unfaithful.
tc: Despite having missed every deadline, the contractor had the ______ to demand a bonus for his work.
Demanding a bonus after missing every deadline shows shameless boldness.
se: I couldn't believe her ______ in criticizing my cooking while eating a second helping.
audacity
Both 'effrontery' and 'audacity' mean shameless boldness, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a sad poem or song, especially one mourning someone who has died
x: At my grandfather's funeral, my cousin read an elegy she had written the night before.
The band's final album feels like an elegy for the city they grew up in.
In our literature seminar we compared Milton's elegy 'Lycidas' with modern poems of grief.
The newspaper's editorial read like an elegy for local journalism, which is vanishing across the country.
At the retirement party, his speech sounded less like a farewell than an elegy for the company's golden years.
tc: Written shortly after the poet's brother died in the war, the poem is a mournful ______ rather than a celebration of victory.
The death and the phrase 'mournful... rather than a celebration' show the blank means a poem of lament.
se: The composer wrote a haunting ______ for the victims of the earthquake.
lament
Both 'elegy' and 'lament' mean a sorrowful piece mourning the dead, so the meaning is the same.

m: to draw out a response, answer, fact or feeling from someone
x: My attempt to elicit a smile from the grumpy shopkeeper failed completely.
The manager's anonymous survey was designed to elicit honest feedback from staff about the new working hours.
Good teachers ask open questions that elicit thoughtful answers rather than memorised facts.
The minister's remarks on fuel prices elicited angry responses from commuters across Dhaka.
Nothing she said could elicit even a hint of sympathy from her older brother.
tc: The detective's gentle, patient questioning was meant to ______ details that the frightened witness had been too nervous to share.
The questioning is aimed at getting details the witness had held back, so the blank must mean 'draw out'.
se: The charity's advertisement was carefully designed to ______ sympathy from viewers.
evoke
Both 'elicit' and 'evoke' mean to bring out a feeling in someone, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: fluent, expressive and persuasive in speaking or writing
x: Even after a long day, my grandfather could give an eloquent account of his village childhood.
Her eloquent presentation persuaded the board to approve the budget for the new project.
The professor's eloquent lectures on history drew students from other departments as well.
In an eloquent editorial, the newspaper urged the government to protect the city's remaining wetlands.
His silence after the argument was more eloquent than any apology he could have offered her.
tc: Although he was usually shy and halting in conversation, he became surprisingly ______ whenever he spoke about his love of poetry.
'Although ... shy and halting' sets up a contrast, so the blank must mean fluent and expressive.
se: The young activist was remarkably ______, explaining complex policy issues in clear and moving language.
articulate
Both 'eloquent' and 'articulate' describe someone who expresses ideas clearly and effectively, giving the same meaning.

m: to make something clear by explaining it in detail
x: My uncle tried to elucidate the rules of chess, but my little cousin only grew more confused.
Could you elucidate what you meant by 'flexible hours' in yesterday's email to the team?
In her thesis, she elucidates the link between river erosion and flooding in northern Bangladesh.
A new study helps elucidate how certain bacteria become resistant to common antibiotics.
She finally elucidated why she had been so distant, and their friendship slowly recovered.
tc: The chapter on quantum theory was so dense that the tutor had to ______ nearly every paragraph for her baffled students.
A dense text and baffled students show that the tutor had to explain it clearly.
se: The spokesperson was asked to ______ the government's position on the new tax.
clarify
Both 'elucidate' and 'clarify' mean to make something clear, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: to try to equal or match someone, usually by imitating them out of admiration
x: As a child, I tried to emulate my older sister in everything, from her handwriting to her taste in music.
Other firms quickly emulated the startup's flexible working policy after seeing how productive its staff became.
Students are encouraged to emulate the clear, concise style of the model essays.
Several countries are now trying to emulate Finland's approach to early childhood education.
He admired his father deeply but never felt he could emulate his patience and generosity.
tc: She admired her mentor so much that she tried to ______ his calm, methodical way of handling difficult clients.
Admiration leading her to copy his way of working shows the blank means imitate.
se: Young designers often try to ______ the style of the masters they admire.
imitate
Both 'emulate' and 'imitate' mean to copy someone you admire, so the meaning stays the same.

m: regularly found in, or native to, a particular place, group or field
x: Lateness is endemic in my family; nobody ever arrives anywhere on time.
Long working hours seem endemic to the banking industry, according to a recent survey.
Critics argue that grade inflation has become endemic at many universities.
The lemur is endemic to Madagascar and is found nowhere else in the wild.
Dengue has become endemic in Dhaka, with cases rising sharply every monsoon season.
tc: Unlike the many species that arrived on visiting ships, this small bird is ______ to the island and lives nowhere else.
The contrast with species brought by ships and 'lives nowhere else' show the blank means native.
se: The kiwi is ______ to New Zealand, where it has lived for millions of years.
native
Both 'endemic to' and 'native to' mean naturally belonging to a place, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to weaken someone or drain them of energy and vitality
x: The sticky heat before the monsoon enervates everyone in Dhaka, and nobody feels like going out.
Endless meetings with no clear outcome tend to enervate even the most enthusiastic staff.
Months of cramming had enervated him, and he slept for almost two days after his finals.
Doctors warn that chronic lack of sleep can enervate the body and weaken the immune system.
The constant arguments with her partner had enervated her, leaving her too tired to care.
tc: Rather than energising the team, the long weekend retreat seemed to ______ them, and they returned more tired than before.
'Rather than energising' and 'more tired than before' show the blank means to drain of energy.
se: A long illness can ______ even a strong person, leaving them barely able to climb the stairs.
weaken
Both 'enervate' and 'weaken' mean to reduce someone's strength, so the sentence means the same.

m: to cause or give rise to a feeling, situation or condition
x: Her kindness to new neighbours engendered a warm sense of community on our street.
The manager's habit of taking credit for others' work engendered resentment among the team.
Good teachers engender curiosity rather than simply delivering facts to their students.
The controversial policy engendered fierce debate both in parliament and in the press.
Years of broken promises had engendered a deep mistrust between the two brothers.
tc: Rather than easing tensions, the leaked memo only served to ______ further suspicion among the employees.
'Rather than easing tensions' signals that the memo created more suspicion, so the blank means cause.
se: Transparent decision-making helps ______ trust between a company and its customers.
foster
Both 'engender' and 'foster' mean to bring about or develop a feeling such as trust, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a person or thing that is mysterious and difficult to understand
x: How my grandmother's cat gets onto the roof remains an enigma to the whole family.
To most of his colleagues, the quiet new director was something of an enigma.
The origin of the ancient script is still an enigma that scholars have failed to solve.
Dark matter remains one of the great enigmas of modern physics.
Even after ten years of marriage, she felt her husband was still an enigma in some ways.
c: a riddle wrapped in an enigma
tc: Although she had lived next door for years, she was a complete ______ to us; we knew nothing about her job, her family or her past.
Knowing nothing about her after years shows she is a mystery.
se: To this day, the disappearance of the ship remains the greatest ______ in the history of the navy.
mystery
Both 'enigma' and 'mystery' mean something that cannot be explained, so the sentence means the same.

m: lasting for only a very short time
x: Social media fame is often ephemeral, and most viral stars are forgotten within months.
Our excitement over the pay rise proved ephemeral once we saw the new tax deductions.
The poet's later work explores the ephemeral nature of youth and happiness.
Mayflies live remarkably ephemeral lives, surviving only a day or two as adults.
Their summer romance was intense but ephemeral, ending as soon as the holidays did.
tc: Unlike the enduring stone monuments of ancient Egypt, the sand sculptures on the beach were ______, washed away by the next tide.
The contrast with 'enduring' and 'washed away by the next tide' show the blank means short-lived.
se: The thrill of buying new clothes is usually ______, fading within a few days.
fleeting
Both 'ephemeral' and 'fleeting' mean lasting only briefly, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: mental calmness and composure, especially in a difficult situation
x: She accepted the news of the flight delay with surprising equanimity and simply opened her book.
A good manager learns to handle both praise and criticism with equanimity.
Regular meditation, the study suggests, can help students face exams with greater equanimity.
The villagers faced the annual floods with an equanimity born of long experience.
After the painful breakup, it took him several months to recover his equanimity.
tc: Though hecklers shouted insults throughout her speech, the candidate responded with remarkable ______, never once raising her voice.
'Never once raising her voice' despite insults shows the blank means calmness.
se: Despite losing the final, the captain spoke to reporters with great ______.
composure
Both 'equanimity' and 'composure' mean calm self-control, so the sentence means the same.

m: unclear or ambiguous, often deliberately, so that it can be understood in more than one way
x: When I asked whether he liked my cooking, my brother gave an equivocal shrug and kept eating.
The CEO's equivocal answer about job cuts only made the staff more anxious.
The results of the clinical trial were equivocal, so researchers called for a larger study.
The government's equivocal stance on the dam project angered both its supporters and its opponents.
Her equivocal reply to his proposal left him unsure whether to hope or give up.
tc: Wanting to avoid offending either side, the spokesperson issued a deliberately ______ statement that could be read in two ways.
'Could be read in two ways' defines the blank as ambiguous.
se: The evidence against the accused was ______, so the judge was reluctant to convict him.
ambiguous
Both 'equivocal' and 'ambiguous' mean open to more than one interpretation, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: having or showing great knowledge gained from study and reading
x: My erudite uncle can talk for hours about anything from Roman history to Bengali poetry.
The new analyst's erudite reports impressed even the most senior partners at the firm.
Her erudite lecture on medieval philosophy was full of references to Latin texts.
The magazine is known for its erudite essays on science, politics and culture.
Although he was deeply erudite, he never made his friends feel ignorant.
tc: Despite leaving school at fifteen, the self-taught historian was remarkably ______, having read thousands of books on the subject.
Having read thousands of books shows the blank means very learned, despite little schooling.
se: The professor was so ______ that her students joked she had read every book in the library.
learned
Both 'erudite' and 'learned' mean deeply knowledgeable from study, so the sentence means the same.

m: understood by or meant for only a small group with special knowledge
x: My cousin collects esoteric facts about old trains that nobody else in the family cares about.
The meeting got bogged down in esoteric details of tax law that only the accountant understood.
Her doctoral thesis dealt with a highly esoteric branch of number theory.
Critics say the court's reasoning is too esoteric for ordinary citizens to follow.
He loves esoteric jazz records, which makes choosing a birthday present for him difficult.
tc: The lecture was so ______ that only the handful of specialists in the audience could follow the speaker's arguments.
Only specialists being able to follow shows the blank means understood by very few.
se: The book discusses ______ points of medieval theology that will interest very few general readers.
arcane
Both 'esoteric' and 'arcane' mean known only to a few specialists, so the meaning stays the same.

m: a speech or piece of writing that praises someone highly, especially someone who has just died
x: At the funeral, my aunt delivered a moving eulogy for her father.
Former colleagues gave warm eulogies at the memorial for the engineer who had founded the firm.
In her essay, the historian offers a eulogy for a vanishing way of village life.
Newspapers around the world published glowing eulogies for the celebrated scientist after her death.
He struggled to write the eulogy because every memory of his best friend made him cry.
tc: Instead of dwelling on the late mayor's flaws, the speaker gave a warm ______ that celebrated his decades of public service.
Celebrating a dead man's service 'instead of dwelling on his flaws' shows the blank means a speech of praise.
se: At the memorial service, her oldest friend delivered a heartfelt ______ that left many in tears.
tribute
Both 'eulogy' and 'tribute' mean a speech honouring someone, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a mild or indirect word used in place of one that seems harsh or unpleasant
x: My grandmother always used the euphemism 'passed away' instead of saying someone had died.
'Let go' is a common euphemism for being fired from a job.
Students analysed the euphemisms that governments use to describe military actions.
Critics argued that 'collateral damage' is simply a euphemism for the deaths of civilians.

exonerate

absolve
Both 'exonerate' and 'absolve' mean to free someone from blame, so the sentence means the same.

advantageous

praise

irrelevant
Both 'extraneous' and 'irrelevant' mean not connected to the matter at hand, so the meaning stays the same.

flippant
Both 'facetious' and 'flippant' describe joking about something serious, so the sentence means the same.

ease

erroneous
Both 'fallacious' and 'erroneous' mean wrong or mistaken, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: very careful about accuracy, detail or cleanliness; hard to please

meticulous

Pilots are trained to be imperturbable, speaking in a steady voice even during severe turbulence.

tc: While everyone else in the control room panicked, the chief engineer stayed ______, calmly reading out instructions.
'While everyone else panicked' sets up a contrast, and 'calmly' confirms the blank means unshakably calm.
se: Throughout the heated debate, the moderator remained ______, never once raising her voice.
unflappable
Both 'imperturbable' and 'unflappable' mean staying calm under pressure, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: not affected or influenced by something, such as criticism, pressure or argument
x: My father seems impervious to the cold and wears sandals even in the middle of winter.
The manager was impervious to complaints from staff about the long hours and endless overtime.
No theory is impervious to evidence; a good scientist must be willing to revise even cherished ideas.
The minister appeared impervious to criticism, pressing ahead with the unpopular tax despite weeks of protests.
She acted impervious to his charm, but her friends noticed she smiled whenever he walked in.
tc: No matter how many people pointed out the flaws in his plan, he remained ______ to their objections and went ahead anyway.
'No matter how many people pointed out the flaws' and 'went ahead anyway' show he was not affected by the objections.
se: The coach seemed ______ to the boos from the crowd and stuck to his strategy.
immune
Both 'impervious to' and 'immune to' mean unaffected by, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: acting or done quickly and without careful thought
x: In an impetuous moment, I quit my job by text message and regretted it by the next morning.
The board worried that the new CEO's impetuous decisions would scare off cautious investors.
My thesis supervisor warned me against an impetuous change of topic so close to the deadline.
Historians still debate whether the general's impetuous attack was an act of bold genius or simple recklessness.
He proposed to her after only two weeks, an impetuous gesture that somehow led to forty happy years.
tc: Unlike her ______ younger brother, who acted on every whim, Maya considered each decision carefully.
'Who acted on every whim' defines the blank, and 'unlike' contrasts it with careful Maya.
se: Selling the house was an ______ decision that she made without consulting anyone.
impulsive
Both 'impetuous' and 'impulsive' describe a decision made suddenly without thought, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: unable to be calmed, satisfied or persuaded to stop opposing
x: My neighbor has been an implacable critic of the new parking rules since the day they were announced.
The company faced implacable opposition from the union, which rejected every offer on the table.
In the novel, the hero is pursued by an implacable enemy who never forgives an old insult.
The two rival parties have remained implacable foes for decades, refusing even to share a stage.
Her anger was implacable; no apology, however sincere, seemed to soften it.
tc: We tried gifts, apologies and long explanations, but her fury was ______ and nothing could soothe it.
'Nothing could soothe it' restates the blank, so it must mean impossible to calm.
se: The rebels faced an ______ foe that refused to negotiate under any circumstances.
unforgiving
Both 'implacable' and 'unforgiving' describe an enemy who cannot be appeased, which fits the refusal to negotiate.

m: suggested or understood without being stated directly
x: There was an implicit agreement between the roommates that whoever cooked would not have to wash the dishes.
Implicit in the manager's praise was a warning that the next report had better be just as good.
Students must learn to identify the implicit assumptions behind an author's argument.
The new law contains an implicit admission that the old system had failed.
Their trust in each other was implicit, never discussed but always deeply felt.
tc: Although he never said it outright, his disapproval was ______ in the way he kept checking his watch during her speech.
'Although he never said it outright' signals that the disapproval was suggested rather than stated.
se: Her silence was an ______ acknowledgment that she had made a mistake.
unspoken
Both 'implicit' and 'unspoken' describe an admission conveyed without words, so the meaning stays the same.

m: to challenge or cast doubt on the truth, honesty or integrity of someone or something
x: I wasn't trying to impugn your cooking; I simply said the curry needed a little more salt.
The auditor's report impugned the accuracy of the figures the finance team had submitted.
In her review, the critic impugned the study's methods, arguing that the sample was far too small.
Opposition lawmakers impugned the integrity of the election commission after the results were announced.
He felt deeply hurt when his own brother impugned his motives for caring for their elderly mother.
tc: The lawyer tried to ______ the witness's honesty by pointing out contradictions in his earlier statements.
Pointing out contradictions is a way of casting doubt, so the blank must mean to call honesty into question.
se: No one would dare to ______ her reputation after decades of honest public service.
question
Both 'impugn' and 'question' mean to cast doubt on her good name, so the sentence means the same.

m: not done on purpose; resulting from carelessness or accident
x: I made an inadvertent mistake on my visa form and had to fill in the whole thing again.
An inadvertent reply-all sent the confidential salary list to the entire department.
The researchers admitted that an inadvertent error in their code had skewed the results.
Officials described the leak of private data as inadvertent, but critics demanded an investigation.
Her inadvertent remark about his weight hurt him more than she ever realized.
tc: The omission of her name from the list was ______, not deliberate; the secretary had simply overlooked it.
'Not deliberate' and 'simply overlooked' tell us the blank means accidental.
se: The company apologized for the ______ release of its customers' email addresses.
accidental
Both 'inadvertent' and 'accidental' mean the release was not intended, so the meaning is the same.

m: continuing without stopping or pausing
x: The incessant rain of the monsoon turned our lane in Dhaka into a shallow river for weeks.
I could not concentrate on my report because of the incessant ringing of the office phones.
Graduate students often complain about the incessant pressure to publish.
Residents near the airport have protested against the incessant noise of planes taking off at night.
His incessant questions about where I had been began to feel less like concern and more like suspicion.
tc: The barking was not occasional but ______, continuing from dusk until dawn without a moment's pause.
'Not occasional but' sets up a contrast, and 'without a moment's pause' confirms the blank means nonstop.
se: The ______ chatter in the library made it impossible to study.
constant
Both 'incessant' and 'constant' describe chatter that never stops, so the sentence means the same.

m: just beginning and not yet fully formed or developed
x: I have an inchoate idea for a novel, but I haven't worked out the plot yet.
At this stage the marketing plan is still inchoate, so please don't share it with the client.
Her dissertation began as an inchoate set of questions about rural-to-urban migration.
The protest movement was inchoate, lacking leaders, a clear message or any real plan.
He felt an inchoate sense of unease about the marriage long before he could explain it.
tc: His plan was still ______: he knew roughly what he wanted, but none of the details had taken shape.
The part after the colon explains the blank: the plan had not yet taken shape.
se: The committee's proposal remains ______ and will need months of work before it can be presented.
undeveloped
Both 'inchoate' and 'undeveloped' mean not yet fully formed, which is why months of work are needed.

m: strange or out of place because it does not fit with its surroundings
x: A pair of bright pink sneakers looked incongruous with his formal black suit.
It seemed incongruous to hold a cheerful office party on the same day as the layoffs.
Critics noted the incongruous mix of medieval costumes and modern slang in the new production.
A gleaming glass tower looks incongruous among the old wooden houses of the historic district.
Her loud laughter felt incongruous in the quiet room where everyone was grieving.
tc: The modern sculpture looked ______ in the ancient temple courtyard, clashing with everything around it.
'Clashing with everything around it' restates the blank, so it must mean out of place.
se: In such a solemn setting, his cheerful whistling seemed ______.
jarring
Both 'incongruous' and 'jarring' describe something that clashes with its surroundings, giving the same meaning.

m: having no interest in or concern about something
x: My cat is completely indifferent to the expensive toys I buy her and prefers the cardboard box.
Customers quickly noticed the indifferent attitude of the staff and took their business elsewhere.
Most of the class seemed indifferent to the lecture, scrolling through their phones for the whole hour.
Many voters have grown indifferent to politics, and turnout in local elections has fallen sharply.
After years of arguments, he had become indifferent to whether she came home or not.
tc: Rather than being passionate about the cause, most citizens were ______, barely noticing the debate at all.
'Rather than being passionate' signals the opposite, and 'barely noticing' confirms a lack of interest.
se: He seemed ______ to the outcome of the match, chatting on the phone while his team lost.
unconcerned
