Both 'indifferent' and 'unconcerned' mean not caring about the result, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: lazy; wanting to avoid activity or effort
x: On holiday I spent an indolent afternoon lying in a hammock with a book I never actually opened.
The new manager vowed to replace indolent employees who did as little work as possible.
Indolent students who skip the readings usually struggle when the exam comes around.
The report blamed an indolent bureaucracy for the long delays in issuing building permits.
Her parents worried that their son, once so energetic, had become indolent since leaving university.
tc: Far from being hardworking, the clerk was so ______ that he rarely finished a single file before lunch.
'Far from being hardworking' signals the opposite, so the blank must mean lazy.
se: The ______ teenager spent the whole summer sleeping until noon and watching television.
lazy
Both 'indolent' and 'lazy' describe someone avoiding effort, so the sentence means the same.

m: too great or intense to be expressed or described in words
x: The ineffable smell of rain on dry earth always takes me back to my childhood.
There is an ineffable quality to her designs that clients love but can never quite describe.
Philosophers have long argued about whether religious experience is ineffable or can be captured in language.
Watching the sun rise over the Sundarbans, she felt an ineffable calm settle over her.
Holding my newborn daughter for the first time, I felt an ineffable joy.
tc: The beauty of the music was ______; even the critics, who usually had plenty to say, could not find words for it.
'Could not find words for it' defines the blank as impossible to put into words.
se: She tried to describe the ______ peace she felt in the mountains but soon gave up.
indescribable
Both 'ineffable' and 'indescribable' mean too intense to express, which is why she gave up describing it.

m: impossible to stop, prevent or change
x: Despite all the anti-aging creams on the market, the inexorable march of time cannot be stopped.
The company's inexorable decline began when it failed to adapt to online shopping.
Students often feel the inexorable approach of exam week as a kind of slow, creeping dread.
Climate scientists warn of an inexorable rise in sea levels that threatens low-lying countries like Bangladesh.
She felt sad watching the inexorable drift between her and her childhood friend after they moved to different cities.
tc: Despite every effort to halt it, the river's erosion of the bank was ______, swallowing a few more meters each year.
'Despite every effort to halt it' shows the erosion could not be stopped.
se: Economists warned that the ______ rise in prices would hurt the poorest families most.
relentless
Both 'inexorable' and 'relentless' describe a rise that keeps going and cannot be stopped, so the meaning is the same.

m: innocent, sincere and trusting, sometimes to the point of being naive
x: It was a little ingenuous of me to believe the seller when he said the car had never been in an accident.
The new intern asked ingenuous questions that made the senior staff smile but also think.
Her ingenuous personal essay, written without irony or pretense, charmed the admissions committee.
Voters who accept every campaign promise at face value are being rather ingenuous.
He loved her ingenuous enthusiasm and the way she trusted everyone she met.
tc: Unlike his scheming older brother, Tom was utterly ______, trusting everyone and never suspecting a trick.
'Unlike his scheming older brother' sets up a contrast, and 'trusting everyone' defines the blank as innocent.
se: The ______ young man believed every word the salesman told him.
naive
Both 'ingenuous' and 'naive' describe someone too trusting, so the sentence means the same.

m: harmful to something, or unfriendly and hostile
x: Late nights and junk food are inimical to good health, as I learned during my final year.
A culture of blame is inimical to innovation because employees become afraid to try new ideas.
Many education researchers argue that rote learning is inimical to genuine understanding.
Critics say the new regulations are inimical to small businesses, which cannot afford the extra paperwork.
His jealousy proved inimical to their marriage, slowly poisoning every conversation they had.
tc: Far from helping the economy, the new tariffs proved ______ to growth, driving away foreign investors.
'Far from helping' signals the opposite, and 'driving away investors' shows the effect was harmful.
se: Constant noise is ______ to concentration, so I study in the quietest corner of the library.
harmful
Both 'inimical to' and 'harmful to' mean damaging, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: harmless; not likely to offend, upset or cause injury
x: What looked like a dangerous spider turned out to be an innocuous little creature that eats mosquitoes.
An innocuous comment in a meeting somehow turned into a week-long argument in the department.
The study found that the food additive, once widely feared, is innocuous at normal levels of consumption.
Officials insisted the leaked chemical was innocuous, but residents near the factory were not convinced.
She asked an innocuous question about his weekend, and he suddenly burst into tears.
tc: The mushroom looked ______, but it was in fact highly poisonous, which shows how deceptive appearances can be.
'But it was in fact highly poisonous' contrasts with the blank, so the blank must mean harmless.
se: The email seemed ______ at first, but it contained a link that installed a virus.
harmless
Both 'innocuous' and 'harmless' describe how the email first appeared, so the meaning is the same.

m: lacking flavor, interest or energy; dull
x: The hospital food was so insipid that my father begged us to bring him some proper biryani from home.
The presentation was full of insipid slogans that nobody in the room remembered five minutes later.
My professor called my first draft insipid and told me to take a stronger position.
Critics dismissed the film as an insipid remake that lacked the wit of the original.
She ended the relationship because their conversations had become insipid and predictable.
tc: The soup was so ______ that even a generous pinch of salt and chili could not give it any taste.
'Could not give it any taste' shows the blank means lacking flavor.
se: The novel's dialogue is ______, so the characters never really come to life.
dull
Both 'insipid' and 'dull' mean lacking interest, which explains why the characters feel lifeless.

m: narrow-minded and uninterested in people, ideas or cultures outside one's own group
x: Our village was so insular that anyone from the next district was considered an outsider.
The engineering team had grown insular, ignoring suggestions from marketing and customers alike.
Some academic departments are criticized for being insular and rarely collaborating with other fields.
Critics warned that an insular foreign policy would leave the country isolated and weaker.
After his divorce he became insular, seeing only two old friends and turning down every invitation.
tc: Rather than welcoming outside ideas, the small town's ______ residents distrusted anything that came from beyond the hills.
'Rather than welcoming outside ideas' and distrust of outsiders show the blank means closed and narrow-minded.
se: The club's ______ culture made new members feel unwelcome.
parochial
Both 'insular' and 'parochial' describe a narrow, inward-looking attitude that shuts out newcomers.

m: hard to control, manage or solve
x: Our old washing machine has an intractable leak that three repairmen have failed to fix.
The project stalled because of an intractable dispute between the two lead engineers.
Mathematicians have worked for centuries on problems that remain intractable today.
Dhaka's traffic congestion has proved an intractable problem for successive city governments.
Their disagreement over where to live became intractable, and eventually they separated.
tc: Unlike most of the puzzles, which the students solved in minutes, this one proved ______, defeating even the teacher.
'Unlike most of the puzzles' sets up a contrast, and 'defeating even the teacher' shows it was very hard to solve.
se: Poverty in the region has proved an ______ problem, resisting decades of foreign aid.
insoluble
Both 'intractable' and 'insoluble' describe a problem that cannot be solved, so the meaning stays the same.

m: refusing to change one's views or to agree to any compromise
x: My landlord remained intransigent about the rent increase, even after I offered to sign a longer lease.
Talks collapsed because both management and the union took an intransigent stand on wages.
The reviewer was intransigent, refusing to accept the paper until every one of his comments was addressed.
Diplomats blamed the intransigent attitude of both governments for the failure of the peace talks.
My father can be intransigent about family traditions, so arguing with him about our Eid plans is pointless.
tc: Although the mediators offered several compromises, the two sides remained ______, refusing to give up a single demand.
'Although' signals a contrast with the offered compromises, and 'refusing to give up a single demand' defines the blank.
se: The senator was ______ on the issue and would not consider any amendments.
inflexible
Both 'intransigent' and 'inflexible' mean unwilling to compromise, so the sentence means the same.

m: fearless and adventurous
x: Our intrepid neighbor climbed onto the roof during the storm to rescue a stranded kitten.
An intrepid reporter spent months undercover to expose the factory's unsafe working conditions.
Intrepid explorers of the nineteenth century mapped rivers that no outsider had ever seen.
Only the most intrepid investors were willing to put money into the company during the crisis.
She was an intrepid traveler who thought nothing of crossing a desert alone.
tc: While most climbers turned back at the first sign of the storm, the ______ few pressed on toward the summit.
'While most climbers turned back' contrasts with those who pressed on, so the blank means fearless.
se: The ______ firefighter ran back into the burning building to find the missing child.
fearless
Both 'intrepid' and 'fearless' describe someone who faces danger without fear, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to overwhelm with a very large amount of something; to flood
x: After my birthday post, friends inundated me with messages and I spent all evening replying.
Our support team was inundated with complaints after the app crashed on launch day.
Professors are often inundated with emails from students in the week before finals.
Heavy monsoon rains inundated large parts of northern Bangladesh, forcing thousands of families from their homes.
When news of their engagement spread, the couple was inundated with advice they had never asked for.
tc: The tiny charity expected a few dozen applications, but news coverage caused thousands of people to ______ its office with letters.
The contrast between 'a few dozen' and 'thousands' shows the blank means to overwhelm.
se: Fans began to ______ the singer's website with requests for a second concert.
flood
Both 'inundate' and 'flood' mean to send an overwhelming number of requests, so the sentence means the same.

m: to make someone used to something unpleasant so that they no longer feel it strongly
x: Growing up next to a railway line inured me to noise, so I can sleep almost anywhere.
Years of working in the emergency room had inured her to the sight of blood.
Constant deadlines during my PhD inured me to pressure that would once have kept me awake.
Some psychologists fear that graphic news coverage inures viewers to real suffering.
He had become so inured to her criticism that he barely heard it anymore.
tc: Soldiers who spend months at the front gradually ______ themselves to danger, until gunfire no longer startles them.
'Until gunfire no longer startles them' shows the blank means to become hardened or accustomed.
se: Living in the Arctic for a decade helped him ______ himself to the bitter cold.
accustom
Both 'inure oneself to' and 'accustom oneself to' mean to get used to something harsh, so the meaning is the same.

m: insulting, abusive or bitterly critical language
x: The driver leaned out of his window and hurled invective at the rickshaw that had cut him off.
The manager's email was a stream of invective that left the whole team demoralized.
Academic debates should rely on evidence, not personal invective against one's opponents.
Online forums are often filled with invective rather than reasoned discussion of the issues.
After the breakup, she was deeply hurt by the invective he posted about her online.
tc: Instead of offering polite criticism, the reviewer unleashed a torrent of ______, calling the author lazy and incompetent.
'Instead of polite criticism' and the insults that follow show the blank means abusive language.
se: The candidate's speech was full of ______ against his rivals, with little discussion of policy.
vitriol
Both 'invective' and 'vitriol' mean bitter, abusive criticism, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: easily made angry; short-tempered
x: Our irascible landlord shouts at anyone who parks even an inch over the line.
The irascible editor was known for tearing up drafts in front of the writers who wrote them.
Students learned to avoid the irascible lab supervisor until he had finished his morning tea.
The irascible senator often lost his temper during televised hearings.
My grandfather grew irascible in his final years, though he was always gentle with the grandchildren.
tc: Unlike his calm and patient wife, Mr. Haque was ______, flying into a rage at the smallest inconvenience.
'Unlike his calm and patient wife' sets up a contrast, and 'flying into a rage' defines the blank.
se: The ______ chef shouted at the waiters whenever an order came back to the kitchen.
irritable
Both 'irascible' and 'irritable' describe someone quick to anger, so the meaning is the same.

m: unable to decide what to do; uncertain and hesitant
x: I stood irresolute in the supermarket aisle, unable to choose between two almost identical brands of rice.
An irresolute manager can paralyze a team by refusing to make even small decisions.
The irresolute student changed his major three times in two years.
The government's irresolute response to the crisis allowed the problem to grow much worse.
She was irresolute about the marriage proposal and asked for a month to think it over.
tc: A strong leader acts quickly in a crisis, but the ______ governor kept postponing his decision while the floodwaters rose.
'But' contrasts him with a strong leader, and 'kept postponing his decision' shows he could not decide.
se: The ______ committee debated for months without reaching a conclusion.
indecisive
Both 'irresolute' and 'indecisive' mean unable to make up one's mind, so the sentence means the same.

m: using very few words
x: When I asked my teenage son how school was, his laconic reply was simply 'fine.'
Her laconic emails, rarely more than a line long, sometimes made colleagues think she was angry.
The professor's laconic comments in the margin, such as 'unclear' and 'why?', terrified his students.
The spokesperson gave a laconic statement to reporters and refused to answer any questions.
He was a laconic man who showed his love through actions rather than words.
tc: Whereas his wife could talk for hours, Rahim was ______, rarely using more than a few words to answer any question.
'Whereas' sets up a contrast with talking for hours, and 'rarely using more than a few words' defines the blank.
se: The general sent a ______ message to his troops: 'Hold the bridge.'
terse
Both 'laconic' and 'terse' describe a message of very few words, so the meaning stays the same.

m: a state of physical or mental tiredness and lack of energy
x: A strange lassitude came over me after the long Friday lunch, and I fell asleep on the sofa.
By the end of the quarter, a general lassitude had settled over the whole office.
Doctors say that lassitude can be an early symptom of several vitamin deficiencies.
Many students complain of lassitude during the humid weeks before the monsoon finally breaks.
After the funeral she sank into a deep lassitude and could barely leave her bed.
tc: The fever had passed, but it left behind a ______ so heavy that she could barely climb the stairs.
'So heavy that she could barely climb the stairs' shows the blank means deep tiredness.
se: In the summer heat, a ______ settled over the town and the streets were nearly empty.
lethargy
Both 'lassitude' and 'lethargy' mean a lack of energy, explaining why the streets were empty.

m: deserving praise
x: Cleaning up the park every Saturday is a laudable habit that more neighbors should share.
The company made a laudable effort to cut its carbon emissions by half.
Her laudable attention to detail made her thesis one of the best in the department.
The government's aims are laudable, but critics say the plan lacks proper funding.
It was laudable of him to apologize first, even though she had started the argument.
tc: Although the project ultimately failed, the volunteers' ______ dedication earned them praise from everyone in the town.
'Earned them praise' shows the blank means deserving praise.
se: Raising money for flood victims is a ______ goal that deserves everyone's support.
commendable
Both 'laudable' and 'commendable' mean worthy of praise, so the sentence means the same.

m: sluggish, drowsy and lacking energy or enthusiasm
x: I always feel lethargic after a heavy lunch of rice and beef curry.
Sales have been lethargic this quarter, and the team is under pressure to find new clients.
Lack of sleep left me too lethargic to concentrate during the morning lecture.
Economists warned that the economy remained lethargic despite repeated cuts in interest rates.
Since losing his job, he has become lethargic and withdrawn, spending most days in bed.
tc: Normally full of energy, the puppy became ______ after its vaccination and slept most of the day.
'Normally full of energy' contrasts with the blank, and 'slept most of the day' confirms it means sluggish.
se: The heat made everyone ______, and few people bothered to leave the shade.
sluggish
Both 'lethargic' and 'sluggish' mean lacking energy, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: humor or lack of seriousness, especially when seriousness is expected
x: A little levity at the dinner table helped ease the tension after our argument.
His attempt at levity during the budget meeting fell flat with the finance director.
The professor's occasional levity kept students awake during long lectures on thermodynamics.
Reporters criticized the official's levity when discussing a disaster that had killed dozens of people.
Even at her father's funeral, she found moments of levity in sharing funny stories about him.
tc: The judge would not tolerate ______ in her courtroom; any joke, however mild, earned a sharp rebuke.
'Any joke, however mild' restates the blank, so it must mean light-hearted humor.
se: His ______ seemed out of place at such a solemn occasion.
flippancy
Both 'levity' and 'flippancy' mean a lack of seriousness, which is why it seemed out of place.

m: very talkative
x: My loquacious aunt can turn a five-minute phone call into an hour-long conversation.
The loquacious salesman talked for so long that I forgot what I had come to buy.
Loquacious students sometimes dominate seminar discussions, leaving quieter classmates no chance to speak.
The usually loquacious minister said very little when reporters asked about the scandal.
He became loquacious after a glass of wine, telling stories he had never shared before.
tc: Unlike her shy sister, who barely spoke, Nadia was ______, happily chatting with anyone who would listen.
'Unlike her shy sister, who barely spoke' sets up a contrast, and 'happily chatting' defines the blank.
se: The ______ taxi driver told us his entire life story before we reached the hotel.
talkative
Both 'loquacious' and 'talkative' describe someone who talks a lot, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: clearly expressed and easy to understand
x: My uncle gave me lucid directions to his village, and I didn't get lost once.
The consultant's lucid presentation helped the board grasp a complex financial problem in minutes.
Her textbook offers a lucid explanation of quantum mechanics for first-year undergraduates.
The report gave a lucid account of how the epidemic spread from city to city.
In a lucid letter, she explained exactly why she needed time apart, and he finally understood.
tc: Whereas his earlier papers were confusing and full of jargon, his latest article is remarkably ______ and easy to follow.
'Whereas' contrasts with 'confusing', and 'easy to follow' confirms the blank means clear.
se: The teacher's ______ explanation helped even the weakest students understand the theorem.
clear
Both 'lucid' and 'clear' describe an explanation that is easy to understand, so the sentence means the same.

m: giving off or full of light; bright and glowing
x: The luminous hands of my old watch let me read the time in the dark.
Our office lobby was redesigned with luminous panels that light up as visitors walk past.
Some deep-sea creatures are luminous, producing their own light to attract prey.
During the wedding season, whole streets in Old Dhaka become luminous with strings of colored lights.
Her face was luminous with happiness when she saw her parents waiting at the airport.
tc: In the pitch-black cave, only the ______ fungi on the walls gave off enough light to see by.
'Gave off enough light' in a 'pitch-black cave' shows the blank means glowing.
se: The bride's ______ smile lit up the entire room.
radiant
Both 'luminous' and 'radiant' describe a smile that seems to shine, so the meaning is the same.

m: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful
x: It was magnanimous of my sister to lend me her car after I had dented it last year.
The CEO was magnanimous in victory, publicly praising the rival firm that had lost the contract.
The professor made the magnanimous decision to list her student as first author on the paper.
After the war, the victorious nation adopted a magnanimous policy toward its former enemy.
He was magnanimous enough to forgive the friend who had spread rumors about him.
tc: Instead of gloating over his defeated rival, the champion was ______, praising his opponent's skill and courage.
'Instead of gloating' signals the opposite, and praising a defeated rival shows generosity of spirit.
se: In a ______ gesture, the winning candidate invited her opponent to join her cabinet.
generous
Both 'magnanimous' and 'generous' describe a big-hearted act toward a rival, so the sentence means the same.

m: easily shaped, influenced or changed
x: Children are malleable, so the habits they learn at home tend to stay with them for life.
The new team leader found her staff malleable and open to changing old routines.
Gold is highly malleable and can be hammered into sheets thinner than tissue paper.
Public opinion is more malleable than many politicians realize, shifting quickly with the news.
In his early twenties he was malleable, easily swayed by whatever his friends believed.
tc: Young minds are ______, which is why teachers have such a powerful influence on how children see the world.
'Which is why teachers have such a powerful influence' shows the blank means easily shaped.
se: Clay is ______ when wet but becomes hard and brittle once it dries.
pliable
Both 'malleable' and 'pliable' mean easily shaped, contrasting with 'hard and brittle'.

m: an independent-minded person who refuses to follow the usual rules or practices
x: My uncle was the family maverick who quit his bank job to open a roadside tea stall.
The company hired a maverick from a rival firm to shake up its slow-moving design team.
Once dismissed as a maverick, the scientist was later proved right about the cause of the disease.
The senator built a reputation as a maverick by voting against her own party on several key bills.
Her friends admired her as a maverick who lived exactly as she pleased.
tc: A true ______, the architect ignored every convention of her profession and designed buildings unlike anything else in the city.
'Ignored every convention of her profession' defines the blank as an independent nonconformist.
se: Known as a ______ in the industry, he refused to follow the strategies his competitors relied on.
nonconformist
Both 'maverick' and 'nonconformist' describe someone who rejects usual practices, so the meaning is the same.

m: not telling the truth; lying
x: The mendacious seller claimed the phone was brand new, but it was full of someone else's photos.
A mendacious report to the board hid the company's mounting losses for nearly two years.
The journal retracted the paper after reviewers exposed the author's mendacious claims about his results.
Voters grew tired of mendacious campaign ads that twisted the truth beyond recognition.
She finally left him after years of mendacious excuses about where he spent his evenings.
tc: Far from being honest, the witness proved ______, inventing details that were easily disproved by video footage.
'Far from being honest' and 'inventing details' show the blank means lying.
se: The politician's ______ statements about the budget fooled very few voters.
dishonest
Both 'mendacious' and 'dishonest' describe untrue statements, so the sentence means the same.

m: a complete change in form, character or appearance
x: After a year of yoga and healthy eating, my cousin underwent a remarkable metamorphosis.
The struggling company's metamorphosis into a tech giant took less than a decade.
In biology class we watched the metamorphosis of a caterpillar into a butterfly.
Dhaka's skyline has undergone a dramatic metamorphosis over the past thirty years.
Falling in love caused a metamorphosis in her; the shy girl became confident and outgoing.
tc: The neighborhood's ______ was so complete that former residents returning after twenty years could not recognize a single street.
Being unable to recognize a single street shows the blank means a total transformation.
se: The old warehouse underwent a ______ and reopened as a stylish art gallery.
transformation
Both 'metamorphosis' and 'transformation' mean a complete change in form, so the meaning is the same.

m: showing great attention to detail; extremely careful and precise
x: My mother keeps meticulous records of every taka she spends on groceries.
Our auditor is meticulous and catches errors that everyone else has missed.
Her meticulous research earned her a full scholarship for graduate study in Canada.
Detectives made a meticulous search of the apartment but found no sign of forced entry.
He was meticulous about remembering birthdays, and his friends loved him for it.
tc: Unlike his careless predecessor, the new accountant was ______, checking every figure twice before signing off.
'Unlike his careless predecessor' sets up a contrast, and 'checking every figure twice' defines the blank.
se: The surgeon's ______ preparation meant that the operation went exactly as planned.
painstaking
Both 'meticulous' and 'painstaking' describe extremely careful work, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a person who dislikes and distrusts other people
x: My neighbor is a bit of a misanthrope and only leaves his house to buy groceries.
Few colleagues liked the misanthrope in accounts who never said good morning to anyone.
Literature students often read Moliere's comedy about a misanthrope who despises the hypocrisy of society.
The reclusive billionaire was described in the press as a misanthrope who trusted no one.
Years of betrayal had turned him into a misanthrope who pushed away even those who loved him.
tc: A true ______, the old writer avoided parties, refused all visitors and declared that humanity was hopeless.
Avoiding people and declaring humanity hopeless defines the blank as someone who dislikes people.
se: Living alone in the forest, the bitter old ______ refused to speak to anyone from the village.
recluse
Both 'misanthrope' and 'recluse' fit someone who shuns other people, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: to make something less severe, serious or painful
x: Drinking plenty of water can help mitigate the effects of a long flight.
The company hired extra staff to mitigate the risk of delays during the busy season.
Engineers are building embankments to mitigate flood damage in coastal Bangladesh.
Students can mitigate exam stress by studying steadily rather than cramming the night before.
A sincere apology did little to mitigate her disappointment at being forgotten on her birthday.
tc: The new drug cannot cure the disease, but it does ______ the pain, making patients far more comfortable.
'Cannot cure' but 'making patients far more comfortable' shows the blank means to lessen.
se: The city planted thousands of trees to ______ the effects of the summer heat.
alleviate
Both 'mitigate' and 'alleviate' mean to make something less severe, so the sentence means the same.

m: to calm someone's anger or anxiety; to soothe
x: I bought my wife flowers to mollify her after I forgot our anniversary.
The airline offered free vouchers to mollify passengers whose flight had been canceled.
The professor tried to mollify anxious students by promising a generous grading curve.
The government's concessions did little to mollify protesters, who stayed in the streets for weeks.
Nothing he said could mollify his mother, who was furious that he had missed his sister's wedding.
tc: Hoping to ______ the furious customer, the manager offered a full refund and a sincere apology.
Offering a refund and apology to a 'furious customer' shows the aim was to calm him down.
se: The coach tried to ______ his angry players by promising them a day off.
placate
Both 'mollify' and 'placate' mean to calm someone's anger, so the meaning stays the same.

m: gloomy, sullen and unwilling to talk
x: My brother is always morose on Monday mornings and barely speaks before his second cup of tea.
The office grew morose after the announcement that this year's bonuses would be cut.
He sat morose in the back of the lecture hall, convinced that he had failed the midterm.
Morose fans trudged out of the stadium after Bangladesh lost the final by a single run.
After their quarrel, she remained morose and withdrawn for days, refusing even to answer his calls.
tc: Usually cheerful and chatty, Karim became ______ after losing his job, sitting silently at dinner every evening.
'Usually cheerful and chatty' contrasts with the blank, and 'sitting silently' shows it means gloomy.
se: The ______ teenager refused to talk to anyone after being grounded.
sullen
Both 'morose' and 'sullen' describe a gloomy, silent mood, so the sentence means the same.

m: ordinary and dull; lacking interest or excitement
x: Most of my weekend was taken up by mundane chores like laundry and paying bills.
Even exciting jobs involve plenty of mundane tasks, such as filling in expense reports.
Historians are increasingly interested in the mundane details of everyday life in the past.
The famous explorer's diaries are surprisingly mundane, full of notes about the weather and food.
She longed to escape her mundane routine and do something truly adventurous.
tc: Fans expected the celebrity's memoir to be thrilling, but it turned out to be a ______ record of meals and errands.
'Expected ... to be thrilling, but' sets up a contrast, so the blank means dull and ordinary.
se: He found the ______ work of data entry so boring that he quit after a week.
routine
Both 'mundane' and 'routine' describe dull, ordinary work, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: extremely generous, especially in giving money or gifts
x: Thanks to a munificent gift from a family friend, I was able to buy my first laptop.
The firm's munificent bonuses made it one of the most desirable employers in the industry.
A munificent donor funded twenty full scholarships for students from rural Bangladesh.
The museum's new wing was built with a munificent grant from a local philanthropist.
He was munificent with his time, always ready to help a friend move house or fix a computer.
tc: Unlike his stingy brother, the merchant was ______, giving away a large part of his fortune to the poor every year.
'Unlike his stingy brother' sets up a contrast, and giving away his fortune shows the blank means very generous.
se: The hospital thanked its ______ benefactor for the donation that paid for the new wing.
generous
Both 'munificent' and 'generous' describe a donor who gives freely, so the sentence means the same.

m: just coming into existence and beginning to develop
x: My nascent interest in cooking began when I had to feed myself during my first year abroad.
The startup is working in the nascent field of quantum computing.
Researchers are studying the nascent stages of language development in infants.
Investors are showing interest in the nascent electric-vehicle industry in Bangladesh.
Their nascent friendship grew stronger over long late-night conversations during the first semester.
tc: The company was still ______, having been founded only a few months earlier and employing just three people.
'Founded only a few months earlier' shows the blank means newly formed and just beginning.
se: The country's ______ democracy faces many challenges after decades of military rule.
emerging
Both 'nascent' and 'emerging' describe a democracy that is just beginning to develop, so the meaning is the same.

m: wicked or criminal, especially in a scheming, underhand way
x: My neighbour swore that the stray cat had nefarious plans for the goldfish in our garden pond.
Auditors uncovered a nefarious scheme in which two managers had been quietly diverting company funds into private accounts.
Our professor warned that data collected for research could easily be put to nefarious uses if it was left unprotected.
Police say the network used fake charities as a front for its nefarious activities, including money laundering and fraud.
She began to suspect that her charming new business partner had nefarious motives behind all his generosity.
tc: Far from being a harmless prank, the hacking was part of a ______ plot to steal thousands of customers' bank details.
'Far from being a harmless prank' and 'plot to steal' show that the blank must mean wicked or criminal.
se: Investigators believe the forged documents were created for ______ purposes rather than by simple mistake.
criminal
Both 'nefarious' and 'criminal' describe purposes that are wrongful and deliberate, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: to cancel out the effect of something or make it ineffective
x: Eating a whole box of doughnuts after the gym rather negates the point of the workout.
A single careless email to the client could negate months of patient relationship-building by our sales team.
A flaw in the control group effectively negated the results of the entire three-year study.
Critics argue that rising inflation has negated the benefit of the government's wage increase for most workers.
His heartfelt apology could not negate the hurt caused by years of broken promises to his family.
tc: The new medication works well on its own, but drinking alcohol can ______ its effects entirely, leaving patients with no relief.
'Works well on its own, but' and 'leaving patients with no relief' show the blank means to cancel out.
se: Constant late-night snacking will ______ any progress you make with your new diet.
undo
Both 'negate' and 'undo' mean to cancel out the progress, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: a beginner or novice in a skill, field, or activity
x: As a neophyte in the kitchen, I managed to burn the rice twice before finally getting it right.
Our firm pairs every neophyte with a senior mentor during the first six months on the job.
Even a neophyte in statistics can follow the author's clear explanation of regression analysis.
Political neophytes often underestimate how much fundraising a national campaign actually requires.
On our first date, he admitted he was a complete neophyte at dancing, which only made me like him more.
tc: Although she had never sailed before, the ______ quickly learned to handle the ropes as well as the seasoned crew.
'Had never sailed before' defines the blank as a beginner, in contrast with 'the seasoned crew'.
se: The software is designed so that even a ______ can build a simple website in under an hour.
novice
Both 'neophyte' and 'novice' mean a beginner, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action
x: My grandfather remains obdurate about never using a smartphone, no matter how often we try to persuade him.
Management stayed obdurate throughout the negotiations, rejecting every proposal the union put forward.
The committee's obdurate refusal to consider new evidence frustrated the young researcher.
Despite international pressure, the regime remained obdurate on the question of releasing political prisoners.
She tried for weeks to reconcile with her brother, but he was obdurate and would not even return her calls.
tc: No amount of pleading could move the ______ landlord, who insisted on evicting the family by Friday.
'No amount of pleading could move' shows the blank must mean stubborn and unyielding.
se: The chairman was ______ in his opposition to the merger, rejecting every compromise the board suggested.
inflexible
Both 'obdurate' and 'inflexible' describe someone who will not change his position, so the meaning is the same.

m: to make something deliberately unclear or confusing, often to hide the truth
x: Whenever I ask my teenage son where he was last night, he obfuscates with vague stories about just hanging out.
The memo was full of jargon that seemed designed to obfuscate the fact that jobs were being cut.
Good academic writing should clarify complex ideas, not obfuscate them behind dense, impenetrable prose.
Critics accused the ministry of obfuscating the true cost of the bridge project by spreading it across several budgets.
Rather than obfuscating her feelings, she finally told him plainly that she wanted to end the relationship.
tc: Instead of answering the question directly, the spokesperson tried to ______ the issue with a flood of irrelevant statistics.
'Instead of answering directly' and 'a flood of irrelevant statistics' show the blank means to make deliberately unclear.
se: The company's lawyers used complex language to ______ the terms of the contract so customers would not notice the hidden fees.
obscure
Both 'obfuscate' and 'obscure' mean to make the terms hard to understand, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: excessively eager to please or obey people in authority; fawning
x: The waiter's obsequious attention became irritating when he interrupted our conversation for the fifth time.
Nobody in the office respected him because of his obsequious habit of agreeing with everything the boss said.
Some graduate students feel pressure to be obsequious toward supervisors who control their funding and references.
The state newspaper's obsequious coverage of the ruling party left readers with little genuine information.
Her new boyfriend was so obsequious toward her parents that her father found him hard to trust.
tc: Unlike his ______ colleagues, who praised every idea the director proposed, Rahim was willing to voice honest disagreement.
'Unlike' and 'praised every idea the director proposed' show the blank means excessively eager to please.
se: The courtiers were ______ in the king's presence, bowing low and laughing at every joke he made.
fawning
Both 'obsequious' and 'fawning' describe exaggerated eagerness to please, so the sentence means the same.

m: stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or behaviour despite persuasion
x: My obstinate little sister refused to wear a raincoat, even though the monsoon clouds were rolling in.
Our project stalled because one obstinate manager refused to approve any changes to the original design.
Professor Karim was obstinate in defending his theory, even after several experiments failed to support it.
Negotiators described both sides as obstinate, with neither willing to budge on the border question.
He can be obstinate when he is hurt, so it took days before he would even talk about the argument.
tc: Though everyone at the table pointed out the flaw in his plan, the ______ captain refused to change course.
'Though everyone pointed out the flaw' and 'refused to change course' show the blank means stubborn.
se: My father is too ______ to admit that he needs reading glasses.
stubborn
Both 'obstinate' and 'stubborn' mean unwilling to give in, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to remove a need or difficulty in advance; to make something unnecessary
x: Keeping a small umbrella in your bag obviates the need to rush for shelter every time it rains.
The new software obviates the tedious manual data entry our team used to do every Friday.
Online access to archives has obviated many of the long trips historians once had to make to distant libraries.
Engineers hope the new flood barriers will obviate the need to evacuate low-lying neighbourhoods every spring.
A frank conversation early on would have obviated months of resentment between the two friends.
tc: Because the new vaccine provides lifelong immunity, it should ______ the need for annual booster shots.
'Provides lifelong immunity' explains why boosters would become unnecessary, so the blank means to make unnecessary.
se: A clear set of written instructions would ______ most of the confusion that new employees face.
prevent
Both 'obviate' and 'prevent' mean to stop the confusion before it arises, so the meaning is the same.

m: annoyingly eager to give unwanted advice or assert authority, especially in trivial matters
x: An officious neighbour knocked on our door to complain that our recycling bin was facing the wrong way.
The officious receptionist insisted that I fill out three forms before she would even tell me the manager's name.
One officious librarian scolded students for whispering, even in the rooms set aside for group study.
Travellers complained of officious border guards who searched their bags repeatedly for no obvious reason.
Her officious mother-in-law kept rearranging the kitchen cupboards and offering advice nobody had asked for.
tc: Visitors found the museum guard ______, constantly telling them where to stand and giving lectures nobody had requested.
'Constantly telling them where to stand' and 'lectures nobody had requested' describe someone annoyingly interfering.
se: Tired of his ______ coworker checking whether he had followed every minor rule, Karim asked to change desks.
meddlesome
Both 'officious' and 'meddlesome' describe someone who interferes where he is not wanted, so the meaning is the same.

m: involving a heavy burden, great effort, or difficulty
x: Looking after three young children while working full-time is an onerous task for any parent.
Many small businesses find the new tax reporting requirements onerous and expensive to meet.
The scholarship came with onerous conditions, including fifteen hours of unpaid lab work every week.
The loan's onerous repayment terms left the country struggling to fund basic public services.
Caring for his ailing father became less onerous once his siblings agreed to share the responsibility.
tc: What had seemed a simple favour soon became ______, consuming every weekend for three months.
The contrast between 'a simple favour' and 'consuming every weekend' shows the blank means burdensome.
se: Filling out the visa paperwork was so ______ that several applicants gave up halfway through.
burdensome
Both 'onerous' and 'burdensome' mean heavy and difficult to bear, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: harsh public criticism or disgrace that follows shameful conduct
x: After posting a rude review of the local bakery, he faced the opprobrium of the entire neighbourhood group chat.
The bank attracted widespread opprobrium for awarding huge bonuses while laying off hundreds of staff.
Her falsified data brought opprobrium not only on her but on everyone in the laboratory.
Despite international opprobrium, the government pressed ahead with building the controversial dam.
He was willing to endure his family's opprobrium rather than marry someone he did not love.
tc: Rather than earning the praise he expected, the senator's speech drew nothing but ______ from both parties.
'Rather than earning the praise' signals that the blank means the opposite: harsh criticism.
se: The club's decision to sell tickets at triple the usual price drew ______ from fans across the country.
condemnation
Both 'opprobrium' and 'condemnation' mean strong public criticism, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to become rigid and unable to change or develop
x: Without new hobbies or friends, my uncle's daily routine began to ossify after he retired.
Companies that stop listening to younger employees risk letting their culture ossify.
Some critics fear that the discipline has ossified around a handful of theories from the 1970s.
Over several decades, the party's leadership ossified into a small circle that resisted any reform.
Their marriage had ossified into polite routine, with neither partner willing to talk about real feelings.
tc: Unless the institution welcomes fresh ideas, its practices will ______ and it will fall behind more flexible rivals.
The contrast with 'fresh ideas' and 'more flexible rivals' shows the blank means to become rigid.
se: Left unchallenged, prejudices tend to ______ over time into beliefs that seem impossible to shift.
harden
Both 'ossify' and 'harden' mean to become fixed and rigid, so the sentence means the same.

m: showy in a way meant to impress others with wealth or importance
x: Some Dhaka families spend fortunes on ostentatious weddings with thousands of guests and several nights of feasting.
He arrived at the interview wearing an ostentatious gold watch that seemed out of place in the modest office.
Her scholarly prose is clear and modest, free of the ostentatious jargon common in her field.
Residents condemned the mayor's ostentatious new office at a time when the city was cutting school budgets.
She loved his quiet kindness, which stood in contrast to his brother's ostentatious displays of generosity.
tc: Although the family was extremely wealthy, their home was surprisingly plain, without any ______ decoration.
'Although extremely wealthy' and 'surprisingly plain' show the blank means showy.
se: With its gold-plated pillars and giant chandeliers, the new hotel lobby struck many guests as ______.
showy
Both 'ostentatious' and 'showy' describe a display meant to impress, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: a person or thing regarded as a perfect example of a particular quality
x: My aunt is a paragon of patience; I have never once seen her lose her temper with her five children.
The new manager was hailed as a paragon of efficiency after she cut processing times in half.
Our textbook presents the ancient city as a paragon of urban planning, with its grid streets and drainage system.
The country was once held up as a paragon of stability, but recent unrest has damaged that image.
He is no paragon of virtue, but he has always been loyal to the people he loves.
tc: Far from being a careless driver, my father is a ______ of caution who always checks his mirrors twice.
'Far from being a careless driver' and 'always checks his mirrors twice' show the blank means a perfect example.
se: Our grandmother was a ______ of generosity, always feeding anyone who came to her door.
model
Both 'paragon' and 'model' mean an ideal example of a quality, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: strongly and often unfairly supporting one party, cause, or person
x: Family dinners became tense whenever my two partisan uncles started arguing about the election.
Staff accused the hiring committee of being partisan when it favoured candidates from the director's old university.
A good historian tries to avoid partisan accounts and weigh evidence from all sides fairly.
Partisan bickering in parliament has delayed the flood relief bill for nearly three months.
Their friendship survived years of partisan disagreement because they agreed never to discuss politics on holidays.
tc: Rather than offering a balanced analysis, the newspaper's coverage was openly ______, praising one party and mocking the other.
'Rather than offering a balanced analysis' and 'praising one party and mocking the other' show the blank means biased.
se: Viewers complained that the debate moderator was ______, interrupting one candidate far more often than the other.
biased
Both 'partisan' and 'biased' mean unfairly favouring one side, so the sentence means the same.

m: the presence of something in only small or insufficient amounts; scarcity
x: Given the paucity of vegetables in the fridge, we ordered pizza instead of cooking dinner.
The startup struggled because of a paucity of experienced engineers willing to work for low salaries.
A paucity of reliable data on rural health makes it hard for researchers to draw firm conclusions.
Aid workers warned that a paucity of clean water could lead to outbreaks of cholera in the camps.
She was hurt by the paucity of affection in her father's letters, which read more like business reports.
tc: Because of the ______ of fossil evidence from that period, scientists can only guess what early mammals looked like.
'Can only guess' shows there is too little evidence, so the blank means scarcity.
se: Historians are frustrated by the ______ of written records from the village before 1900.
scarcity
Both 'paucity' and 'scarcity' mean too small an amount, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: too concerned with minor details or rules, often to show off one's learning
x: My friend is so pedantic that he corrected the grammar on a birthday card I gave him.
The editor's pedantic comments about comma placement distracted from the real problems in the report.
Students found the lecturer pedantic, since he spent most of each class correcting their pronunciation of Latin terms.
Critics said the court's pedantic reading of the law ignored the obvious intention behind it.
I love her, but she can be pedantic when we argue, pointing out that I said 'always' when I meant 'often'.
tc: His ______ insistence on correcting every tiny factual slip made the friendly discussion feel like an exam.
'Correcting every tiny factual slip' describes excessive attention to minor details, which defines the blank.
se: The reviewer was criticized for being ______, focusing on minor spelling slips instead of the book's argument.
fussy
Both 'pedantic' and 'fussy' describe someone overly concerned with small details, so the meaning stays the same.

m: a strong liking for something or a habitual tendency to do it
x: My roommate has a penchant for spicy food and adds chilli flakes to almost everything she cooks.
Our director's penchant for last-minute changes means we rarely finish a presentation before midnight.
As a schoolboy, he showed a penchant for mathematics long before he chose to study engineering.
The novelist is known for her penchant for complex plots and unreliable narrators.
His penchant for grand romantic gestures delighted her at first but later felt a little overwhelming.
tc: Given her ______ for adventure, no one was surprised when she quit her desk job to trek across the Himalayas.
'No one was surprised' that she chose an adventurous trek, so the blank means a strong liking.
se: Ever since childhood, Tanvir has had a ______ for taking apart radios to see how they work.
fondness
Both 'penchant' and 'fondness' mean a strong liking, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: extreme poverty; destitution
x: After losing his job and savings, he spent his final years in penury, living in a single rented room.
The factory's sudden collapse plunged hundreds of workers and their families into penury.
Her thesis documents the penury of mill workers in nineteenth-century Manchester.
Rising food prices have pushed millions of families from modest comfort toward penury.
She never forgot the penury of her childhood, which made her careful with every taka she earned.
tc: Once one of the richest merchants in the city, he ended his life in ______, unable even to pay for his own funeral.
The contrast with 'one of the richest merchants' and 'unable to pay for his own funeral' shows the blank means extreme poverty.
se: The novel follows a once-wealthy family that is reduced to ______ after a series of bad investments.
destitution
Both 'penury' and 'destitution' mean extreme poverty, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: lasting for a very long time or constantly recurring
x: Finding a parking space near the market is a perennial headache for residents of our street.
Late expense reports are a perennial complaint from the finance department.
The debate over nature versus nurture remains a perennial topic in psychology seminars.
Flooding is a perennial problem in low-lying parts of the city during the rainy season.
Their perennial disagreement about where to spend the holidays flares up again every December.
tc: Unlike passing fashions that disappear after a season, these classic designs have ______ appeal.
'Unlike passing fashions that disappear after a season' shows the blank means long-lasting.
se: Traffic congestion is a ______ problem that every new city government promises to solve.
persistent
Both 'perennial' and 'persistent' describe a problem that keeps continuing, so the meaning is the same.

m: deceitful and untrustworthy; guilty of betraying trust
x: I felt betrayed when my perfidious roommate told everyone the secret I had shared only with him.
Our perfidious accountant had been selling confidential client data to a competitor for years.
The epic portrays the general as a perfidious ally who switched sides the moment the battle turned.
Many citizens viewed the treaty violation as a perfidious act that destroyed decades of trust.
Discovering her partner's perfidious affair left her unable to trust anyone for a long time.
tc: Although he had sworn to protect the king, the ______ knight secretly opened the castle gates to the enemy.
'Although he had sworn to protect the king' contrasts with his betrayal, so the blank means treacherous.
se: The hero of the novel is ruined by a ______ friend who sells his plans to the enemy.
treacherous
Both 'perfidious' and 'treacherous' describe someone who betrays trust, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: done with minimal effort or care, merely as a routine duty
x: He gave the dishes a perfunctory rinse and left them, still greasy, on the rack.
My manager's perfunctory review of the report missed several serious errors.
The examiner gave only a perfunctory glance at my thesis before signing the approval form.
Inspectors carried out a perfunctory check of the building, which collapsed six months later.
Her perfunctory 'love you' at the end of the call told him she was still upset.
tc: Expecting a thorough investigation, the victims were outraged by the police's ______ inquiry, which lasted less than an hour.
'Expecting a thorough investigation' and 'lasted less than an hour' show the blank means done with little effort.
se: The doctor gave me only a ______ examination before writing a prescription and calling the next patient.
cursory
Both 'perfunctory' and 'cursory' mean quick and careless, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: allowing liquids or gases to pass through; open to outside influence
x: Our tent turned out to be permeable, and we woke up soaked after the first night of rain.
At a small startup, the line between work and personal time is often highly permeable.
Students placed the cells in salt water to test how permeable their membranes were.
Engineers recommend permeable pavements that let rainwater soak into the ground instead of flooding the streets.
He found that the boundaries in his family were permeable, with everyone's problems quickly becoming everyone else's.
tc: Unlike clay, which holds water at the surface, sandy soil is highly ______, letting rain drain away quickly.
'Unlike clay, which holds water' and 'letting rain drain away' show the blank means allowing liquid to pass through.
se: The jacket's fabric proved surprisingly ______, letting the rain soak straight through to my shirt.
porous
Both 'permeable' and 'porous' mean letting water pass through, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: spreading widely through every part of a place, group, or thing
x: The smell of frying onions was pervasive, reaching every room in the apartment.
A pervasive culture of overwork left many employees exhausted and close to quitting.
Researchers studied the pervasive influence of social media on how teenagers form friendships.
Corruption remains pervasive in the sector, despite several high-profile arrests.
He struggled with a pervasive sense of loneliness after moving abroad for his master's degree.
tc: Far from being confined to a few departments, the problem of low morale was ______ across the entire organization.
'Far from being confined to a few departments' shows the blank means spread throughout.
se: Fear of the new disease was ______ in the city, affecting how people shopped, travelled, and worked.
widespread
Both 'pervasive' and 'widespread' mean spread throughout, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: calm and unemotional by temperament; not easily excited or upset
x: Even when the power went out during dinner, my phlegmatic husband simply lit a candle and kept eating.
A phlegmatic project manager is invaluable when deadlines slip and everyone else starts to panic.
My phlegmatic examiner showed no reaction at all as I stumbled through my answer.
The captain's phlegmatic response to the storm reassured the frightened passengers.
She sometimes wished her phlegmatic boyfriend would show a little more excitement about their plans.
tc: While her sister panicked at every small setback, Nadia was ______, rarely showing alarm even in a crisis.
'While her sister panicked' sets up a contrast, and 'rarely showing alarm' defines the blank as calm.
se: Known for his ______ nature, the pilot quietly informed passengers that one engine had failed.
calm
Both 'phlegmatic' and 'calm' describe someone who stays unruffled, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to make someone less angry or hostile, usually by doing something to please them
x: I tried to placate my crying nephew with ice cream, but he only wanted his mother.
The airline offered free vouchers to placate passengers who had been stuck at the gate for six hours.
The university extended the deadline to placate students who complained about the server outage.
The government's small concessions failed to placate the protesters, who stayed in the streets.
He bought her flowers to placate her after forgetting their anniversary, but she wanted an apology.
tc: The manager offered a full refund in an attempt to ______ the furious customer, who had threatened to post a scathing review.
Offering a refund to a 'furious customer' shows the blank means to calm someone's anger.
se: The company raised salaries slightly to ______ workers who were threatening to strike.
appease
Both 'placate' and 'appease' mean to calm discontent by giving something, so the meaning is the same.

m: a remark used so often that it has become dull and meaningless
x: When my exam results were poor, my uncle offered only the platitude that everything happens for a reason.
The CEO's speech was full of platitudes about teamwork but said nothing about the layoffs.
My essay was marked down for relying on platitudes instead of careful analysis.
Voters are tired of politicians who answer hard questions with comforting platitudes.
Grieving people often need someone to listen, not platitudes about time healing all wounds.
tc: Instead of offering fresh ideas, the report simply repeated the familiar ______ that people are our greatest asset.
'Instead of offering fresh ideas' and 'familiar' show the blank means an overused, unoriginal remark.
se: Rather than giving real advice, the counsellor offered the tired ______ that it would all work out in the end.
cliché
Both 'platitude' and 'cliché' mean an overused, empty remark, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: an excessive amount of something; more than is needed
x: The new supermarket offers a plethora of cereal brands, which makes choosing breakfast oddly stressful.
Every Monday morning, our inbox fills with a plethora of meeting invitations.
Students now have a plethora of online resources, from video lectures to practice tests.
The city faces a plethora of problems, including traffic, pollution, and a shortage of affordable housing.
After the breakup, she received a plethora of well-meaning advice from friends she barely spoke to.
tc: Unlike last year, when there were too few applicants, this year the department received a ______ of applications.
'Unlike last year, when there were too few' signals a contrast, so the blank means an overabundance.
se: Shoppers can feel overwhelmed by the ______ of options available in a modern supermarket.
glut
Both 'plethora' and 'glut' mean an excessive amount, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to fall straight down very quickly; to decrease rapidly in value or amount
x: My phone slipped from my hand and plummeted down the stairwell, landing with a sickening crack.
Sales plummeted after a rival launched a cheaper version of our product.
Exam scores plummeted in the semester after the school cut its tutoring programme.
The currency plummeted against the dollar after the central bank's surprise announcement.
His confidence plummeted when his girlfriend said she needed time to think about their future.
tc: Once the scandal broke, the company's share price began to ______, losing half its value in a single afternoon.
'Losing half its value in a single afternoon' shows the blank means to fall sharply.
se: Temperatures in the desert can ______ after sunset, so campers should bring warm clothing.
plunge
Both 'plummet' and 'plunge' mean to drop suddenly and steeply, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: dealing with problems sensibly and realistically, based on practical rather than theoretical considerations
x: Instead of buying a new car, we took the pragmatic option and repaired the old one.
Our team leader is pragmatic; she prefers a working solution today over a perfect one next year.
Engineering students learn to take a pragmatic approach, balancing ideal designs against cost and time.
Faced with a budget crisis, the city council made pragmatic cuts rather than ideological ones.
Choosing a university near home was a pragmatic decision, since it meant he could still help his parents.
tc: Unlike her idealistic colleagues, who wanted to rebuild the whole system, Farah took a ______ view and focused on fixes that could be made immediately.
'Unlike her idealistic colleagues' and 'fixes that could be made immediately' show the blank means practical.
se: Rather than chasing a perfect design, the engineers adopted a ______ approach and used parts that were already available.
practical
Both 'pragmatic' and 'practical' describe a realistic, workable approach, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: not secure or stable; dangerously likely to fall, collapse, or fail
x: Our cat sat in a precarious position on the edge of the bookshelf, eyeing the vase below.
Many freelancers live on precarious incomes that change dramatically from month to month.
Without a scholarship, his place in the doctoral programme was precarious.
The ceasefire remains precarious, and both sides accuse each other of violations.
Their friendship was in a precarious state after the argument over money.
tc: With only a one-seat majority, the government's hold on power is ______, and a single defection could bring it down.
'Only a one-seat majority' and 'a single defection could bring it down' show the blank means insecure.
se: The ladder looked ______, balanced on two uneven bricks in the muddy ground.
unstable
Both 'precarious' and 'unstable' mean likely to fall, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to cause something, usually bad, to happen suddenly or sooner than expected
x: A minor disagreement over the TV remote precipitated a full-blown family argument.
The chief executive's sudden resignation precipitated a sharp fall in the company's share price.
Discovering a calculation error precipitated a complete review of the research team's findings.
Economists warn that rising interest rates could precipitate a recession next year.
Losing his job precipitated a period of depression that lasted nearly a year.
tc: Although tensions had been building for months, a single border incident was enough to ______ open conflict.
'Tensions had been building' and 'a single incident was enough' show the blank means to bring about suddenly.
se: Experts fear that the bank's collapse could ______ a wider financial crisis across the region.
trigger
Both 'precipitate' and 'trigger' mean to set off a sudden event, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: a person or thing that comes before and leads to a later, more developed one
x: A tickle in my throat is usually a precursor to a full-blown cold.
The small pilot project was a precursor to the company-wide software rollout.
Historians regard early printing presses as a precursor of today's mass media.
Seismologists study small tremors that may be precursors of larger earthquakes.
Their long late-night phone calls turned out to be a precursor to the romance that followed.
tc: Just as dark clouds often signal rain, these small market fluctuations may be a ______ of a larger downturn.
The comparison with clouds that 'signal rain' shows the blank means something that comes before and signals what follows.
se: The abacus is sometimes described as a ______ of the modern calculator.
forerunner
Both 'precursor' and 'forerunner' mean an earlier version that led to a later one, so the meaning is the same.

m: overstepping proper limits by being too confident or taking too much for granted
x: It was presumptuous of our guest to rearrange the living room furniture without asking.
My colleague made the presumptuous assumption that he would lead the project before the manager had decided.
It would be presumptuous to claim that one small study has solved such a complex problem.
Commentators called the party's victory speech presumptuous, since votes were still being counted.
Would it be presumptuous of me to invite her to meet my parents after only two dates?
tc: Although he had only just been hired, the ______ intern began telling senior partners how to run the firm.
'Although he had only just been hired' contrasts with his bold behaviour, so the blank means overstepping limits.
se: It seemed ______ of him to book a table for two before she had even agreed to the date.
forward
Both 'presumptuous' and 'forward' mean overly bold in assuming something, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to speak or act evasively in order to avoid telling the truth
x: When I asked my son whether he had finished his homework, he began to prevaricate about being mostly done.
Rather than prevaricate, the manager admitted that the project was months behind schedule.
Asked whether he had copied the essay, the student prevaricated, claiming he could not remember his sources.
The minister prevaricated for weeks before finally admitting that the figures had been wrong.
She knew he was prevaricating when he gave three different explanations for why he had come home late.
tc: Instead of giving a straight answer, the witness continued to ______, offering vague replies that avoided the question.
'Instead of giving a straight answer' and 'vague replies that avoided the question' define the blank as being evasive.
se: When pressed about the missing funds, the treasurer began to ______, giving answers that were deliberately vague.
equivocate
Both 'prevaricate' and 'equivocate' mean to avoid the truth with evasive language, so the meaning is the same.

m: in its original, unspoiled condition; perfectly clean and fresh
x: My mother keeps the front room in pristine condition, reserved strictly for guests.
The used laptop I bought online arrived in pristine condition, without a single scratch.
Biologists collected samples from a pristine forest that had never been logged.
Tourism threatens the island's pristine beaches, where plastic waste is starting to wash up.
He kept her old letters in pristine shape, as if they were the most precious things he owned.
tc: Although the house was over a century old, its original woodwork was ______, as if it had been installed yesterday.
'Although over a century old' and 'as if installed yesterday' show the blank means in perfect original condition.
se: Collectors pay huge sums for comic books that are still in ______ condition.
immaculate
Both 'pristine' and 'immaculate' mean perfectly clean and undamaged, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: strong moral principles; complete honesty and decency
x: Our local shopkeeper is known for his probity; he once ran after me to return extra change.
The firm hires auditors of unquestioned probity to review its accounts each year.
The committee investigating the research grant found nothing to cast doubt on the scientist's probity.
Voters increasingly demand financial probity from those who manage public funds.
Her father's probity shaped her values, teaching her never to lie even when it was easier.
tc: The judge's reputation for ______ was so strong that even her critics never suggested she could be bribed.
'Never suggested she could be bribed' points to a reputation for honesty, which defines the blank.
se: Investors trusted the fund manager because of his long record of ______ and careful accounting.
integrity
Both 'probity' and 'integrity' mean strong honesty, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: spending money or resources recklessly; wastefully extravagant
x: My prodigal cousin spent his entire first salary on designer sneakers within a week.
The board criticized the department's prodigal use of company funds on luxury travel.
As a student, he was prodigal with his time, wasting whole semesters before he finally buckled down.
Critics accused the government of being prodigal with taxpayers' money on vanity projects.
His father forgave him for his prodigal ways and welcomed him back into the family business.
tc: Unlike her ______ brother, who wasted his inheritance within a year, Mitu saved every penny she received.
'Unlike' and 'wasted his inheritance within a year' show the blank means wastefully extravagant.
se: The new finance minister promised to end the government's ______ spending on unnecessary projects.
wasteful
Both 'prodigal' and 'wasteful' describe reckless spending, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: remarkably or impressively great in size, amount, or degree
x: My little brother has a prodigious appetite and can eat four plates of biryani at a wedding.
She completed a prodigious amount of work during her first month at the firm.
The young mathematician displayed a prodigious talent for solving problems that stumped her professors.
Building the bridge required a prodigious effort from thousands of engineers and workers.
His prodigious memory for birthdays made him everyone's favourite uncle.
tc: Though he was only twelve, the boy had a ______ ability to memorize entire books after a single reading.
'Though he was only twelve' and 'memorize entire books after a single reading' show the blank means remarkably great.
se: The athlete's ______ strength allowed her to lift twice her own body weight.
phenomenal
Both 'prodigious' and 'phenomenal' mean extraordinarily great, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: very great or intense; showing deep insight or understanding
x: Moving to a new city had a profound effect on my daily routine and sense of independence.
The merger brought profound changes to the way our department operated.
Her lecture offered a profound insight into how language shapes the way we think.
The pandemic had a profound impact on education systems around the world.
He felt a profound sense of loss after his grandmother died last winter.
tc: Far from being superficial, the novel offers ______ reflections on grief, memory, and forgiveness.
'Far from being superficial' signals that the blank means deep and insightful.
se: The discovery of antibiotics had a ______ effect on modern medicine.
far-reaching
Both 'profound' and 'far-reaching' describe a very great effect, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: plentiful or abundant; given or expressed very freely
x: The waiter offered profuse apologies after spilling tea all over my shirt.
She received profuse thanks from her colleagues for covering their shifts over the holidays.
In the clinical case study, the patient's profuse sweating prompted doctors to test for infection.
Unusually heavy rains brought profuse blooms to the normally barren desert this spring.
His profuse compliments made her suspect that he wanted something from her.
tc: Although the shrub produced only a few flowers last year, this spring its blossoms were ______, covering every branch.
'Although only a few flowers last year' and 'covering every branch' show the blank means abundant.
se: The guests were embarrassed by their host's ______ apologies for serving dinner a few minutes late.
effusive
Both 'profuse' and 'effusive' describe apologies poured out excessively, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to increase rapidly in number; to multiply or spread quickly
x: Coffee shops have proliferated in our neighbourhood, with three new ones opening this year alone.
Since the reorganization, meetings have proliferated until there is barely any time left for actual work.
Cancer cells proliferate uncontrollably, which is why early detection matters so much.
Fake news stories tend to proliferate on social media during election campaigns.
Small misunderstandings proliferated between them once they stopped talking openly.
tc: Once the regulations were relaxed, small private colleges began to ______, and dozens opened within a few years.
'Dozens opened within a few years' shows the blank means to increase rapidly in number.
se: Weeds will quickly ______ in the garden if you stop pulling them out each week.
multiply
Both 'proliferate' and 'multiply' mean to increase rapidly in number, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: a natural tendency to behave in a particular way
x: Our dog has an unfortunate propensity to chew shoes whenever we leave her alone.
His propensity for missing deadlines eventually cost him the promotion.
Researchers studied whether a propensity for risk-taking is shaped more by genes or by upbringing.
Low-lying coastal cities have a greater propensity to flood as sea levels rise.
She has a propensity to apologize too often, even when she has done nothing wrong.
tc: Given his ______ to exaggerate, nobody believed him when he said he had caught a fish as big as a car.
'Nobody believed him' suggests his habit of exaggerating, so the blank means a natural tendency.
se: Teenagers often have a ______ to take risks that most adults would avoid.
tendency
Both 'propensity' and 'tendency' mean a natural inclination, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to win or regain someone's favour by doing something that pleases them
x: I brought my sister her favourite sweets to propitiate her after borrowing her laptop without asking.
The firm offered a large discount to propitiate a major client angered by the delayed shipment.
Anthropologists study rituals that ancient farmers performed to propitiate the gods of rain.
The government cut fuel taxes in an effort to propitiate voters before the election.
He tried to propitiate his in-laws by learning to cook their favourite dishes.
tc: Fearing the anger of the spirits, the villagers left offerings at the shrine to ______ them before planting season.
'Fearing the anger of the spirits' and 'left offerings' show the blank means to win their favour.
se: The young king sent lavish gifts to ______ his powerful neighbour and avoid war.
appease
Both 'propitiate' and 'appease' mean to win favour and soften hostility, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: behaviour that follows accepted standards of what is correct or morally proper
x: My grandmother was a stickler for propriety and insisted that we never put our elbows on the dinner table.
Colleagues raised questions about the propriety of the director hiring his own nephew.
The ethics board reviewed the propriety of using patient data without explicit consent.
Opposition leaders questioned the propriety of a minister accepting free flights from a construction company.
Out of a sense of propriety, he waited a full year after his divorce before dating again.
tc: Although the guests were close friends, the formal dinner was conducted with strict ______, and no one dared tell a joke.
'Formal dinner' and 'no one dared tell a joke' show the blank means correct, proper behaviour.
se: Victorian novels often depict characters who are obsessed with social ______ and terrified of scandal.
decorum
Both 'propriety' and 'decorum' mean conformity to accepted standards of behaviour, so the meaning is the same.

m: to forbid something officially, especially by law or rule
x: Our building's rules proscribe pets, so we had to find a new home for the kitten.
Company policy proscribes accepting gifts from suppliers worth more than fifty dollars.
The university's honour code strictly proscribes any collaboration on take-home exams.
The international treaty proscribes the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances.
Her religion proscribes alcohol, so she happily drank juice while her friends ordered wine.
tc: Rather than merely discouraging the practice, the new regulations explicitly ______ it, making violations punishable by heavy fines.
'Rather than merely discouraging' and 'punishable by heavy fines' show the blank means to forbid.
se: Many schools ______ the use of mobile phones during exams.
prohibit
Both 'proscribe' and 'prohibit' mean to forbid officially, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: having a sharp, strong smell or taste; (of remarks) sharply critical

Someone left a pungent cheese in the office fridge, and nobody could eat lunch in peace.
Our chemistry lab had a pungent odour after a student accidentally spilled ammonia.
The columnist is known for her pungent criticism of wasteful government spending.
His pungent remarks about her cooking hurt more than he realized.
tc: Unlike the mild onions grown in the valley, these wild ones are so ______ that their smell brings tears to your eyes.
'Unlike the mild onions' and 'brings tears to your eyes' show the blank means sharply strong in smell.
se: A ______ smell of burning rubber drifted from the factory chimney.
acrid
Both 'pungent' and 'acrid' describe a sharp, strong smell, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to argue or raise objections about a trivial matter
x: My brother and I quibbled over who had been given the bigger slice of cake.
