Reviewers quibbled with minor details of the methodology but praised the study overall.
Lawmakers quibbled over a single clause while the larger reform bill stalled.
They often quibbled about trivial things, like which way the toilet paper should hang.
tc: The overall plan was excellent, so it seemed petty to ______ about the font used on the cover page.
'It seemed petty' and the trivial matter of 'the font' show the blank means to object over something minor.
se: Rather than ______ over a few dollars, the buyer simply agreed to the seller's price.
bicker
Both 'quibble' and 'bicker' mean to argue over something petty, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: in a state of inactivity or rest; temporarily dormant
x: Once the baby finally fell asleep, the house was quiescent for the first time all day.
Trading remained quiescent through the holiday week, with very few deals being made.
After a week of exams, our usually noisy hostel was strangely quiescent.
The volcano has been quiescent for centuries, but scientists continue to monitor it closely.
His old jealousy, quiescent for years, flared up when she mentioned her former boyfriend.
tc: The virus can remain ______ in the body for years before suddenly becoming active again.
'Before suddenly becoming active again' shows the blank means inactive or dormant.
se: The rebel movement was ______ for nearly a decade before violence broke out again.
dormant
Both 'quiescent' and 'dormant' mean temporarily inactive, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: stubbornly uncooperative toward authority, rules, or control
x: Getting my recalcitrant toddler into his car seat each morning is a daily battle.
Our project leader struggled to manage a recalcitrant team that ignored every new procedure.
Teachers devised creative strategies for engaging recalcitrant students who refused to participate.
The central government faced recalcitrant provinces that refused to implement the new tax.
He became recalcitrant whenever his parents mentioned marriage, changing the subject immediately.
tc: Unlike his cooperative classmates, the ______ boy refused to follow even the simplest instructions.
'Unlike his cooperative classmates' and 'refused to follow even the simplest instructions' show the blank means stubbornly uncooperative.
se: The coach struggled to discipline a few ______ players who skipped practice and ignored team rules.
unruly
Both 'recalcitrant' and 'unruly' describe people who resist discipline, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to publicly withdraw a statement or belief that one previously held
x: After a week of online backlash, the blogger recanted his claim that the vaccine caused infertility.
Despite pressure from her manager, the analyst refused to recant her criticism of the flawed sales forecast.
Galileo was forced to recant his view that the Earth moves around the Sun.
The key witness recanted his testimony, telling the court he had been threatened into lying.
Even when his friends laughed at him, Rafi would not recant his belief that Bangladesh could win the World Cup.
tc: Having insisted for years that his experiment was flawless, the scientist was finally forced to ______ when other labs failed to reproduce his results.
'Having insisted for years' together with the failed replications shows he had to take back his earlier claim.
se: Faced with overwhelming evidence, the witness decided to ______ her earlier statement.
retract
Both 'recant' and 'retract' mean to formally take back a statement, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: a person who lives alone and deliberately avoids the company of other people
x: My neighbour became something of a recluse after his wife died, rarely leaving the house except for groceries.
Once a sociable team leader, she turned into a recluse who worked from home and skipped every office party.
The novelist lived as a recluse for decades, refusing interviews and answering fan letters only through his lawyer.
Researchers found that older adults who become recluses face a far higher risk of depression and heart disease.
I'm not a recluse; I just need a quiet weekend now and then to recharge.
tc: Far from being the party-loving celebrity the tabloids imagined, the singer was a ______ who had not left her country estate in years.
'Far from being the party-loving celebrity' and 'had not left her country estate in years' point to someone who shuns company.
se: After retiring, the old professor lived like a ______, seeing no one but his housekeeper.
hermit
A 'recluse' and a 'hermit' are both people who withdraw from society, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: little known or obscure; understood only by people with specialized knowledge
x: His lecture on medieval tax law was so recondite that half the students stopped taking notes.
The contract was full of recondite legal terms that our team needed a lawyer to interpret.
She enjoys recondite trivia, like the names of extinct languages once spoken in the Andes.
What was once a recondite branch of mathematics now underpins the encryption that secures online banking.
He tried to impress her with recondite references to French poets, but she just found him pretentious.
tc: Although the professor's research was ______, understood by perhaps a dozen specialists worldwide, he could explain its basics to any curious teenager.
'understood by perhaps a dozen specialists worldwide' restates the blank, so it must mean obscure and specialized.
se: The book is packed with ______ details about Byzantine court rituals that few historians even know.
arcane
Both 'recondite' and 'arcane' describe knowledge known only to a few, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: stubbornly resistant to authority, control, or treatment
x: The refractory mule refused to move no matter how hard the farmer pulled on its rope.
Managers struggled to deal with a refractory employee who ignored every new policy.
The teacher finally sent the most refractory students to the principal's office after they disrupted class again.
Doctors are testing a new drug for patients whose epilepsy has proved refractory to standard treatment.
As a teenager, I was refractory and moody, rejecting every piece of advice my parents offered.
tc: Unlike his docile older brother, the boy was so ______ that no tutor could make him sit still for a lesson.
'Unlike his docile older brother' sets up a contrast, so the blank must mean stubbornly unmanageable.
se: The new governor faced a ______ legislature that blocked every reform he proposed.
recalcitrant
Both 'refractory' and 'recalcitrant' mean stubbornly resisting control, so the sentence means the same.

m: to prove that a statement, claim, or argument is wrong
x: She calmly refuted every accusation by producing bank statements for each expense.
In the meeting, our engineer refuted the client's claim that the bridge design was unsafe.
Your essay should not only present your thesis but also refute the strongest counterargument.
New data from the telescope appear to refute the theory that the planet has no atmosphere.
No matter how carefully I refuted his assumptions, my father insisted I would regret leaving my job.
tc: The defense lawyer did not merely question the prosecution's evidence; she set out to ______ it completely with security camera footage.
'did not merely question' signals going further than doubt, to proving the evidence wrong.
se: The study was designed to ______ the popular belief that cold weather causes colds.
disprove
Both 'refute' and 'disprove' mean to show a belief is false, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to move someone or something to a lower or less important position
x: After the new TV arrived, the old one was relegated to the guest room.
When the project failed, the junior engineer was relegated to filing reports instead of designing systems.
Many textbooks relegate the contributions of women scientists to a brief footnote.
The club was relegated to the second division after losing its final match of the season.
She hated being relegated to the role of listener whenever her older sister was around.
tc: Fearing that the new manager would ______ her to routine paperwork, the ambitious analyst began applying for other jobs.
'Fearing' plus 'routine paperwork' and her ambition show the blank means push down to a lesser role.
se: Critics feared the new curriculum would ______ art and music to the margins of the school day.
consign
Both 'relegate' and 'consign' mean to push something to an inferior place, giving the same meaning.

m: to express disapproval of or disappointment with someone's actions
x: My mother never shouted; she simply reproached me with a look that made me feel terrible.

Professors rarely reproach students publicly, preferring to discuss poor work in private.
Opposition leaders reproached the government for its slow response to the flooding in the north.
He still reproaches himself for not calling his grandfather in the weeks before he died.
tc: Rather than praise the intern for staying late, the supervisor chose to ______ him for the careless errors in his report.
'Rather than praise' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean express disapproval.
se: The coach did not ______ the players for losing; instead, he reminded them how far they had come.
rebuke
Both 'reproach' and 'rebuke' mean to criticize someone for their behaviour, so the sentence means the same.

m: to reject something or refuse to accept or be associated with it
x: She repudiated the rumours that she was leaving the company, calling them completely baseless.
The party leader repudiated the extremist group that had endorsed him.
In his later work, the philosopher repudiated many of the ideas that had made him famous.
After the scandal, the company repudiated the contract signed by its former chief executive.
He felt deeply hurt when his own son repudiated the family's values and moved abroad.
tc: Although he once championed the theory, the economist came to ______ it entirely after seeing its effects on the poor.
'Although he once championed' contrasts with the blank, which must mean reject.
se: The candidate was quick to ______ the hateful comments made by one of his supporters.
disavow
Both 'repudiate' and 'disavow' mean to publicly reject any connection with something, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to officially cancel or revoke a law, order, decision, or agreement
x: The university rescinded his admission offer after discovering he had faked his transcripts.
Management rescinded the new dress code after a week of complaints from staff.
Parliament voted to rescind the controversial law that had restricted public protests.
When the bank rescinded its loan offer, we had to postpone buying the flat.
Hurt by his rude remark, she rescinded her invitation and spent her birthday with other friends.
tc: The city council voted to ______ the parking fee only a month after introducing it, admitting the policy had been a mistake.
'admitting the policy had been a mistake' shows the council officially cancelled it.
se: The company was forced to ______ its decision to cut staff holidays.
revoke
Both 'rescind' and 'revoke' mean to officially cancel a decision, so the sentence means the same.

m: unwilling to speak openly about one's thoughts or feelings; reserved
x: My grandfather was reticent about the war and changed the subject whenever we asked.
Normally reticent in meetings, Nadia surprised everyone by presenting a bold plan for the new product.
Many students are reticent in seminars, worried that their questions will sound foolish.
Officials remained reticent about the cause of the explosion until the investigation was complete.
He is reticent with strangers but warm and talkative once you get to know him.
tc: Though she spoke freely about her career, the actress was ______ about her private life, refusing to answer any personal questions.
The contrast with 'spoke freely' and the phrase 'refusing to answer' show the blank means unwilling to talk.
se: The usually ______ engineer astonished his colleagues with a passionate speech at the farewell party.
reserved
Both 'reticent' and 'reserved' describe someone who rarely shares his feelings, so the meaning stays the same.

m: feeling or showing deep respect, often mixed with awe
x: Visitors walked through the old mosque in reverent silence, admiring its carved arches.
The new hires spoke of the company's founder in almost reverent tones.
Students listened with reverent attention as the visiting scientist described her early experiments.
The museum's reverent treatment of the ancient manuscripts includes strict limits on light and humidity.
He kept his late father's watch in a drawer, handling it with reverent care whenever he took it out.
tc: Far from mocking the old traditions, the young director treated them in a ______ manner, as though they were sacred.
'Far from mocking' and 'as though they were sacred' show the blank means deeply respectful.
se: The crowd fell into a ______ hush as the elderly poet stepped up to the microphone.
respectful
Both 'reverent' and 'respectful' describe a silence showing deep respect, so the sentence means the same.

m: having or showing sharp judgment and practical wisdom
x: My aunt gave me sagacious advice: never sign anything you haven't read twice.
A sagacious investor, she sold her shares months before the market crashed.
The professor's sagacious comments helped me see the flaw in my research design.
Voters wanted a sagacious leader who could steer the country through the economic crisis.
Looking back, I realise how sagacious my father was when he urged me to study engineering.

se: The company's ______ annual report said nothing about the factory closures that had angered workers.
bland
Both 'anodyne' and 'bland' mean safely dull and unprovocative, so the sentence means the same.

m: formal approval or praise
x: My grandmother's approbation mattered more to me than any trophy, so her quiet nod after the recital meant everything.
The new hiring policy won the approbation of the board, though several managers privately grumbled about it.
Her thesis earned the approbation of examiners who were notoriously hard to please.
The plan to widen the roads around Dhaka met with public approbation until residents learned how many trees would be felled.
Teenagers often crave the approbation of their peers far more than any praise from their parents.
tc: Far from criticizing the proposal, the committee greeted it with warm ______ and voted to fund it immediately.
'Far from criticizing' signals the opposite of criticism, so the blank must mean approval or praise.
se: The young architect's design received the ______ of the city council, which praised its elegance and practicality.
approval
Both 'approbation' and 'approval' mean official acceptance and praise, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: showing great care, steady effort and persistence in work
x: Thanks to her assiduous note-taking, she could reconstruct every lecture of the semester before the final exam.
An assiduous gardener, my father checks his tomato plants every morning before breakfast.
The auditor's assiduous review of the accounts uncovered a pattern of small but suspicious payments.
Scientists spent a decade in assiduous research before they could explain the decline of the frog population.
He was assiduous in his attentions to her, remembering every birthday and calling whenever she felt low.
tc: Unlike his careless roommate, Rafiq was ______, reviewing every problem set twice before submitting it.
'Unlike his careless roommate' sets up a contrast, and 'reviewing every problem set twice' shows the blank means hardworking and careful.
se: Only through ______ practice over many years did she become a concert pianist.
diligent
Both 'assiduous' and 'diligent' describe steady, careful effort, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: hostile and aggressive; eager to argue or fight
x: After a few drinks, the normally quiet man became belligerent and started arguing with strangers.
The client's belligerent emails made the whole team dread opening their inboxes on Monday mornings.
Diplomats worried that the government's belligerent rhetoric could push the region toward open conflict.
In the seminar, one belligerent student challenged every point the visiting professor made, often rudely.
She grew tired of her brother's belligerent tone whenever anyone questioned his decisions.
tc: Although he had been ______ at the start of the meeting, shouting at everyone, he ended it calm and apologetic.
'Shouting at everyone' and the contrast with 'calm and apologetic' show the blank means hostile and aggressive.
se: The ______ customer refused to calm down and kept threatening the waiter.
aggressive
Both 'belligerent' and 'aggressive' describe someone hostile and ready to fight, producing the same meaning.

m: relating to the pleasant, peaceful aspects of the countryside and country life
x: We spent a bucolic weekend at my uncle's village home, waking to birdsong and fresh date-palm juice.
The company's retreat was held at a bucolic farm, a welcome change from the glass towers of the city.
Romantic poets often idealized bucolic life, ignoring the hardship that real farmers endured.
Developers plan to turn the bucolic valley into a housing estate, much to the dismay of locals.
He dreamed of retiring to a bucolic cottage where he could read, garden and forget about deadlines.
tc: Tired of the noise and smog of the city, she longed for a ______ life of meadows, cows and quiet lanes.
The contrast with the noisy city and the details 'meadows, cows and quiet lanes' point to a word meaning pleasantly rural.
se: The painting depicts a ______ scene of shepherds resting beside a stream.
pastoral
Both 'bucolic' and 'pastoral' describe peaceful country life, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: a false statement made deliberately to damage someone's reputation; slander
x: The rumor that she had cheated on the exam was pure calumny, spread by a jealous classmate.
The senior engineer sued the blogger for calumny after false accusations of bribery appeared online.
Historians now regard many of the charges against the deposed king as calumny invented by his enemies.
Election campaigns too often descend into calumny, with candidates trading lies instead of policies.
He could forgive honest criticism, but the calumnies his former friend spread about him were harder to bear.
tc: The accusations were not merely mistaken but deliberate ______, invented to ruin the mayor's reputation.
'Deliberate' and 'invented to ruin the mayor's reputation' define the blank as malicious false statements.
se: The journalist lost his job after publishing ______ about a local businessman that he knew to be false.
slander
Both 'calumny' and 'slander' mean false statements meant to damage a reputation, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to raise petty, trivial objections or find fault unnecessarily
x: It seems petty to cavil about the font when the report itself is excellent.
My aunt will always cavil at the wedding food, no matter how much the family spends on it.
Reviewers caviled at minor errors in the footnotes but praised the book's central argument.
Rather than caviling over the budget's details, the opposition should propose a real alternative.
She knew he loved her, but his habit of caviling at everything she cooked slowly wore her down.
tc: The plan was so sound that even its harshest critics could only ______ about trivial details.
'So sound' and 'trivial details' show the critics could make only petty objections.
se: Instead of praising the excellent design, the manager chose to ______ over the color of one button.
quibble
Both 'cavil' and 'quibble' mean to object to something trivial, giving the same meaning.

m: cautious or wary, especially about possible risks or dangers
x: After being cheated once, she is chary of lending money to anyone, even close friends.
Investors have grown chary of tech start-ups that promise profits but never deliver them.
Many students are chary of asking questions in class for fear of looking foolish.
Doctors are increasingly chary of prescribing antibiotics for ordinary colds and coughs.
Having been hurt before, he was chary of opening his heart to someone new.
tc: Burned by two failed partnerships, the entrepreneur was ______ of signing any new contract without a lawyer present.
'Burned by two failed partnerships' gives a cause for caution, so the blank means wary.
se: Parents are often ______ of letting young children walk to school alone.
wary
Both 'chary of' and 'wary of' mean cautious about a risk, so the sentence means the same.

m: an unrealistic hope or idea that can never be achieved; an illusion
x: For many commuters, a quick drive across Dhaka at rush hour remains a chimera.
The promise of a paperless office turned out to be a chimera; we print more than ever.
Some physicists argue that a final theory of everything may be nothing more than a chimera.
Peace between the two factions seemed a chimera until both leaders unexpectedly agreed to talks.
He chased the chimera of perfect love for years and overlooked the good people around him.
tc: The investors finally realized that the promised overnight profits were a ______, an illusion with no basis in reality.
The restatement 'an illusion with no basis in reality' defines the blank.
se: Total job security has become a ______ in today's economy.
fantasy
Both 'chimera' and 'fantasy' mean something hoped for but unreal, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: excessive greed, especially for money or possessions
x: The landlord's cupidity knew no bounds; he raised the rent every year without fixing anything.
Several executives were jailed when their cupidity led them to falsify the company's earnings.
Economists debate whether markets channel human cupidity into useful work or simply reward it.
The scam worked by appealing to the cupidity of people who believed they could double their savings in a month.
She realized, too late, that her suitor's affection was driven less by love than by cupidity.
tc: Unlike his generous brother, who gave away most of his salary, Karim was known for his ______, hoarding every taka he earned.
The contrast with 'generous' and the phrase 'hoarding every taka' show the blank means greed.
se: The scandal exposed the ______ of officials who had pocketed funds meant for flood victims.
greed
Both 'cupidity' and 'greed' mean an excessive desire for money, so the meaning is the same.

m: to raise objections or show reluctance to agree
x: When I offered to pay for dinner, my friend demurred, insisting it was her turn.
Several board members demurred at the proposal to cut research funding.
The professor asked for volunteers to present first, but most of the students demurred.
Asked whether he would run for office, the retired judge politely demurred.
She demurred when her parents suggested an arranged match, saying she wanted to finish her master's first.
tc: Although most of the staff welcomed the new schedule, a few were quick to ______, arguing that it ignored parents' needs.
'Although most... welcomed' sets up a contrast, and 'arguing that' shows the blank means to object.
se: When asked to sign the agreement, the lawyer was quick to ______, pointing out several unfair clauses.
object
Both 'demur' and 'object' mean to express disagreement, so the sentence has the same meaning.

m: a person who dabbles in a subject or art without serious commitment or real expertise
x: My cousin is a dilettante who takes up a new hobby every month and finishes none of them.
The board wanted a serious engineer, not a dilettante who had read a few articles about software.
Critics dismissed him as a dilettante, yet his amateur research on local birds proved remarkably accurate.
Serious scholars resent dilettantes who publish confident books on subjects they barely understand.
She admired his curiosity but feared he was a dilettante who would soon lose interest in her too.
tc: Unlike a true expert, who spends years mastering a craft, a ______ merely dabbles in it for fun.
The contrast with 'a true expert' and the phrase 'merely dabbles' define the blank.
se: The gallery owner had no patience for the ______ who claimed to love art but knew nothing about it.
dabbler
Both 'dilettante' and 'dabbler' mean someone with shallow interest and no real expertise.

m: a speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something very highly
x: At the retirement dinner, her former student delivered a moving encomium to her decades of teaching.
The CEO's email to staff was an encomium to the team that had rescued the failing project.
The journal published an encomium to the late physicist, praising both his discoveries and his kindness.
Reviewers poured encomiums on the debut novel, calling it the finest of the decade.
His wedding toast was such a heartfelt encomium to his wife that half the guests were in tears.
tc: Far from criticizing the coach, the players' speech was a glowing ______ to his leadership.
'Far from criticizing' and 'glowing' signal that the blank is a speech of high praise.
se: The article was a lengthy ______ to the city's founding mayor, listing all his achievements.
tribute
Both 'encomium' and 'tribute' mean a piece of writing that honors someone, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to use vague or ambiguous language to avoid committing oneself or telling the truth
x: When I asked whether he had finished the report, he began to equivocate, which told me he hadn't.
Asked directly about the layoffs, the manager equivocated, promising only to 'review all options.'
The minister equivocated for weeks before finally admitting that the vaccine supply had run short.
Good scientific writing states its conclusions plainly instead of equivocating at every step.
She hated the way he equivocated whenever she asked where their relationship was going.
tc: Instead of giving a straight yes or no, the spokesman continued to ______, hiding behind vague phrases.
'Instead of giving a straight yes or no' and 'vague phrases' show the blank means to speak evasively.
se: Pressed by reporters about the missing funds, the official tried to ______ rather than answer directly.
prevaricate
Both 'equivocate' and 'prevaricate' mean to avoid a direct answer, so the sentence means the same.

m: silly and pointless, often in a smug or thoughtless way
x: He made a fatuous remark about the weather just as everyone was discussing the funeral.
The consultant's fatuous slogan, 'Synergize for success,' was mocked throughout the office.
Reviewers called the paper's conclusions fatuous, since they ignored the study's own data.
The politician's fatuous promise to end poverty within a year won applause but convinced no economist.
She was tired of his fatuous grin whenever she tried to have a serious conversation.
tc: Rather than offering a thoughtful answer, the candidate gave a ______ reply that showed he had not considered the question at all.
'Rather than offering a thoughtful answer' signals the blank means foolish and empty.
se: Everyone groaned at his ______ joke about the boss's haircut.
inane
Both 'fatuous' and 'inane' mean silly and pointless, producing the same meaning.

m: lacking initiative, strength of character or a sense of responsibility; ineffective
x: Her feckless brother borrowed money from everyone and never held a job for more than a month.
Staff blamed the feckless management for letting the project drift without clear goals.
Critics described the government's feckless response to the flooding as a betrayal of rural families.
My feckless study habits caught up with me when finals arrived and I had read nothing.
She finally left her feckless husband, tired of carrying every responsibility in the household alone.
tc: Unlike her hardworking sister, Nadia was ______, drifting from job to job without any sense of responsibility.
The contrast with 'hardworking' and the phrase 'without any sense of responsibility' define the blank.
se: The coach was sacked after another season of ______ leadership that left the team without direction.
ineffectual
Both 'feckless' and 'ineffectual' describe weak, ineffective leadership, so the meaning is the same.

m: highly fertile; producing a great deal of growth, offspring or new ideas
x: The fecund soil of the river delta yields three rice harvests a year.
The brainstorming session was unusually fecund, producing more ideas than the team could possibly test.
Darwin's notebooks reveal a fecund mind that leaped from barnacles to orchids to earthworms.
Rabbits are famously fecund, which is why they spread so quickly in the wild.
For the novelist, her childhood memories proved a fecund source of stories.
tc: Unlike the barren hills to the north, the river valley was remarkably ______, producing abundant crops every year.
The contrast with 'barren' and the phrase 'producing abundant crops' show the blank means fertile.
se: The 1920s were a ______ period for the composer, who wrote six symphonies in a decade.
productive
Both 'fecund' and 'productive' describe a time of great creative output, so the sentence means the same.

m: fluent and easy in speech but shallow, insincere or too simple
x: When I asked why he was late again, he gave a glib excuse about traffic and changed the subject.
The salesman's glib answers made us suspicious of everything he claimed about the car.
It is too glib to say that poverty is simply the result of laziness.
The professor warned us against glib conclusions drawn from a single small survey.
Her apology sounded glib, as if she had rehearsed it without really feeling sorry.
tc: The candidate's replies were ______ rather than thoughtful: smooth and confident but lacking any real substance.
The restatement 'smooth and confident but lacking any real substance' defines the blank.
se: Critics dismissed the report's ______ explanation of the crisis as far too simple.
facile
Both 'glib' and 'facile' mean superficially easy and shallow, so the meaning stays the same.

m: unlucky and unfortunate
x: The hapless tourist lost his wallet, his passport and his luggage on the first day of the trip.
Some hapless intern was blamed for the server crash, though the fault lay with senior staff.
During the monsoon, hapless commuters waded through knee-deep water to reach their offices.
The documentary follows a hapless team of researchers whose every experiment seems to fail.
He felt sorry for his hapless friend, who had been dumped by text message on his birthday.
tc: Everything that could go wrong did go wrong for the ______ traveler, who missed three connecting flights in a row.
'Everything that could go wrong did go wrong' shows the blank means unlucky.
se: The ______ goalkeeper slipped on the wet grass and let in an easy goal.
unlucky
Both 'hapless' and 'unlucky' describe someone suffering misfortune, giving the same meaning.

m: a person or thing that signals or announces that something is coming
x: The first robin on the lawn is often seen as a harbinger of spring.
A sudden drop in orders was the harbinger of the layoffs that followed months later.
Rising sea temperatures may be a harbinger of more violent storms in the decades ahead.
In the history seminar, we discussed how the printing press served as a harbinger of the Reformation.
Her silence at dinner was a harbinger of the argument that erupted later that night.
tc: The dark clouds massing on the horizon were a ______ of the storm that would strike the coast that evening.
The clouds appear before the storm arrives, so the blank means a sign of something to come.
se: Many investors saw the bank's collapse as a ______ of a wider financial crisis.
portent
Both 'harbinger' and 'portent' mean a sign of a coming event, so the sentence means the same.

m: rude and disrespectful, especially toward someone who deserves respect
x: The impudent boy stuck out his tongue when his teacher asked him to sit down.
An impudent new hire told the director, in front of everyone, that his strategy was outdated.
The examiner was startled by the impudent tone of the student's appeal letter.
The magazine was fined for an impudent cartoon mocking the country's highest court.
She laughed at his impudent question about her age and refused to answer it.
tc: Instead of the respectful reply his grandfather expected, the teenager gave an ______ answer that made everyone at the table gasp.
'Instead of the respectful reply' sets up a contrast, so the blank means disrespectful.
se: The teacher punished the ______ student who mocked her accent in class.
insolent
Both 'impudent' and 'insolent' mean rudely disrespectful, producing the same meaning.

m: showing a relaxed, casual lack of concern; carefree
x: He strolled into the exam hall twenty minutes late, insouciant as ever, with a cup of tea in his hand.
Her insouciant attitude toward deadlines eventually cost her the promotion.
Scientists are alarmed by the public's insouciant response to warnings about antibiotic resistance.
With an insouciant shrug, she told her parents she had quit medical school to become a painter.
On weekends, my roommate adopts an insouciant air, ignoring dishes, laundry and bills alike.
tc: While everyone else panicked as the deadline approached, Tariq remained ______, chatting and sipping coffee as if nothing were wrong.
The contrast with 'everyone else panicked' and 'as if nothing were wrong' show the blank means unconcerned.
se: She gave a ______ wave as she drove off, apparently untroubled by the dent in the car.
nonchalant
Both 'insouciant' and 'nonchalant' mean casually unconcerned, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: having a long-established habit or quality that is unlikely to change
x: My uncle is an inveterate gambler who still bets on every cricket match, despite losing thousands.
As an inveterate optimist, our manager believes every delayed project will somehow finish on time.
Researchers found that inveterate smokers were far less likely to respond to warning labels.
The professor was an inveterate note-taker, filling dozens of notebooks during every conference.
Her inveterate jealousy slowly poisoned a relationship that had started so happily.
tc: Having lied about everything since childhood, Javed was an ______ liar whom no one believed anymore.
'Since childhood' shows a long-established habit, which is what the blank describes.
se: Doctors find ______ smokers the hardest patients to persuade to quit.
habitual
Both 'inveterate' and 'habitual' describe a deeply ingrained habit, so the sentence means the same.

m: extreme, aggressive patriotism, especially support for a warlike foreign policy
x: My father switches off the TV whenever the commentary on a cricket match slides into jingoism.
The advertising agency was criticized for jingoism after its campaign mocked a neighboring country.
Historians argue that jingoism in the popular press helped drag Europe into war in 1914.
In her thesis, she traced how school textbooks can quietly encourage jingoism.
He loved his country deeply but despised the jingoism of those who wanted to bomb its rivals.
tc: The editorial warned that the government's aggressive ______ could easily turn patriotic pride into a reckless war.
'Aggressive', 'patriotic pride' and 'reckless war' point to warlike, extreme patriotism.
se: As the border dispute escalated, a wave of ______ swept through the tabloids, which called for immediate military action.
chauvinism
Both 'jingoism' and 'chauvinism' here mean aggressive national pride, so the meaning is the same.

m: lacking enthusiasm and effort; lazily careless
x: His lackadaisical approach to cleaning meant the kitchen sink was always piled with dishes.
The manager warned that lackadaisical work on safety checks would no longer be tolerated.
After a lackadaisical first semester, he buckled down and earned top marks.
Officials were accused of a lackadaisical response to early reports of the outbreak.
She found his lackadaisical replies to her messages hurtful, as if he could hardly be bothered.
tc: The coach was furious at the team's ______ performance; the players had barely bothered to chase the ball.
'Barely bothered to chase the ball' explains the blank as lazy and lacking effort.
se: Her ______ attitude toward her studies worried her parents, who had expected far more effort.
apathetic
Both 'lackadaisical' and 'apathetic' describe an attitude lacking interest and effort, so the meaning holds.

m: generosity in giving money or gifts, or the gifts themselves
x: The village school was rebuilt thanks to the largess of a former student who made his fortune abroad.
Employees were surprised by the company's sudden largess: a bonus for everyone at the end of a bad year.
Many universities depend on the largess of wealthy alumni to fund new laboratories.
Critics say the government's pre-election largess is simply a bribe paid with taxpayers' money.
My aunt's largess at Eid is legendary; every child in the family leaves with crisp new banknotes.
tc: The museum, normally short of funds, was saved by the ______ of an anonymous donor who gave it ten million dollars.
'Gave it ten million dollars' shows the blank means generous giving.
se: The orphanage survived for decades on the ______ of local merchants.
generosity
Both 'largess' and 'generosity' mean freely given gifts or money, so the sentence means the same.

m: lacking moral restraint, especially in sexual behavior
x: Victorian critics condemned the novel as licentious, though modern readers find it rather tame.
The emperor's licentious court scandalized the common people, who struggled to feed their families.
The festival was once famous for its licentious revelry, but today it is a family-friendly event.
The company tightened its code of conduct after licentious behavior at an office party led to complaints.
Her parents worried that the city's licentious nightlife would lead their daughter astray.
tc: Unlike his ______ predecessor, whose court was notorious for scandal and excess, the new king lived a modest, disciplined life.
The contrast with 'a modest, disciplined life' and 'scandal and excess' show the blank means morally unrestrained.
se: The preacher denounced the town's ______ behavior, warning that excess and immorality would ruin it.
dissolute
Both 'licentious' and 'dissolute' mean lacking moral restraint, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: completely clear, like clean water, or (of writing) clear and easy to understand
x: We swam in a limpid mountain lake where you could see pebbles twenty feet below.
The manager praised the intern's limpid summary, which explained the whole problem on a single page.
Her limpid prose makes even difficult ideas in philosophy feel accessible.
Researchers found that the once limpid river had turned murky with industrial waste.
He looked into her limpid eyes and knew at once that she was telling the truth.
tc: Unlike the murky ponds near the factory, the mountain stream was ______, every stone on its bed visible.
The contrast with 'murky' and 'every stone on its bed visible' show the blank means perfectly clear.
se: Readers praised the author's ______ style, which made complex science easy to follow.
lucid
Both 'limpid' and 'lucid' describe writing that is clear and easy to understand.

m: to treat someone as a celebrity or hero and give them great public attention
x: After scoring a century in his debut match, the young batsman was lionized across the country.
The tech industry tends to lionize founders while forgetting the engineers who actually build the products.
Students lionized the visiting poet, crowding around her for autographs after the lecture.
Historians warn against lionizing explorers whose expeditions brought suffering to local peoples.
He enjoyed being lionized at parties, but at home he felt lonely and unappreciated.
tc: The public, which had once ignored the inventor, began to ______ him as a national hero after his discovery saved thousands of lives.
The contrast with 'once ignored' and the phrase 'as a national hero' show the blank means to treat as a celebrity.
se: Young fans tend to ______ footballers, treating them as heroes beyond criticism.
idolize
Both 'lionize' and 'idolize' mean to treat someone as a hero, so the meaning is the same.

m: looking or sounding sad and gloomy, often in an exaggerated way
x: The basset hound gave us a lugubrious look when we left without taking him for a walk.
Nobody enjoyed the meeting, thanks to the finance director's lugubrious forecast for the year.
The orchestra played a lugubrious melody that suited the solemn memorial service.
Critics found the film too lugubrious, with two hours of rain, funerals and silent grief.
His lugubrious sighs whenever she went out with friends made her feel guilty for having fun.
tc: Rather than the cheerful tune we expected at the wedding, the band played a ______ dirge that left everyone feeling glum.
The contrast with 'cheerful' and the words 'dirge' and 'glum' show the blank means mournful.
se: The old man's ______ face suggested he had just received terrible news.
mournful
Both 'lugubrious' and 'mournful' mean looking sad and gloomy, so the sentence means the same.

m: self-pityingly or tearfully sentimental, often because of drinking too much
x: By midnight, my uncle had grown maudlin and was weeping over old wedding photographs.
The farewell speech became so maudlin that colleagues began quietly checking their phones.
Critics dismissed the novel's ending as maudlin, a cheap attempt to make readers cry.
Some news channels turn every tragedy into maudlin entertainment, complete with sad music and slow-motion replays.
She sent him a maudlin text late at night, which she deeply regretted the next morning.
tc: The director avoided the ______ sentimentality of most war films, presenting grief with restraint and dignity.
The contrast with 'restraint and dignity' shows the blank means overly tearful and sentimental.
se: His speech grew so ______ that even his closest friends rolled their eyes at the tears.
mawkish
Both 'maudlin' and 'mawkish' mean excessively sentimental, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behavior
x: My mercurial roommate can be laughing one minute and slamming doors the next.
Working for a mercurial boss means never knowing whether a mistake will be forgiven or punished.
Markets have been mercurial this year, swinging wildly on every rumor of an interest-rate cut.
The professor's mercurial grading made it impossible to predict how any essay would be marked.
She loved his creativity but found his mercurial temper exhausting.
tc: Unlike her calm, steady brother, Mitu was ______, cheerful at breakfast and furious by lunch.
The contrast with 'calm, steady' and the sudden mood swing show the blank means unpredictable.
se: The ______ striker could win a match on his own one week and disappear entirely the next.
erratic
Both 'mercurial' and 'erratic' describe unpredictable performance, so the meaning is the same.

m: a small amount of something, especially something good or desirable
x: With a modicum of planning, you can cook healthy meals for the whole week in two hours on Sunday.
Anyone with a modicum of common sense would have backed up the files before updating the system.
The study achieved only a modicum of success, reducing symptoms in a handful of patients.
Even a modicum of rainfall would save the region's crops from total failure.
All she wanted from him was a modicum of respect, not grand romantic gestures.
tc: The report was full of exaggerations, though it did contain a ______ of truth, just enough to make it believable.
'Just enough to make it believable' shows the blank means a small amount.
se: If the minister had shown even a ______ of humility, the protests might have ended sooner.
shred
Both 'modicum' and 'shred' mean a tiny amount, so 'even a ___ of humility' means the same.

m: lacking foresight or wider understanding; focused only on the short term
x: Skipping breakfast to save ten minutes is a myopic habit that leaves you exhausted by noon.
Cutting the training budget was a myopic decision that hurt productivity for years.
Critics called the policy myopic because it ignored the long-term cost of rising sea levels.
Focusing only on GRE vocabulary while ignoring reading practice is a myopic study strategy.
His myopic focus on his career blinded him to his wife's growing unhappiness.
tc: Rather than planning for future growth, the company's ______ managers cared only about the next quarter's profits.
'Rather than planning for future growth' and 'only about the next quarter' show the blank means short-sighted.
se: Economists warned that slashing education spending was a ______ policy that would harm the country for decades.
short-sighted
Both 'myopic' and 'short-sighted' mean ignoring long-term consequences, giving the same meaning.

m: strong public criticism or abuse, and the disgrace that results from it
x: After the scandal, the once-popular coach faced a storm of obloquy from fans and journalists alike.
She endured months of online obloquy at work simply for defending an unpopular colleague.
The scientist's theory met with obloquy at first but was vindicated decades later.
No politician wants to risk the obloquy that follows a broken campaign promise.
He bore the obloquy of his neighbors with quiet dignity, convinced he had done the right thing.
tc: Once celebrated as a hero, the general now faced public ______ after the details of the massacre came to light.
The contrast with 'once celebrated as a hero' shows the blank means harsh public criticism.
se: The company's decision to dump waste in the river brought it widespread ______ from environmental groups.
condemnation
Both 'obloquy' and 'condemnation' mean strong public criticism, so the sentence means the same.

m: noisy, unruly and difficult to control
x: The obstreperous toddler screamed all through the flight from Dhaka to Singapore.
An obstreperous shareholder kept interrupting the annual meeting with shouted questions.
The teacher finally separated the two obstreperous boys who had disrupted every lesson that week.
Police removed several obstreperous fans who had thrown bottles onto the pitch.
She loved her brother, but his obstreperous behavior at family dinners embarrassed her constantly.
tc: The normally quiet class became ______ when the substitute teacher arrived, shouting and refusing to sit down.
The contrast with 'normally quiet' and the details 'shouting and refusing to sit down' define the blank.
se: Security guards escorted the ______ guest out of the restaurant after he began shouting at the staff.
unruly
Both 'obstreperous' and 'unruly' mean noisy and hard to control, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a public speech or piece of writing that praises someone or something highly
x: My friend's review of the new café was less a review than a panegyric to its mango lassi.
The annual report opened with a panegyric to the chairman that embarrassed even his allies.
