tc: Although the comment was meant only as a joke, the professor took ______ and left the room in stony silence.
'Although... meant only as a joke' and leaving 'in stony silence' show he felt offended.
se: Many readers took ______ at the article's suggestion that rural people are poorly educated.
offense
'Took umbrage at' and 'took offense at' both mean felt insulted, so the sentence means the same.

m: shockingly unfair, unreasonable, or unjust; not acceptable by any moral standard
x: Charging elderly customers triple the normal price is simply unconscionable.
The company kept workers waiting an unconscionable length of time for their unpaid wages.
Ethicists argued that withholding the drug from the control group would be unconscionable.
It is unconscionable that children still die from diseases that are easily preventable.
Breaking his promise to his dying father seemed unconscionable to him, so he stayed in the village.
tc: While some price rises are understandable, the pharmacy's decision to triple the cost of insulin during the crisis was ______.
'While some price rises are understandable' sets up a contrast, so the blank means morally unacceptable.
se: Keeping patients waiting fourteen hours for emergency treatment is ______.
indefensible
Both 'unconscionable' and 'indefensible' mean impossible to justify morally, so the meaning is the same.

m: (of a position or argument) not able to be maintained or defended
x: Living with five roommates in a one-bedroom flat became untenable after the first month.
His position as manager became untenable once the fraud was discovered.
Her thesis rested on the untenable assumption that one small sample represented the whole population.
New evidence of toxic waste made the government's claim that the river was safe completely untenable.
She realized the relationship was untenable when they could no longer talk without fighting.
tc: Once the new data contradicted every one of his claims, the scientist's theory became ______.
'Contradicted every one of his claims' shows the theory could no longer be defended.
se: With losses mounting every month, the company's current strategy is clearly ______.
unsustainable
Both 'untenable' and 'unsustainable' mean the strategy cannot be maintained, giving the same meaning.

m: to scold or criticize someone severely
x: My mother upbraided me for coming home after midnight without calling.
The supervisor upbraided the technician for skipping the routine safety checks.
The professor upbraided students who had copied their lab reports from the internet.
Editorials upbraided the city council for ignoring warnings about the crumbling bridge.
She silently upbraided herself for ever doubting her best friend's loyalty.
tc: Instead of praising the junior doctor for her quick thinking, the consultant chose to ______ her for not following protocol.
'Instead of praising' signals the opposite, so the blank means to scold.
se: The coach did not hesitate to ______ the players who arrived late for training.
scold
Both 'upbraid' and 'scold' mean to criticize sharply, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: showing a lack of thought or intelligence; empty of meaning
x: He stared at the television with a vacuous expression, barely hearing a word I said.
The meeting produced nothing but vacuous slogans about 'synergy' and 'innovation.'
Reviewers dismissed the essay as vacuous, full of big words but lacking any real argument.
Voters are tired of vacuous campaign promises that never turn into actual policies.
She broke up with him after realizing their conversations were pleasant but vacuous.
tc: Although the speech sounded impressive, it was essentially ______, offering no real ideas or evidence.
'Although... sounded impressive' and 'offering no real ideas' point to a word meaning empty.
se: The celebrity's interview was so ______ that I couldn't remember a single thing she said.
vapid
Both 'vacuous' and 'vapid' mean lacking substance or intelligence, so the meaning is the same.

m: open to bribery; willing to act dishonestly for money
x: At that border crossing, venal officials expect a bribe from almost every truck driver.
The audit uncovered a venal purchasing manager who had taken kickbacks from suppliers.
Historians describe the late empire as hopelessly venal, with offices openly sold to the highest bidder.
The investigation exposed venal judges who sold favorable verdicts to wealthy defendants.
She was heartbroken to discover that her fiance's devotion was venal and tied entirely to her family's money.
tc: Unlike his honest predecessor, the new customs chief was ______ and approved any shipment for the right bribe.
The contrast with 'honest' and 'for the right bribe' point to a word meaning corruptible.
se: Reformers hoped to clean up the ______ bureaucracy that demanded payment for every permit.
corrupt
Both 'venal' and 'corrupt' describe officials who take bribes, so the sentence means the same.

m: to annoy, frustrate, or worry someone
x: It really vexes me when people talk loudly on their phones in the cinema.
A recurring software crash vexed the IT team for weeks.
This problem in number theory has vexed mathematicians for more than a century.
Rising food prices continue to vex families across the country.
She was vexed that her brother had forgotten her birthday yet again.
tc: Though he usually ignored small annoyances, the constant dripping of the tap began to ______ him beyond endurance.
'Though he usually ignored small annoyances' and 'beyond endurance' show the blank means to irritate.
se: Her colleague's habit of interrupting her in meetings never failed to ______ her.
irritate
Both 'vex' and 'irritate' mean to annoy, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: filled with bitter, harsh criticism or malice
x: My neighbor left a vitriolic note on my car because I parked slightly over the line.
The CEO's vitriolic email to the staff was leaked to the press within an hour.
The scholar's vitriolic review of his rival's book shocked the editors of the journal.
Online debates about the election have become increasingly vitriolic, with insults replacing arguments.
After the divorce, their exchanges grew so vitriolic that their children dreaded every phone call.
tc: Far from offering gentle suggestions, the critic's review was ______, attacking the director with personal insults.
'Far from offering gentle suggestions' and 'personal insults' signal bitter, harsh criticism.
se: The candidate launched a ______ attack on his opponent's record.
scathing
Both 'vitriolic' and 'scathing' describe fiercely harsh criticism, so the meaning is the same.

m: talking fluently, readily, and at length
x: Our voluble taxi driver told us his entire life story before we reached the airport.
She is quiet in meetings but becomes voluble once the formal agenda is over.
Students liked the voluble lecturer, though he often ran out of time before reaching the main point.
Several voluble critics of the policy appeared on talk shows every night that week.
After a few minutes with her old friends, the shy girl became surprisingly voluble.
tc: Normally ______ and full of stories, my uncle was oddly silent at the funeral.
The contrast with 'oddly silent' and 'full of stories' show the blank means talkative.
se: The ______ host kept the conversation flowing all evening.
talkative
Both 'voluble' and 'talkative' describe someone who talks readily, giving the same meaning.

m: deliberate and unprovoked, especially of cruel, violent, or destructive acts
x: Someone smashed every streetlight on our lane in an act of wanton vandalism.
The company was accused of wanton disregard for its workers' safety.
Researchers documented the wanton destruction of mangroves along the southern coast.
The wanton killing of elephants for ivory has drawn international condemnation.
Her wanton cruelty toward her younger brother deeply worried their parents.
tc: The attack served no purpose and was completely unprovoked; it was an act of ______ violence.
'Served no purpose and was completely unprovoked' defines senseless, deliberate violence.
se: The soldiers were condemned for the ______ destruction of villages that posed no threat.
gratuitous
Both 'wanton' and 'gratuitous' mean done without reason or provocation, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: the highest point reached; the peak
x: At the zenith of summer, the afternoon heat leaves the streets almost empty.
Her career reached its zenith when she was appointed head of the research division.
Many historians consider the Mughal Empire to have been at its zenith under Akbar.
Astronomers explain that the sun reaches its zenith around noon, when shadows are shortest.
Their friendship was at its zenith during university, before work and marriage pulled them apart.
tc: From the ______ of his fame in the 1980s, the singer slowly declined into obscurity.
'Slowly declined into obscurity' shows he started from the highest point of his fame.
se: The empire was at its ______ when it controlled trade routes across three continents.
peak
Both 'zenith' and 'peak' mean the highest point, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a state of temporary suspension or inactivity
x: Our plans to renovate the kitchen are in abeyance until we save more money.
The merger has been held in abeyance while regulators review the deal.
The university placed the new grading policy in abeyance after strong student protests.
The law remains in abeyance pending a ruling from the Supreme Court.
Her doubts about the marriage were in abeyance for a while but returned after the wedding.
tc: The construction project was not cancelled but merely held in ______ until new funding could be found.
'Not cancelled but merely held... until' signals a temporary pause.
se: The old harvest festival fell into ______ during the war but was revived in the 1960s.
dormancy
Both 'fell into abeyance' and 'fell into dormancy' describe a temporary inactive state, so the meaning is the same.

m: of doubtful truth, although widely told or believed
x: The story that my grandfather once wrestled a tiger is almost certainly apocryphal.
An apocryphal tale circulates in the office about a manager who fired someone by text message.
Historians now regard the famous quotation as apocryphal, since it appears in no contemporary source.
Health experts warned that apocryphal claims about garlic curing the virus were dangerous.
She enjoyed her father's apocryphal stories about his student days, even though she believed only half of them.
tc: Although the tale is repeated in every biography, historians have found no evidence for it and consider it ______.
'Repeated in every biography' yet 'no evidence for it' defines a widely told but doubtful story.
se: The widely told story about the inventor's dream is probably ______, since no record of it exists.
fictitious
Both 'apocryphal' and 'fictitious' mean the story is likely not true, giving the same meaning.

m: natural and sincere; without guile, deception, or pretense
x: The child's artless remark that the cake tasted like a shoe made everyone laugh.
Clients trusted her artless manner more than the polished pitches of her rivals.
The poet's early work has an artless charm that his later, more sophisticated poems lack.
Voters warmed to the young candidate's artless honesty about her own mistakes.
He was charmed by her artless delight in simple things, like the first rain of the monsoon.
tc: Unlike her scheming cousins, who were always plotting, Mina was ______ and said exactly what she thought.
The contrast with 'scheming' and 'always plotting' shows the blank means free of guile.
se: The villagers' ______ hospitality, offered with no expectation of reward, touched the visitors deeply.
guileless
Both 'artless' and 'guileless' mean sincere and without hidden motives, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: respected and impressive; marked by dignity and grandeur
x: We lowered our voices as we entered the august reading room of the old university library.
Being invited to address such an august body of judges was the highlight of her career.
The journal is an august publication with more than two centuries of history.
The ceremony took place in the presence of august guests from around the world.
My grandfather looked august in his white panjabi as he led the family prayers on Eid.
tc: Founded in 1660 and counting many Nobel laureates among its members, the society is one of the most ______ institutions in Europe.
Its long history and Nobel laureate members show the blank means highly respected and dignified.
se: The young scholar felt honored to speak before the ______ members of the academy.
distinguished
Both 'august' and 'distinguished' describe highly respected people, so the sentence means the same.

m: self-evident or unquestionable; accepted as true without proof
x: In our family it is axiomatic that guests are fed before anyone else.
Every salesperson treats it as axiomatic that keeping a customer is cheaper than finding a new one.
In Euclidean geometry, it is axiomatic that parallel lines never meet.
For decades, most economists regarded the benefits of free trade as axiomatic.
She held it as axiomatic that true friends always tell each other the truth.
tc: No one in the lab ever questioned the principle; it was considered ______ that results must be repeated before publication.
'No one... ever questioned the principle' restates the idea of something accepted without proof.
se: Among investors, it is ______ that higher returns come with higher risk.
self-evident
Both 'axiomatic' and 'self-evident' mean obviously true without proof, giving the same meaning.

m: blissfully happy; showing great joy and serenity
x: After finishing her final exam, my sister lay on the sofa with a beatific smile.
When the boss announced two extra holidays, a beatific calm settled over the office.
The art historian compared the beatific faces of the saints in several Renaissance paintings.
Photographs showed the freed prisoner wearing a beatific expression as he hugged his family.
Holding her newborn son, she looked up at her husband with a beatific glow.
tc: Far from looking anxious about the surgery, the old man lay in bed with a ______ smile of perfect peace.
'Far from looking anxious' and 'perfect peace' point to a blissfully serene expression.
se: The child's ______ expression as she tasted the ice cream made everyone laugh.
blissful
Both 'beatific' and 'blissful' describe a look of pure joy, so the meaning stays the same.

m: to cheat or defraud someone, especially out of money
x: A fake repairman bilked my elderly neighbor out of thousands of taka.
The accountant was arrested for bilking his employer through a series of fake invoices.
Researchers studied how online scams bilk students who are desperate for scholarships.
Prosecutors say the firm bilked investors out of millions with a fake property scheme.
She felt bilked by her former partner, who had quietly emptied their joint account.
tc: The so-called charity turned out to be a scam designed to ______ generous donors out of their money.
'Turned out to be a scam' shows the blank means to cheat or defraud.
se: The gang used fake lottery calls to ______ pensioners out of their savings.
swindle
Both 'bilk' and 'swindle' mean to cheat someone out of money, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: cheerfully careless or unconcerned, often about something that deserves attention
x: He showed a blithe disregard for the speed limit as he drove us to the airport.
Her blithe assurance that the report would be done on time worried the whole team.
The study criticizes the blithe assumption that technology alone can solve climate change.
Officials made blithe promises that the floodwaters would recede within days.
She was blithe about the breakup, laughing it off as if it had never mattered.
tc: Although everyone else was alarmed by the storm warning, he remained ______, joking that nothing bad would happen.
'Although everyone else was alarmed' and his joking show the blank means carelessly unconcerned.
se: The developers showed a ______ disregard for the residents who would lose their homes.
casual
'Blithe disregard' and 'casual disregard' both mean careless indifference, giving the same meaning.

m: to polish by rubbing; especially, to improve or enhance a reputation or image
x: My father spent the morning burnishing the brass doorknob until it gleamed.
The company hired a public relations firm to burnish its image after the scandal.
She published three papers in a year to burnish her credentials before applying for tenure.
The government hopes hosting the cricket tournament will burnish the country's international reputation.
He tried to burnish his reputation with her family by bringing generous gifts to every visit.
tc: After the scandal damaged his standing, the senator launched a charity campaign to ______ his reputation.
A campaign launched 'after the scandal damaged his standing' must aim to improve his image.
se: The university hopes the new research center will ______ its reputation abroad.
enhance
Both 'burnish' and 'enhance' mean to improve a reputation, so the sentence means the same.

m: to persuade someone by flattery or gentle coaxing
x: We had to cajole our son into eating his vegetables with promises of ice cream.
She cajoled her manager into approving an extra week of leave.
The supervisor cajoled exhausted students into finishing the experiment before midnight.
Diplomats spent weeks trying to cajole both sides into returning to the negotiating table.
He cajoled his grandmother into telling stories about her childhood in the village.
tc: Rather than ordering her staff to stay late, she tried to ______ them with compliments and free pizza.
'Rather than ordering' and 'compliments and free pizza' point to persuading by flattery.
se: Parents often try to ______ toddlers into going to sleep with stories and treats.
coax
Both 'cajole' and 'coax' mean to persuade gently, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: inexperienced and immature, usually describing a young person
x: As a callow eighteen-year-old, I thought I knew everything about money.
The callow new hire made promises to clients that the company could not keep.
In his callow undergraduate essays, he relied on big words instead of clear thinking.
Critics dismissed the callow candidate as far too young to lead a country in crisis.
Looking back, she was embarrassed by the callow love letters she had written at sixteen.
tc: Though he was now a seasoned diplomat, he still remembered the ______ youth who had arrived in London knowing nothing.
The contrast with 'seasoned diplomat' and 'knowing nothing' show the blank means immature and inexperienced.
se: The team was full of ______ players who had never faced the pressure of a final.
inexperienced
Both 'callow' and 'inexperienced' describe players lacking experience, so the meaning is the same.

m: a small, exclusive group of people with shared interests
x: My aunt has a coterie of friends who meet every Thursday to play cards and gossip.
The CEO relied on a small coterie of advisers and rarely listened to anyone else.
A coterie of graduate students gathered around the famous professor after every lecture.
Real power in the party is concentrated in a coterie of senior leaders.
She felt excluded from the coterie of popular girls who sat together at lunch.
tc: Rather than consulting the whole department, the director made decisions with a tight ______ of loyal assistants.
The contrast with 'the whole department' and 'tight' point to a small, exclusive group.
se: The poet shared her work only with a small ______ of trusted friends.
circle
Both 'coterie' and 'circle' mean a small, close group, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: causing harm or damage
x: Staying up late every night has had a deleterious effect on my concentration.
Long hours without breaks can be deleterious to employees' health.
The study found that the pesticide had deleterious effects on bee populations.
Air pollution in Dhaka has deleterious consequences for children's lungs.
Constant criticism from his father had a deleterious impact on his self-esteem.
tc: Far from being beneficial, the new diet proved ______ to patients with heart disease.
'Far from being beneficial' signals the opposite, so the blank means harmful.
se: Excessive screen time may have ______ effects on young children's sleep.
harmful
Both 'deleterious' and 'harmful' mean causing damage, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a slow, mournful song or piece of music, especially one for the dead
x: The rain dripping from the roof sounded like a slow dirge all night.
His farewell speech at the office party sounded more like a dirge than a celebration.
Music students studied how composers use minor keys to give a dirge its mournful tone.
A brass band played a solemn dirge as the coffin passed through the streets.
She played the old dirge on the piano every year on the anniversary of her mother's death.
tc: Instead of a cheerful tune, the band played a slow, mournful ______ as the procession made its way to the cemetery.
'Instead of a cheerful tune', 'mournful' and 'cemetery' point to a funeral song.
se: The villagers sang an ancient ______ for the fishermen lost at sea.
lament
Both 'dirge' and 'lament' mean a song of mourning, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: dissatisfied with those in authority and no longer willing to support them
x: After the third fare increase, many disaffected commuters stopped using the new bus service.
Disaffected employees often leave quietly rather than raising complaints with their managers.
The survey found many students disaffected with a curriculum that ignores practical skills.
Extremist groups often recruit among disaffected young men with few job prospects.
Years of being ignored left her disaffected and distant from her once-close family.
tc: Once loyal supporters of the party, many voters had become ______ after years of broken promises.
'Once loyal' and 'years of broken promises' signal a loss of support and satisfaction.
se: The rebel leader drew support from ______ soldiers who had not been paid for months.
disgruntled
Both 'disaffected' and 'disgruntled' describe people resentful toward authority, so the meaning is the same.

m: rigidly applying a theory or belief without regard to practical considerations
x: My uncle is doctrinaire about diet and refuses to eat anything his favorite book forbids.
The new manager's doctrinaire approach ignored the realities of the factory floor.
Her supervisor was too doctrinaire to accept any method outside his own school of thought.
Critics say doctrinaire economic policies, applied without regard to local conditions, worsened the crisis.
Their friendship cooled when he became increasingly doctrinaire about politics.
tc: Rather than adapting her theory to the new evidence, the economist remained ______, insisting that the model could not be wrong.
'Rather than adapting' and 'insisting that the model could not be wrong' signal rigid adherence to theory.
se: The party's ______ leaders refused to consider any compromise that conflicted with their ideology.
dogmatic
Both 'doctrinaire' and 'dogmatic' mean rigidly attached to a doctrine, so the sentence means the same.

m: something regarded as worthless; rubbish
x: Most of what's on television tonight is dross, so let's read instead.
The editor's job is to separate useful reports from the dross that floods her inbox.
Among the dross of hastily written essays, the examiner occasionally found a genuinely original idea.
Critics complained that the festival screened too much commercial dross and too few serious films.
She learned to ignore the dross of online gossip and focus on the friends who mattered.
c: separate the gold from the dross
tc: Only a handful of the hundreds of submissions were brilliant; the rest was ______ that the judges quickly discarded.
The contrast with 'brilliant' and 'quickly discarded' show the blank means worthless material.
se: Amid all the ______ in the secondhand shop, she found a valuable first edition.
junk
Both 'dross' and 'junk' mean worthless items, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: outstandingly bad; shocking
x: Forgetting my best friend's wedding was an egregious mistake I'll never live down.
The auditor found several egregious errors in the company's financial statements.
The journal retracted the paper after discovering egregious flaws in its data.
Human rights groups documented egregious abuses in the detention centers.
His egregious lie about his past finally destroyed her trust in him.
tc: This was not a minor oversight but a truly ______ blunder that cost the company millions.
'Not a minor oversight' and 'cost the company millions' signal an outstandingly bad mistake.
se: The referee's ______ error decided the outcome of the match.
glaring
Both 'egregious' and 'glaring' describe an obvious, shocking mistake, giving the same meaning.

m: to deliberately avoid or keep away from something, usually on principle
x: My grandmother eschews sugar in her tea, insisting that it ruins the flavour of good leaves.
Our new manager eschews long meetings and prefers quick updates over chat.
Good academic writing eschews jargon whenever a plain word will do the job.
Several candidates eschewed negative advertising, choosing instead to focus on local issues.
Since the breakup, she has eschewed social gatherings and spent most evenings alone with her books.
tc: A lifelong pacifist, he urged his followers to ______ violence in all its forms, even in self-defence.
'A lifelong pacifist' tells us he wants people to avoid violence, so the blank means to shun or avoid.
se: Hoping to stay healthy, the athlete chose to ______ fried food entirely during the season.
shun
Both 'eschew' and 'shun' mean to deliberately avoid, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: very small in amount; scanty or meagre
x: After rent and bills, what remained of my monthly salary was exiguous at best.
The startup survived its first year on an exiguous budget and a lot of unpaid overtime.
Historians have only exiguous records of the village before the nineteenth century.
Farmers in the region struggled to feed their families on exiguous harvests after the drought.
His letters home grew exiguous, a few hurried lines at most, and his mother worried constantly.
tc: Far from being generous, the charity's grant was so ______ that it barely covered the cost of stationery.
'Far from being generous' and 'barely covered' show the grant was tiny, so the blank means scanty.
se: The research team had to work with ______ funding, so they cut the number of field trips in half.
meagre
Both 'exiguous' and 'meagre' mean very small in amount, which explains why the trips were cut.

m: still in existence; surviving from an earlier time
x: Only three letters from my great-grandfather are extant, kept in a tin box in my aunt's cupboard.
The firm's oldest extant contract dates from 1952 and now hangs framed in the lobby.
Scholars compared every extant manuscript of the poem to reconstruct the original text.
Of the many mosques built during the Sultanate period, only a handful remain extant in Bangladesh.
She treasures the few extant photographs of her parents' wedding, faded but still precious.
tc: Although most of the playwright's works were lost in the fire, two of his comedies are still ______ and are performed today.
'Although most ... were lost' sets up a contrast, so the blank must mean still surviving.
se: Only a few ______ copies of the first edition can be found in libraries today.
surviving
Both 'extant' and 'surviving' describe copies that still exist, giving the same meaning.

m: irritable and quarrelsome; difficult to control or keep in order
x: By evening the children were tired and fractious, squabbling over every toy in the house.
Meetings became increasingly fractious as the two departments argued over the shrinking budget.
The seminar grew fractious when students began attacking each other personally instead of the arguments.
The coalition was too fractious to agree on a single candidate for prime minister.
Their once warm friendship turned fractious after a long dispute over borrowed money.
tc: Unlike his calm and cooperative brother, the boy was ______, picking fights with anyone who crossed him.
'Unlike his calm and cooperative brother' and 'picking fights' show the blank means quarrelsome.
se: The committee was so ______ that it could not even agree on when to hold its next meeting.
quarrelsome
Both 'fractious' and 'quarrelsome' describe a group that argues constantly, so the meaning is the same.

m: socially awkward; lacking grace, tact or sophistication
x: It felt gauche to ask the host how much the house had cost, so I said nothing.
His gauche remark about the director's weight during the client dinner made everyone wince.
As a first-year student, I was painfully gauche at departmental parties and hid near the snacks.
Many viewers found the official's attempt at humour during the memorial service gauche and insensitive.
She found his gauche manners endearing rather than embarrassing when they first met.
tc: Far from the polished diplomat his colleagues expected, the new envoy was ______, often blurting out tactless comments at receptions.
'Far from the polished diplomat' and 'tactless comments' show the blank means socially awkward.
se: At sixteen he was shy and ______, never knowing what to say to adults at parties.
awkward
Both 'gauche' and 'awkward' describe social clumsiness, so the sentence means the same.

m: using pompous, showy or extravagant language to impress others
x: My uncle gives grandiloquent speeches at every family wedding, quoting poets nobody has read.
The chief executive's grandiloquent memo promised a 'new dawn' but said nothing about salaries.
The professor warned us that grandiloquent prose often hides a lack of clear ideas.
Voters grew tired of the candidate's grandiloquent promises and wanted concrete plans instead.
His grandiloquent love letters made her laugh far more than they moved her.
tc: The novelist's early books were ______, stuffed with ornate phrases, but her later style became admirably plain.
'Stuffed with ornate phrases' and the contrast with 'admirably plain' show the blank means pompous in language.
se: The politician's ______ speech was full of lofty phrases but contained no real policy.
bombastic
Both 'grandiloquent' and 'bombastic' mean inflated and showy in language, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: innocent and honest; without any cunning or intention to deceive
x: The guileless child told the shopkeeper exactly how much money his mother had given him.
A guileless new intern believed the prank email announcing free lunches for a whole year.
Some readers find the novel's guileless narrator charming, while others find him hard to believe.
Fraudsters often target guileless pensioners who trust anyone claiming to call from their bank.
What drew her to him was his guileless honesty; he simply could not tell a lie.
tc: Unlike his scheming brothers, Joseph was ______, trusting everyone and never hiding his intentions.
The contrast with 'scheming brothers' and 'never hiding his intentions' shows the blank means free of deceit.
se: With her ______ smile and open manner, she seemed incapable of telling a lie.
innocent
Both 'guileless' and 'innocent' describe someone without deceit, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: a biography or account that praises its subject excessively and ignores their faults
x: My aunt's speech at Grandpa's birthday was pure hagiography; she forgot every one of his faults.
The company's official history reads like a hagiography of its founder.
Reviewers criticized the new biography as hagiography rather than serious scholarship.
State television aired a hagiography of the late general, ignoring the controversies of his rule.
When you are newly in love, describing your partner can easily turn into hagiography.
tc: Rather than offering a balanced portrait, the author wrote a ______, presenting the general as flawless.
'Rather than a balanced portrait' and 'presenting the general as flawless' show the blank means an idealizing biography.
se: The documentary is less a balanced account than a ______ of the company's founder.
glorification
Both 'hagiography' and 'glorification' mean an uncritical, flattering portrayal, so the meaning is the same.

m: overly theatrical or melodramatic in behaviour or emotion
x: My little brother gave a histrionic performance of agony whenever he was asked to wash the dishes.
Her histrionic outburst in the meeting over a slightly missed deadline surprised everyone.
Our writing tutor advised us to avoid histrionic language in the conclusions of our essays.
Commentators dismissed the senator's histrionic warnings as a bid for attention.
He was tired of her histrionic threats to leave every time they disagreed.
tc: Her ______ sobbing seemed out of proportion to the minor scratch on her car, and her friends rolled their eyes.
'Out of proportion to the minor scratch' shows the reaction was exaggerated and theatrical.
se: The player's ______ fall, clutching his leg as if he had been shot, fooled nobody, including the referee.
theatrical
Both 'histrionic' and 'theatrical' describe an exaggerated, staged reaction, so the meaning stays the same.

m: excessive pride or self-confidence that often leads to a downfall
x: It was pure hubris to think I could cook a five-course dinner without a recipe.
The project collapsed because of the director's hubris; he refused to listen to any warnings.
Greek tragedy often shows heroes destroyed by hubris and their defiance of the gods.

tc: Although the two partners had once been close friends, their bitter lawsuit left nothing but ______ between them.
'Although ... close friends' and 'bitter lawsuit' show the blank means lasting resentment.
se: The negotiations were conducted with surprisingly little ______, given how fiercely the two sides had fought.
acrimony
Both 'rancor' and 'acrimony' mean bitterness between people, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: an immoral or unprincipled person
x: My uncle was the family reprobate, always borrowing money he never intended to repay.
The new hire turned out to be a reprobate who padded his expense reports every month.
The novel's hero is a charming reprobate who gambles away his entire inheritance.
The judge described the defendant as a reprobate with no remorse for his crimes.
She knew he was a reprobate, yet she could not stop loving him.
tc: Though his family hoped prison would reform him, he remained an unrepentant ______, cheating and lying as before.
'Unrepentant' and 'cheating and lying as before' show the blank means an immoral person.
se: Everyone in the village warned her not to marry the ______ who had cheated half the town.
scoundrel
Both 'reprobate' and 'scoundrel' mean a dishonest, immoral person, so the meaning is the same.

m: restless and impatient, especially under delay or control
x: The passengers grew restive as the flight sat on the runway for a third hour.
Staff became restive when management postponed the pay review yet again.
By the end of the two-hour lecture, the students were noticeably restive.
The restive crowd outside parliament began chanting as the vote was delayed.
After years in the same job, he felt restive and longed for something new.
tc: After waiting nearly two hours for the delayed concert to begin, the audience became ______, stamping their feet and shouting at the stage.
The long delay and the stamping and shouting show the blank means restless and impatient.
se: The horses grew ______ as the storm approached, pawing the ground and tossing their heads.
restless
Both 'restive' and 'restless' mean unable to stay calm and still, so the sentence means the same.

m: referring to sex in a rude but humorous, irreverent way
x: My uncle's ribald jokes at the wedding made the older guests cough awkwardly.
The office party grew ribald after midnight, and the manager sensibly went home.
Students are often surprised by how ribald some of Chaucer's tales turn out to be.
The comedy show drew complaints for its ribald humour in a family time slot.
She blushed at the ribald teasing of her friends on the night before her wedding.
tc: The sailors' songs were far too ______ for the children's choir, full of crude jokes about love and drink.
'Far too ... for the children's choir' and 'crude jokes' show the blank means rudely humorous.
se: The comedian's ______ humour delighted the late-night crowd but would never be allowed on daytime television.
bawdy
Both 'ribald' and 'bawdy' describe coarse, sexual humour, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: making a show of being morally superior to other people
x: My brother-in-law gave me a sanctimonious lecture about sugar while finishing his third slice of cake.
Nobody in the office enjoyed the manager's sanctimonious emails about punctuality, since he himself rarely arrived before ten.
The professor warned us that a sanctimonious tone would weaken even the best-argued essay.
Critics dismissed the senator's sanctimonious speech on ethics, pointing out that his own campaign was under investigation.
She grew tired of her friend's sanctimonious remarks about how she chose to spend her money.
tc: Rather than offering genuine help, the neighbor delivered a ______ sermon about how he would never have let his own garden fall into such disrepair.
A smug 'sermon' about his own superior conduct, given instead of real help, points to a self-righteous attitude.
se: Voters tuned out the candidate's ______ speeches about family values and personal responsibility.
self-righteous
Both 'sanctimonious' and 'self-righteous' describe moralizing from a position of claimed superiority, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: making scandalous, abusive claims intended to damage someone's reputation
x: The tabloid printed scurrilous rumors about the actor's private life without a shred of evidence.
Someone circulated a scurrilous email about the new director, and HR is now trying to trace it.
Historians have shown that many scurrilous pamphlets of the eighteenth century were paid for by political rivals.
During the election, scurrilous posts about both candidates spread rapidly across Facebook groups in Dhaka.
He was deeply hurt when an old friend repeated scurrilous gossip about his divorce.
tc: The newspaper was forced to pay damages after a court ruled that its ______ article had falsely accused the mayor of taking bribes.
'Falsely accused' and 'pay damages' show the article was damaging and untrue, that is, defamatory.
se: The politician's lawyers threatened to sue over the ______ claims published on the anonymous blog.
defamatory
Both 'scurrilous' and 'defamatory' describe false, damaging claims about a person, which is why lawyers would threaten to sue.

m: showing steady, careful and persistent effort
x: Thanks to her sedulous attention to detail, the wedding went off without a single hitch.
The audit team was sedulous in checking every invoice, which took longer but uncovered several errors.
A sedulous researcher, he spent three years cataloguing every manuscript in the library's archive.
Scientists praised the sedulous monitoring of river levels that helped officials warn villages before the monsoon floods.
His sedulous care for his ailing mother impressed everyone who visited the family.
tc: Unlike his careless predecessor, the new editor was ______, checking every fact and rereading each page twice before publication.
The contrast with 'careless' and the description of checking every fact point to diligent, persistent effort.
se: The book's accuracy owes much to the author's ______ research in archives across three continents.
diligent
Both 'sedulous' and 'diligent' mean careful and hardworking, so the research is praised in the same way.

m: given to moralizing in a pompous, preachy way
x: My uncle's sententious advice at dinner usually begins with 'When I was your age.'
The speech was so sententious that half the employees stopped listening after the first few minutes.
Reviewers found the novel's ending sententious, as if the author were lecturing readers rather than telling a story.
Commentators mocked the minister's sententious remarks about thrift, given his famously lavish lifestyle.
She loved her grandfather dearly, but his sententious letters full of proverbs always made her smile.
tc: The film's message about kindness would have been more moving had the director not filled it with ______ speeches that lectured the audience at every turn.
'Lectured the audience at every turn' signals pompous, preachy moralizing.
se: The graduation speaker's ______ advice about hard work and humility bored the restless students.
preachy
Both 'sententious' and 'preachy' describe tiresome moral lecturing, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to satisfy a thirst, desire or craving
x: After the long hike, we stopped at a roadside stall to slake our thirst with green coconut water.
No amount of overtime pay could slake his ambition to run the company one day.
Students hoping to slake their curiosity about black holes packed the lecture hall.
The new reservoir was built to slake the growing city's demand for clean water.
Her letters, however frequent, never quite slaked his longing to see her again.
tc: After a whole day in the desert without water, the travelers rushed to the well to ______ their burning thirst.
The cause, a day without water, makes clear that they wanted to satisfy their thirst.
se: A cold glass of lemonade was all she needed to ______ her thirst on that sweltering afternoon.
quench
Both 'slake' and 'quench' mean to satisfy thirst, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: conceited and overconfident but immature and poorly informed
x: His sophomoric jokes about the bride's family made everyone at the wedding table cringe.
The consultant's sophomoric analysis ignored basic market data, so the board quickly rejected it.
My thesis supervisor said the first draft read like a sophomoric essay full of big words and little substance.
Critics called the party's economic manifesto sophomoric, arguing that it promised everything and explained nothing.
Looking back, she was embarrassed by the sophomoric love poems she had written at nineteen.
tc: Although the author clearly thinks his arguments are profound, they are in fact ______, relying on clichés and half-understood theories.
The contrast between thinking the arguments profound and their reliance on clichés signals immature pretension.
se: The comedian's ______ humor, built mostly on bathroom jokes, failed to impress the audience.
juvenile
Both 'sophomoric' and 'juvenile' describe childish, immature humor, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: false or fake though appearing genuine; based on faulty reasoning
x: The so-called antique turned out to be spurious, made in a factory only two years ago.
Several spurious expense claims were found during the annual audit, and the employee was dismissed.
Statisticians warn that two trends rising together can easily produce a spurious correlation.
Health officials debunked the spurious claim that drinking hot water cures the virus.
He kept offering spurious excuses for missing her birthday, but she knew he had simply forgotten.
tc: Although the document bore an official seal, experts soon showed it to be ______, a clever forgery produced decades later.
'A clever forgery' restates the blank: the document only looked genuine but was fake.
se: The court dismissed the lawsuit, noting that it rested on ______ evidence that had clearly been fabricated.
bogus
Both 'spurious' and 'bogus' mean fake, so the evidence is described the same way.

m: so excellent or beautiful that it inspires awe
x: We watched a sublime sunset over the Bay of Bengal from the beach at Cox's Bazar.
Our team's pitch was good, but the winning agency's presentation was simply sublime.
The lecture on Bach's cello suites helped us hear why critics so often call the music sublime.
Astronomers described the new images of the distant nebula as nothing short of sublime.
Holding her newborn daughter for the first time was the most sublime moment of her life.

'Not merely competent but' and listeners moved to tears show the blank means awe-inspiringly excellent.
se: Standing at the edge of the canyon at dawn, the hikers felt they were witnessing something truly ______.
magnificent
Both 'sublime' and 'magnificent' describe a sight of awe-inspiring beauty, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: behaving as though one is superior to others; disdainful
x: The waiter gave us a supercilious look when we asked for the cheapest wine on the menu.
Her supercilious manner in meetings made junior colleagues reluctant to share their ideas.
Some senior students were supercilious toward newcomers, treating their questions as beneath notice.
The ambassador's supercilious remarks about smaller nations at the summit drew sharp criticism.
He found her family supercilious at first, but they warmed to him after a few visits.
tc: Although she was kind to her friends, she was ______ toward strangers, treating them with a disdain that made her seem arrogant.
'Disdain' and 'arrogant' restate the blank, contrasted with her kindness to friends.
se: The salesman's ______ attitude toward customers who couldn't afford luxury cars cost the showroom many sales.
condescending
Both 'supercilious' and 'condescending' describe treating others as inferior, so the sentence means the same.

m: an excessive amount of something; more than is needed or wanted

Our office suffers from a surfeit of meetings and a shortage of actual decisions.
Students today face a surfeit of information but often lack the skills to evaluate it.
A surfeit of cheap oil on the world market has pushed prices to a three-year low.
She felt there was a surfeit of advice from relatives about her marriage and too little real support.
tc: Far from lacking candidates, the committee faced a ______ of applicants, more than five hundred for just two positions.
'Far from lacking' and 'more than five hundred for just two positions' indicate an excess.
se: The market already has a ______ of smartphone brands, so another newcomer is unlikely to succeed.
glut
Both 'surfeit' and 'glut' mean an oversupply, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: showy but cheap and of poor quality; also sordid or shabby
x: The hotel lobby was decorated with tawdry plastic chandeliers and fake gold paint.
The agency's tawdry advertising campaign damaged the brand more than it helped.
Our literature professor dismissed the bestseller as a tawdry romance with no believable characters.
Reporters uncovered the tawdry details of the bribery scandal that brought down the city council.
She was embarrassed by the tawdry necklace her cousin insisted she wear to the reception.

The definition after the colon, flimsy trinkets in loud colors, describes something showy but cheap.
se: Guests were unimpressed by the ______ decorations, which looked expensive from afar but cheap up close.
tacky
Both 'tawdry' and 'tacky' describe cheap, showy decoration, so the meaning is the same.

m: promoting a particular point of view, especially a controversial one; biased
x: My uncle forwards tendentious articles to the family WhatsApp group almost every morning.

Reviewers criticized the historian's tendentious reading of the sources, which ignored any evidence against his thesis.
The documentary was accused of offering a tendentious account of the war.
Their discussions about money grew tendentious, with each partner citing only the facts that supported their own side.

'Far from being an impartial study' and the selective use of data reveal a biased report.
se: The committee rejected the article as ______, saying it ignored every fact that contradicted its conclusion.
biased
Both 'tendentious' and 'biased' describe writing slanted toward one view, so the sentence means the same.

m: to promote or praise something insistently, often more than it deserves

The contrast with disappointing independent trials shows the company is insistently praising the drug.

trumpet
Both 'tout' and 'trumpet' mean to praise loudly and publicly, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

The chess club paired every tyro with an experienced mentor for the season.

novice
Both 'tyro' and 'novice' mean a beginner, so the sentence means the same either way.

dull
Both 'vapid' and 'dull' describe characters without interest or life, so the sentence means the same.

The contrast with 'once hailed as a hero' signals harsh public attack.

malign

falter
Both 'waver' and 'falter' mean to lose firmness of resolve, so the sentence means the same.

m: dislike or fear of people from other countries or cultures

nativism
Both 'xenophobia' and 'nativism' describe hostility to foreigners in favor of native-born people, so the meaning holds.

m: giving or expressing a warning or mild reproof

His mother gave him an admonitory look when he reached for a third sweet.

se: The coach's ______ words before the match reminded players of what happened the last time they grew complacent.
cautionary
Both 'admonitory' and 'cautionary' describe words meant as a warning, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to solemnly renounce a belief, cause, habit or claim

se: Before he could rejoin the party, he had to publicly ______ his earlier support for the extremists.
renounce
Both 'abjure' and 'renounce' mean to formally give up a position, so the sentence means the same.

The contrast between 'meant to last a century' and 'within months' shows the treaty is being abolished.
se: Critics fear the new emergency law will ______ citizens' right to a fair trial.
revoke
Both 'abrogate' and 'revoke' mean to formally cancel a right, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to accept or agree to something reluctantly but without protest

Rather than fight the restructuring, most managers quietly acquiesced and kept their objections to themselves.
The department acquiesced to the students' request for an extra week before exams.
Under international pressure, the government acquiesced in the release of the detained journalists.

se: Faced with the union's threat of a strike, the management had little choice but to ______.
yield

m: refusing to change one's mind; unyielding

The client is adamant that the logo must be green, despite our designer's objections.

Despite mounting evidence, the company remains adamant that its product is safe.
He was adamant that he would never forgive his brother, but they reconciled a year later.

Repeated pleading had no effect, which signals an unyielding stance.
se: The coach was ______ that no player would skip training, regardless of exams.
firm
Both 'adamant' and 'firm' express an unshakable position, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: clever or skillful in using the hands or the mind

An adroit negotiator, she secured a better deal without upsetting the client.
His adroit handling of tricky questions impressed the thesis committee.
The diplomat's adroit response defused what could have become an international incident.
Being adroit with words, he always knew how to cheer up his friends after a bad day.

The contrast with 'clumsy' and his ability to fix almost anything show the blank means skillful.

deft

m: friendly, good-natured and easy to talk to

The affable professor invited students to his office for tea and informal discussion.
Despite his affable public image, the actor was reportedly difficult to work with on set.
Her affable nature made it easy for her to make friends in a new city.

The contrast with 'cold and aloof' and 'chatting warmly' show the blank means friendly.
se: The hotel's ______ owner greeted every guest by name and recommended places to eat.
amiable
Both 'affable' and 'amiable' describe a warm, friendly person, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: open and responsive to suggestion; easily persuaded

se: The landlord seemed ______ to lowering the rent if we signed a two-year lease.
agreeable

m: something or someone that is intensely disliked or loathed

Lying was anathema to her, so she told him the truth even though it hurt.

A career spent fighting for press freedom shows she loathed censorship.
se: To the purist chef, frozen vegetables were an ______ that would never enter his kitchen.
abomination
Both 'anathema' and 'abomination' mean something detested, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: the direct opposite of someone or something

The contrast between a calm coach and one who screamed shows the blank means direct opposite.
se: Her careful, methodical approach is the ______ of her partner's impulsive style.
opposite
Both 'antithesis' and 'opposite' mean the exact reverse, so the sentence means the same.

m: apt; especially relevant and appropriate to the situation
x: She always finds an apposite quotation for every birthday card she writes.

The judge cited an apposite precedent from a similar case decided ten years earlier.
His apposite joke broke the tension at an otherwise awkward family meeting.
tc: Instead of rambling about unrelated topics, the speaker made a few ______ points that addressed the audience's concerns directly.
The contrast with 'unrelated topics' and points that 'addressed the audience's concerns directly' show the blank means relevant.
se: The editor praised the author for choosing an ______ title that captured the novel's theme perfectly.
apt
Both 'apposite' and 'apt' mean well suited to the situation, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: great enthusiasm, passion or eagerness

The young researcher's ardor for genetics showed on every page of her proposal.
Revolutionary ardor swept through the capital in the weeks before the election.
Over the years, their romantic ardor gave way to a deep and steady affection.
tc: Her initial ______ for the job faded quickly once she discovered the long hours and tedious paperwork.
Something that 'faded quickly' once drawbacks appeared must have been initial enthusiasm.
se: Not even a week of rain could dampen the volunteers' ______ for the clean-up campaign.
enthusiasm
Both 'ardor' and 'enthusiasm' mean eager energy, so the sentence means the same.

m: a position of dominant power or influence over others

The marketing team's growing ascendancy within the company has frustrated many engineers.
Economic historians trace the ascendancy of the British textile industry in the nineteenth century.
The party's ascendancy in parliament allowed it to pass laws with little opposition.
In their friendship, she always seemed to have the ascendancy, deciding where they went and what they did.
tc: After decades of decline, the city regained its ______, once again dominating the region's trade and politics.
'Once again dominating' restates the blank: a position of dominant power.
se: By the end of the decade, the newer technology had achieved clear ______ over its rivals.
dominance
Both 'ascendancy' and 'dominance' mean a controlling, superior position, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a damaging remark or attack on someone's character or reputation

Reviewers cast aspersions on the study's methods without offering any evidence.
The minister denied the aspersions against his department and promised a full inquiry.
Her aunt kept making aspersions about her fiancé's family, which upset everyone at the gathering.

se: The article contained a thinly veiled ______ on the senator's honesty.
slur
Both 'aspersion' and 'slur' mean a damaging remark about someone's character, so the sentence means the same.

m: a willingness to take bold risks; also, shameless or rude boldness
x: She had the audacity to ask for a raise on her very first day.
It took real audacity for the small startup to bid against the industry giants.
The student's audacity in questioning the professor's data turned out to be justified.
Investigators were stunned by the audacity of the thieves, who robbed the bank in broad daylight.
He admired her audacity in leaving a secure job to travel the world.
tc: Most beginners would never dare challenge the champion, but the young player had the ______ to propose a match on live television.
The contrast with beginners who 'would never dare' shows the blank means bold daring.
se: I can't believe he had the ______ to criticize my work when he hadn't even read it.
nerve
Both 'audacity' and 'nerve' mean shameless boldness in this phrase, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: extreme greed for wealth or material gain
x: My grandfather often warned us that avarice ruins families faster than poverty does.
The firm collapsed because of the avarice of executives who inflated profits to earn bonuses.
Many classic novels explore how avarice corrupts otherwise decent characters.
Environmentalists blamed corporate avarice for the destruction of the mangrove forest.
She eventually realized that his apparent generosity was only a mask for avarice.
tc: Driven by ______, the landlord raised the rent again and again, caring only about squeezing more money from his tenants.
'Caring only about squeezing more money' defines extreme greed.
se: The film portrays a banker whose ______ leads him to cheat even his closest friends.
greed
Both 'avarice' and 'greed' mean an excessive desire for money, so the sentence means the same.

m: extremely elaborate, ornate or complicated
x: The restaurant's menu was so baroque that I needed ten minutes just to understand the starters.
Our company's baroque approval process means even buying pens requires three signatures.
Editors asked him to simplify his baroque prose, which buried every idea under layers of adjectives.
Critics say the country's baroque tax code favors those who can afford expensive accountants.
Their wedding plans became increasingly baroque, with six outfit changes and three separate receptions.
tc: Readers who prefer simple, direct prose will find the novelist's ______ sentences, crowded with clauses and ornate imagery, exhausting.
The contrast with 'simple, direct prose' and 'crowded with clauses and ornate imagery' signal elaborate complexity.
se: The film's ______ plot, full of twists and subplots, left many viewers confused.
convoluted
Both 'baroque' and 'convoluted' describe an overly complicated plot, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: aggressive, hostile and eager to fight
x: After two cups of strong coffee, my usually calm uncle becomes almost bellicose about politics.
His bellicose tone in negotiations alienated potential partners who had come ready to compromise.
Historians examine how bellicose rhetoric in the press helped push the nation toward war.
The general's bellicose statements about reclaiming lost territory alarmed neighboring countries.
She had grown tired of her husband's bellicose reactions to every small disagreement.
tc: Instead of seeking peace, the dictator issued increasingly ______ threats, promising to invade if his demands were not met.
'Instead of seeking peace' and threats to invade show the blank means aggressive and warlike.
se: The fans grew ______ after the referee's controversial decision, and police had to separate the rival groups.
belligerent
Both 'bellicose' and 'belligerent' mean ready to fight, so the sentence means the same.

m: pompous, high-sounding language with little real meaning, used to impress
x: Strip away the bombast, and my brother's business plan is just selling tea online.
The CEO's speech was mostly bombast, full of promises but empty of figures.
Our professor warned that bombast is no substitute for a clear, well-supported argument.
Voters seem tired of political bombast and want practical solutions instead.
Her letters to him were sincere and simple, free of the bombast that filled his.
tc: Behind the senator's ______, with its grand phrases about destiny and greatness, lay a remarkably thin set of policies.
'Grand phrases' contrasted with 'a remarkably thin set of policies' point to pompous, empty language.
se: The critic dismissed the manifesto as pure ______, impressive in tone but empty of substance.
grandiloquence
Both 'bombast' and 'grandiloquence' mean inflated, pompous language, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: excessively complicated and detailed, often in a devious or secretive way
x: Getting a new passport can feel byzantine, with forms, queues and signatures at every step.
The company's byzantine reporting structure leaves nobody sure who their boss actually is.
The university's byzantine rules for transferring credits confuse even the academic advisers.
Journalists struggled to explain the byzantine financial arrangements behind the merger.
Their family politics were byzantine, full of old grudges and secret alliances among the cousins.
tc: The tax system was so ______ that even professional accountants struggled to follow its tangled rules and exceptions.
'Tangled rules and exceptions' that baffle even professionals show excessive complexity.
se: Applicants must navigate a ______ maze of regulations before they can open a small business.
labyrinthine
Both 'byzantine' and 'labyrinthine' describe something bewilderingly complex, so the sentence means the same.

m: the quality of being open, honest and frank
x: I appreciated my doctor's candor about the risks of the surgery.
Her candor in performance reviews made her unpopular with some but respected by most.
The professor admired the candor with which the student admitted the mistakes in her lab report.
The minister's unusual candor about the economic crisis surprised reporters.
Their friendship survived because of their candor, even when the truth was painful.
tc: Rather than giving evasive answers, the CEO spoke with surprising ______, admitting that the company had made serious mistakes.
The contrast with 'evasive answers' and the open admission of mistakes indicate frankness.
se: We were grateful for the inspector's ______ about the building's structural problems.
frankness
Both 'candor' and 'frankness' mean open honesty, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: accepted as authoritative or standard; conforming to established rules
x: For many in Kolkata and Dhaka, biryani with potatoes is the canonical version of the dish.
Our team follows the canonical approach to code review, with two approvals before any merge.
Students are expected to read the canonical texts of political philosophy before joining this seminar.
Physicists still regard this experiment as the canonical test of the theory.
In her family, the canonical story of how her parents met changed slightly every time it was told.
tc: Although many versions of the legend exist, scholars treat the oldest manuscript as the ______ one, against which all others are judged.
Being the version 'against which all others are judged' indicates the authoritative standard.
se: This textbook remains the ______ reference for students learning organic chemistry.
standard
Both 'canonical' and 'standard' mean the generally accepted authority, so the sentence means the same.

m: to surrender or give in, especially after a period of resistance
x: After an hour of pleading, I capitulated and bought my daughter the ice cream.
Management finally capitulated to the workers' demands after a ten-day strike.
Rather than capitulate to his critics, the scientist published more data supporting his theory.
The besieged city capitulated after its food supplies ran out.
She swore she would never capitulate in their argument over where to spend the holidays.
tc: Though the garrison had held out bravely for months, starvation forced it to ______ at last.
'Held out bravely' contrasted with being forced by starvation 'at last' shows surrender after resistance.
se: The government refused to ______ to the protesters' demands, despite weeks of demonstrations.
yield
Both 'capitulate to' and 'yield to' mean to give in to demands, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: intellectual rather than emotional or physical
x: My brother prefers cerebral board games like chess to anything involving running.
Her cerebral approach to management sometimes made her seem cold to her team.
The course is highly cerebral, focusing on abstract theory rather than practical skills.
Critics praised the film as a cerebral thriller that rewards close attention.
He loved their cerebral conversations, but sometimes wished she would just laugh at his jokes.
tc: Unlike his emotional, passionate rival, the chess champion was coolly ______, analyzing every position with detached logic.
The contrast with 'emotional, passionate' and 'detached logic' show the blank means intellectual.
se: The novel is more ______ than most romances, exploring philosophical questions rather than passionate love scenes.
intellectual
Both 'cerebral' and 'intellectual' mean appealing to the mind rather than the emotions, so the sentence means the same.

m: a person with excessive, prejudiced loyalty to their own country, group or sex
x: My aunt calls my uncle a chauvinist because he never lifts a finger in the kitchen.
The old manager was a chauvinist who assumed the women on the team would take the meeting notes.
The historian describes the nineteenth-century writer as a chauvinist who believed his nation superior to all others.
Commentators labeled the party leader a chauvinist after his dismissive remarks about foreign workers.
She broke off the engagement after realizing he was a chauvinist who expected her to quit her job.
tc: Convinced that his own country was superior to every other, the commentator was an unapologetic ______ who sneered at foreign cultures.
Believing his own country superior and sneering at other cultures defines a prejudiced patriot.
se: The general, a fierce ______, insisted that his nation had never lost a just war and never would.
jingoist
Both 'chauvinist' and 'jingoist' describe someone with aggressive, excessive national pride, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: making a loud, confused noise; loudly and insistently demanding
x: The clamorous fish market near our house wakes the whole neighborhood before dawn.
The conference call became so clamorous that nobody could hear what the client was saying.
The lecture hall grew clamorous as students argued about the surprise exam.
Clamorous demands for reform followed the release of the corruption report.
Her clamorous family reunions were exhausting but always full of love.
tc: The once quiet square became ______ as thousands of protesters arrived, shouting slogans and beating drums.
The contrast with 'once quiet' and the shouting, drumming crowd show the blank means loud.
se: A ______ crowd gathered outside the stadium, chanting and shouting for tickets.
raucous
Both 'clamorous' and 'raucous' describe a loud, disorderly crowd, so the sentence means the same.

m: to come together and form one whole
x: Over dinner, our vague holiday ideas began to coalesce into a real plan.
After months of debate, the team's opinions coalesced around a single design.
In the early universe, clouds of gas coalesced to form the first stars.
Several small opposition groups coalesced into a single party before the election.
Her scattered feelings for him slowly coalesced into something she recognized as love.
tc: Instead of remaining separate, the scattered droplets began to ______ into a single large pool on the table.
'Instead of remaining separate' and 'a single large pool' signal merging into one.
se: Diverse protest movements eventually began to ______ into one powerful coalition.
merge
Both 'coalesce' and 'merge' mean to come together as one, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: secret cooperation between people for a dishonest or illegal purpose
x: The two brothers acted in collusion to hide the broken vase from their mother.
Regulators fined the companies for collusion in fixing the price of cement.
The professor suspected collusion when two students submitted nearly identical answers.
An inquiry found evidence of collusion between police officers and smugglers at the border.
She felt betrayed when she discovered the collusion between her best friend and her ex.
tc: The two firms claimed to be fierce competitors, but their identical price rises suggested secret ______.
The contrast between claiming to be competitors and raising prices identically points to secret cooperation.
se: The officials were charged with ______ after it emerged they had secretly helped the contractor win the bid.
conspiracy
Both 'collusion' and 'conspiracy' mean secret cooperation for an illegal purpose, so the sentence means the same.

m: eager to please others or to accept their wishes without protest
x: My complaisant roommate agrees to whatever movie the rest of us choose.
The board was too complaisant, approving every proposal the CEO put forward.
A complaisant reviewer might have accepted the paper, but this one demanded new experiments.
Critics accused the media of being complaisant toward the government during the crisis.
She was so complaisant in the relationship that she rarely voiced her own wishes.
tc: Unlike her outspoken sister, Nadia was ______, always going along with whatever others wanted rather than voicing objections.
The contrast with 'outspoken' and her habit of going along with others signal eagerness to please.
se: The ______ landlord agreed to every request his tenants made, no matter how unreasonable.
obliging
Both 'complaisant' and 'obliging' describe someone eager to accommodate others, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a feeling of guilt or moral hesitation about doing something wrong
x: He ate the last piece of cake without the slightest compunction.
The manager showed no compunction about taking credit for his team's work.
Some students feel no compunction about copying answers from the internet.
The smugglers had no compunction about endangering the lives of the migrants they carried.
She felt a twinge of compunction after snapping at her mother on the phone.
tc: A ruthless operator, the trader felt no ______ about deceiving his clients and slept soundly no matter whom he had ruined.
'Ruthless' and sleeping soundly after ruining people show he felt no guilt.
se: The thief seemed to feel no ______ as he took money from the charity box.
remorse
Both 'compunction' and 'remorse' mean a feeling of guilt, so the sentence means the same.

m: a large, destructive fire; also, a large-scale conflict
x: A tiny kitchen fire in the old building turned into a conflagration within minutes.
After the warehouse conflagration, the company introduced strict fire-safety drills for all staff.
Students studied how the Great Fire of London, a famous conflagration, reshaped city planning.
Diplomats feared the border skirmish could spark a wider regional conflagration.
Their small quarrel grew into a family conflagration that lasted for years.
tc: What began as a single spark in the dry grass soon became a ______ that destroyed hundreds of homes.
The contrast between 'a single spark' and a fire that destroyed hundreds of homes indicates a huge blaze.
se: Firefighters battled the ______ for three days before it was finally brought under control.
inferno
Both 'conflagration' and 'inferno' mean a huge, raging fire, so the meaning is unchanged.
